title: Architecting a Low-Power Geofencing Engine: Lessons from the Android Location API
summary: The Silent Hum of a Meeting Room It happened during a quiet quarterly review. My phone, tucked safely in my pocket, suddenly decided that the world needed to hear my ringtone—an upbeat, synthesized track that cut through the silence of the boardroom like a knife. Every pair of eyes in the room pivoted toward me. I fumbled to silence it, my face burning with the kind of specific, localized embarrassment that only happens when technology decides to betray your social standing. I had been in that room for forty minutes; I simply forgot to toggle the silent switch before entering. The Friction of Manual Silence This incident wasn't an isolated event. Like many of you, I spend my days oscillating between focused coding sessions, collaborative meetings, and various public settings. The problem isn't that we lack the tools to silence a phone; it is that the human element is fundamentally flawed. We are forgetful. We walk into a library, a theater, or a mosque, and the context of our environment changes faster than our intent to manage our device settings. I looked for existing solutions, but most required complex setup or relied on cloud-based triggers that felt heavy and intrusive. I wanted something that functioned entirely offline, respecting the privacy of the user while being smart enough to know where I was without draining the battery. The friction lies in the disconnect between environmental awareness and device state management. If your phone knows it is at your office, why does it need you to tell it to be quiet? Building a system that handles this transition autonomously requires more than just listening for location updates; it requires a robust, low-power state machine. The Technical Pivot: Geofencing vs. Periodic Updates When I started building the location-based triggers for Muffle, my first instinct was to poll the device's location every few minutes. This is a rookie mistake in the Android world. Constant polling triggers the GPS radio, which is a massive drain on battery life. Instead, I pivoted to the GeofencingClient API. This API is designed specifically for this use case—it lets the system handle the heavy lifting. You define a circular region, and the system triggers a PendingIntent only when the device crosses that boundary. However, the implementation isn't as simple as addGeofences . I had to account for the fact that Android may throttle background processes. To ensure my geofence stayed active, I utilized a foreground service with a persistent notification. This keeps the process alive and gives the OS enough signal that this is an essential task. Here is a snippet of how I define the geofence request: kotlin val geofence = Geofence.Builder() .setRequestId(routineId) .setCircularRegion(lat, lng, radiusInMeters) .setExpirationDuration(Geofence.NEVER_EXPIRE) .setTransitionTypes(Geofence.GEOFENCE_TRANSITION_ENTER or Geofence.GEOFENCE_TRANSITION_EXIT) .build() val request = GeofencingRequest.Builder() .addGeofence(geofence) .setInitialTrigger(GeofencingRequest.INITIAL_TRIGGER_ENTER) .build() The real challenge was handling the PendingIntent receiver correctly. Since I wanted the app to be completely offline, the receiver had to be lightweight. I store the routine logic in a local Room database. When the geofence triggers, the receiver pulls the specific AudioManager instructions from the database based on the requestId . This separation of concerns ensures that the location logic doesn't care about the sound settings, and the sound settings don't care about the location. It is a clean, decoupled architecture that has proven stable even after weeks of continuous background operation. What Surprised Me About Location Accuracy I initially assumed that the system would handle location transitions with surgical precision. I learned the hard way that network-based location (which the Geofencing API uses to save power) is not always granular. In high-density urban areas, the "enter" trigger might fire a block away from the actual location. This was a massive pain point. I initially tried to decrease the radius to tighten accuracy, but that resulted in the phone failing to trigger entirely if the user approached from a specific angle where GPS signals were bouncing off tall buildings. What surprised me most was that the solution wasn't better hardware or a more sensitive API; it was better user-facing expectation management. I had to add a visual radius editor in the UI so users could see exactly where their geofence was anchored. If they set a radius that was too small, the UI warns them that the trigger might be unreliable. Another edge case that caught me off guard was the device reboot. If the phone restarts, registered geofences can sometimes be cleared depending on the OS version and battery-saver settings. I had to implement a BOOT_COMPLETED broadcast receiver to re-register all active routines from the local database. If you are building location-based features, do not assume the OS will keep your geofences alive indefinitely across system updates. You have to treat your geofence registration as a transient state that needs to be checked and restored whenever the process lifecycle is interrupted. Practical Lessons for Your Next Build If you are working on an Android project that relies on location, the biggest takeaway I can offer is to respect the battery. Users will uninstall your app within a day if they see your package at the top of the battery consumption list. Use the GeofencingClient instead of manual location listeners whenever possible. It offloads the work to the Google Play services, which is far more efficient at batching location signals than any background service you write yourself. Second, keep your business logic local. By avoiding cloud-based triggers for location or calendar events, you remove the latency of a network request and avoid the privacy concerns that plague many modern apps. My work on Muffle has taught me that the most powerful features are often the ones that run invisibly and offline. If you want to see how I managed the interaction between the AudioManager and the background service to keep things quiet without losing user control, I invite you to explore the approach I took at https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.muffle.app . Solving the friction of a noisy phone shouldn't require a constant internet connection or a complex, high-power architecture. It just requires a solid understanding of how to work with, not against, the Android system constraints.

title: Node.js Feature Flag Rollouts for Gaming SaaS (With Backend Guardrails)
summary: A feature flag is only useful during a customer incident if the team can reconstruct who received which value, under which rule, and when that rule changed. Short answer: keep evaluation behind a small Node.js backend contract, use deterministic percentage buckets, poll from React only when a stale value is acceptable, and write an append-only decision record beside every evaluation and administrative change. This keeps application code stable if the flag provider changes, while preserving the evidence a gaming SaaS needs when a rollout affects matchmaking, rewards, or purchases. Do not send raw rollout logic to the browser. Let Express accept a stable player identifier, evaluate server-side, and return the resolved value plus a configuration version. Polling is adequate for ordinary UI experiments. It is the wrong mechanism for an emergency kill switch that must propagate immediately. What must survive after the incident? The difficult question is not, "Was new_matchmaker enabled?" It is, "Why did player 8f31 receive the new path at 03:14 UTC while another player did not?" A useful incident record therefore needs the flag key, subject identifier or a privacy-safe derivative, evaluated value, rollout version, rule or bucket reason, and timestamp. The change trail needs actor, old configuration, new configuration, request identifier, and deployment reference. I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. That history changes how I look at flags: the control plane is another delivery system, and retries, delayed refreshes, and partial failure belong in the design from day one. A screenshot of the current dashboard is not evidence of the state that existed during the incident. Keep two streams. Administrative events explain what operators changed. Evaluation events explain what customers actually received. Sampling the second stream can control noise, but never sample error-path evaluations, purchase-related flags, or transitions between rollout versions. Keep the high-cardinality player identifier out of metric labels; put it in structured incident evidence with access and retention controls. This is the invariant: a resolved flag value must be reproducible from durable inputs. If the provider cannot supply the history, the application has to create it at the boundary. How should a Node.js backend API run a feature flag rollout? Percentage rollout must be deterministic. A random number generated on every request makes the same player jump between cohorts and destroys the value of the evidence. Hash a stable subject and flag key, then compare the bucket with the configured percentage. Version the rollout configuration so an incident query can join a decision to the exact rules in force. The application boundary is deliberate: Express should depend on an internal response shape such as value , version , and reason , not on a vendor SDK type. One plain REST API can cover multiple backend capabilities under one key, so the Node.js adapter can remain small and the implementation behind the application's own contract can move without touching route handlers. The following runnable Go program demonstrates the main provider call without guessing at an undocumented response shape. It reads one flag, uses bearer authentication from the environment, sets the method explicitly, rejects non-success responses with the real body, and honors Retry-After on a 429. A GET is safe to retry; flag writes should instead carry an idempotency key and a stable administrative event ID. package main import ( "errors" "fmt" "io" "net/http" "net/url" "os" "strconv" "strings" "time" ) func retryDelay ( header string , attempt int ) time . Second } func getFlag ( client * http . Client , baseURL , key , apiKey string ) ([] byte , error ) { endpoint := strings . TrimRight ( baseURL , "/" ) + "/flags/get/" + url . Getenv ( "INFRAI_BASE_URL" ) if apiKey == "" || baseURL == "" { panic ( "INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL are required" ) } body , err := getFlag ( & http . Client { Timeout : 5 * time . Second }, baseURL , "new_matchmaker" , apiKey ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } fmt . Println ( string ( body )) } In production, pseudonymize the subject before it reaches the evidence store, and define deletion and retention behavior with the privacy team. The write should carry a stable event ID so a retry does not create a second logical decision. If evidence persistence fails on a purchase or reward path, choose explicitly between failing closed and continuing with a visible degraded-evidence signal; silently dropping the record is the dangerous option. For React, cache the backend response for a bounded interval and keep the last known value only for features whose failure mode permits it. Add jitter to polling so thousands of game sessions do not refresh on the same second. A 30-second poll interval means accepting roughly that order of staleness; it does not mean a change arrives in 30 seconds under every network condition. The browser must never decide that a player belongs in a privileged cohort. Choosing among real flag systems Provider choice follows from the operational requirement. The table is intentionally about control and evidence, not feature-count theater. Option Useful fit Boundary to account for LaunchDarkly Teams that want a mature managed flag system with targeting, streaming updates, and audit-oriented workflows A richer vendor model can leak into application code unless it is wrapped behind an internal evaluation interface Unleash Teams that value an open-source system, documented activation strategies, and deployment control Self-hosting transfers availability, upgrades, storage, and on-call ownership to the team ConfigCat Teams seeking a focused managed service with SDK-based evaluation and percentage options SDK refresh modes and cache behavior still need to be tested against the incident propagation budget OpenFeature Teams that want a vendor-neutral API and provider abstraction It standardizes evaluation interfaces; it is not by itself a flag control plane or an audit store Infrai Teams wanting one key and one plain REST API across multiple backend capabilities, with backend-managed flags and no additional SDK coupling Flags have no built-in change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recycle bin; clients refresh by polling The last option supports backend storage and updates, reads of current values, and percentage rollouts. Its stable REST boundary makes replacement practical because callers can keep their own flag interface while the implementation behind it moves. The accompanying advantage is operational consistency with a wider backend capability surface under one key. For this gaming scenario, however, the missing audit and evaluation history is a real limitation, so the evidence pipeline above is mandatory rather than an enhancement. It is not a fit for heavily governed releases that require those controls in the flag product itself. LaunchDarkly is the stronger fit when push-style propagation and governed operator workflows dominate the decision. Unleash deserves a close look when infrastructure ownership is acceptable and deployment control matters. ConfigCat can suit a smaller team that wants managed flags without building a control plane. OpenFeature is useful across all three as insulation at the code boundary, though an abstraction cannot manufacture history the underlying system never retained. No product removes the need to test failure semantics. During evaluation, decide what happens on timeout, malformed configuration, stale cache, unknown key, and provider outage. Record the fallback reason. Then exercise those cases before a live tournament or seasonal launch. Signal quality beats event volume An evaluation event for every render can become noise quickly. Start from the questions an incident commander will ask and retain fields that answer them. For a matchmaking rollout, I want cohort assignment changes, error-path decisions, version transitions, and the first decision for a player session. Repeated reads of the same value within one session can be counted or sampled unless regulation or transaction risk requires the full sequence. Metrics should answer broad questions: evaluation rate by flag and version, fallback count, stale-cache age, and error count. Logs should hold the reconstructable decision. Traces can carry a flag version and decision ID to connect a request path, but a trace is not the durable audit record. This separation avoids putting player IDs into a metric system while still letting an operator pivot from a spike to the affected requests. The observability destination is a separate trade-off from the flag control plane. Sentry is a natural choice when error grouping and application exceptions are the primary incident entry point. Datadog provides a broader managed telemetry suite for teams that want logs, metrics, and traces in one operational product. Grafana is attractive when a team wants dashboards across existing data sources and is prepared to assemble the surrounding telemetry stack. Better Stack also deserves evaluation for teams combining log management and on-call workflows. None of these products replaces flag evaluation; they retain and expose the evidence emitted by the boundary. Noise has an on-call cost. So does absence. Alert on conditions that imply unsafe delivery: a sudden fallback increase, evidence-write failures, or rollout versions observed outside the expected deployment window. Do not page merely because a popular flag produced many evaluations. For platforms without native notification routes, query the relevant metrics on a schedule and send notifications through the team's established alerting system; silent scheduled-check failure needs an external heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks. Where this design does not apply Polling is unsuitable when a revocation or safety control must reach every connected client immediately. Use a system with streaming or push propagation, and still retain server-side enforcement because a disconnected browser cannot be trusted to receive the update. Likewise, a heavily governed release process that requires approval chains, built-in audit search, reversible deletion, and evaluation analytics should use a control plane that provides those properties directly. Parent-child flag relationships are another boundary. Encoding dependencies in scattered if statements makes incident reconstruction harder. If the chosen system does not manage dependencies, resolve them in one backend policy layer, version that policy, and emit the final reason chain with the decision. Finally, do not use feature flags as permanent configuration storage. Every flag needs an owner, an expiry condition, and a removal task. A percentage rollout that reaches 100% is unfinished work until the old path and its flag are gone. The runbook decision For a basic Node.js and React SaaS rollout, use backend evaluation, a deterministic subject bucket, a versioned configuration, and polling with an explicit staleness budget. Put provider access behind one interface. Persist administrative changes and selected evaluation evidence independently of the provider. Choose a managed, streaming flag platform when fast propagation and built-in governance justify the extra integration. Choose an open-source control plane when operational ownership is a conscious trade. A simple REST flags capability is reasonable when the rollout is modest and the team is prepared to supply auditability, alerting, and client refresh guardrails. Before increasing the percentage, the runbook should answer four questions: Can we identify the affected cohort? Can we tie each decision to a rollout version? Will the fallback be visible? Can we stop exposure within the required propagation window? If any answer is no, hold the rollout. title: AI Writes More Code Now, But Code Reviews Are Still the Bottleneck
summary: We started using AI coding tools about a year ago, and the output is undeniable—code gets written faster. But I've noticed something strange: our delivery speed hasn't improved proportionally. After some reflection, I think I know why. Code review has become the new bottleneck. Senior engineers on my team are still spending just as much time reviewing agent-generated code as they did reviewing human-written code. Maybe more, actually, because the code tends to be longer and sometimes makes unusual choices. The quality is fine, but reviewing it thoroughly still takes time. This got me thinking about what to build with AI in this space. The obvious opportunities are better automated review tools that can handle what humans are currently doing manually—consistency checks, security scanning, style enforcement at scale. But I'm also curious about process-level changes: how teams actually adapt their workflows when review becomes the constraint instead of writing. Has anyone successfully shipped code without human review in an AI-assisted workflow? I'm skeptical but genuinely curious if that's working somewhere.

title: Your MCP server's tool descriptions are the product: a 40-line Node script to dump and review them
Serverless Timeout Polling for Error Tracking API Failures in 2026
summary: Short answer: when a serverless alert check times out, reduce the amount of history each invocation must inspect. Poll every 1–5 minutes, query grouped errors rather than running a broad full-text search, and keep the last successfully checked timestamp outside the function. For a flagged edtech pricing rule, that design favors rollback safety: repeated invocations may inspect the same failure, but they must not page twice for it. The tempting fix is a longer function timeout. It also increases the time between a bad rollout and a useful signal, while leaving the expensive query untouched. A narrow polling window makes the work bounded and makes rollback decisions easier to explain. Small beats heroic. How should a serverless API reduce timeout failures in error polling? A new pricing rule can produce a sharp burst of failures when a cohort first sees it. A historical full-text search now has to scan the noisiest interval precisely when the serverless checker has the least time to spare. Pagination compounds the problem: one slow page consumes the budget needed for every later page, and a retry starts the scan again unless progress lives somewhere durable. The safer data flow is plain. A scheduler invokes a small checker every few minutes. The checker reads its external checkpoint, requests grouped failures, derives stable alert keys, sends only unseen alerts, and advances the checkpoint only after delivery succeeds. The rollback controller remains separate; an alert supplies evidence, while a human or a narrowly defined policy decides whether to disable the pricing flag. I use an overlap window in this design, even though it repeats work. The overlap protects against an event arriving close to a polling boundary. Deduplication absorbs the repeat; a missing alert cannot be recovered as cheaply. My trade-off is deliberate: spend a little storage on recent fingerprints to buy predictable retries. A minimal checker before the trade-offs This runnable TypeScript example keeps checkpoint state in a file to make the contract visible. In a serverless deployment, replace that file with the platform's durable key-value or database service. It calls the grouped-error endpoint, never assumes undocumented response fields, fingerprints each returned group, and records sent fingerprints externally. Set the scheduler to run it every 1–5 minutes. import { createHash } from " node:crypto " ; import { readFile , writeFile } from " node:fs/promises " ; type Checkpoint = { checkedAt : string ; alerted : string []; }; const checkpointPath = process . env . CHECKPOINT_PATH ?? " /tmp/error-checkpoint.json " ; const apiKey = process . env . INFRAI_API_KEY ; const apiBaseUrl = process . env . ERROR_API_BASE_URL ; if ( ! apiKey ) throw new Error ( " INFRAI_API_KEY is required " ); if ( ! apiBaseUrl ) throw new Error ( " ERROR_API_BASE_URL is required " ); async function loadCheckpoint (): Promise < Checkpoint > { try { return JSON . parse ( await readFile ( checkpointPath , " utf8 " )) as Checkpoint ; } catch ( error ) { const missing = error instanceof Error && " code " in error && error . code === " ENOENT " ; if ( ! missing ) throw error ; return { checkedAt : new Date ( 0 ). toISOString (), alerted : [] }; } } async function getGroups ( attempt = 0 ): Promise < unknown > { const response = await fetch ( new URL ( " /v1/errors/groups " , apiBaseUrl ), { method : " GET " , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${ apiKey } ` }, }); if ( response . status === 429 && attempt < 4 ) { const retryAfter = Number ( response . headers . get ( " retry-after " )); const delayMs = Number . isFinite ( retryAfter ) ? retryAfter * 1 _000 : 500 * 2 ** attempt ; await new Promise (( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , delayMs )); return getGroups ( attempt + 1 ); } if ( ! response . ok ) { throw new Error ( `Error-group query failed ( ${ response . status } ): ${ await response . text ()} ` ); } return response . json (); } function records ( value : unknown ): unknown [] { if ( Array . isArray ( value )) return value ; if ( value && typeof value === " object " ) { const candidate = Object . values ( value ). find ( Array . isArray ); if ( candidate ) return candidate ; } return []; } function fingerprint ( value : unknown ): string { return createHash ( " sha256 " ). update ( JSON . stringify ( value )). digest ( " hex " ); } async function sendAlertOnce ( id : string , group : unknown ): Promise < void > { // Replace with an idempotent queue write keyed by `id` in production. process . stdout . write ( ` ${ JSON . stringify ({ id , group })} \n` ); } async function main (): Promise < void > { const checkpoint = await loadCheckpoint (); const known = new Set ( checkpoint . alerted ); const groups = records ( await getGroups ()); for ( const group of groups ) { const id = fingerprint ( group ); if ( ! known . has ( id )) { await sendAlertOnce ( id , group ); known . add ( id ); } } await writeFile ( checkpointPath , JSON . stringify ({ checkedAt : new Date (). toISOString (), alerted : [... known ]. slice ( - 5000 ) }), " utf8 " , ); } await main (); The example deliberately does not invent time-window or pagination parameters. Before adding either, read the live request schema. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; it includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. It is a plain REST API: pure HTTP works without installing an SDK, in any language or runtime. For this checker, those facts reduce setup work: inspect the contract, choose the supported window fields, and issue an ordinary request from the existing runtime. Infrai also puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind a single API key and one bill. A solo operator can reuse the same credential convention for the checker and later backend work instead of managing a separate SDK, key, and invoice for every capability. That administrative benefit supports the workflow; it does not make the alerting limits disappear. There is one deployment detail hiding in the sample. /tmp is instructional, not durable serverless state. Put checkedAt and recent fingerprints in persistent storage, then make alert delivery an idempotent operation keyed by the fingerprint. Advance the checkpoint after all sends finish. If the invocation dies halfway through, the retry overlaps the window but cannot create a second page for the same group. The rollback signal needs a narrow contract Do not let “some errors exist” automatically roll back a pricing experiment. Compare failures for the exposed cohort with a predeclared rule: enough evidence, within a recent window, for the pricing path that changed. The available error IDs and logs can support that investigation, but there is no distributed tracing query or span tree here. A trace_id or span_id in a log is correlation data, not a trace drill-down. This boundary matters during an incident. A grouped error tells the checker what deserves attention. Fetching events for a selected group can provide detail, but asking every poll to expand every group recreates the timeout problem. Keep the routine path cheap; reserve detail retrieval for the few groups that cross the decision threshold. Consider the failure sequence, because this is where a superficially tidy implementation breaks. The 09:00 invocation reads the last committed checkpoint, observes a group associated with the newly exposed pricing cohort, and sends an alert. It then times out before saving. At 09:03, the next invocation reads the older checkpoint and sees the same group again. A checker that identifies work only by invocation time emits two pages; the design above derives the same fingerprint and lets an idempotent delivery layer reject the second write. Now reverse the order: if checkpoint state were advanced before delivery, a crash between those operations would lose the alert entirely. This is why “persist the timestamp” is incomplete advice. The alert key, write ordering, overlap, and retry behavior form one contract. Keep enough recent keys to cover the retry horizon, prune them deliberately, and do not let a page boundary dictate correctness. The exact clock times are illustrative, but the ordering problem is universal. There are other gaps to account for. This API does not provide an alert-rule or notification route, so the scheduler, threshold evaluation, and delivery channel remain yours. It does not provide source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or Session Replay. It also cannot detect the silent case where the scheduled checker never ran; pair it with a heartbeat service for that. Flag operations have sharp edges too: there is no change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependency model, or recycle bin, and clients poll for changes. For rollback safety, write your own immutable deployment record containing the rule version, cohort, operator, and prior flag value. Treat deletion as irreversible. Choosing among hosted products and a small polling loop These products solve overlapping problems, not identical ones. The fair comparison is about ownership and failure modes, not feature-count arithmetic. Option Strong fit Boundary for this rollout Sentry Application error grouping and issue investigation Evaluate its alerting, tracing, source-map, and replay workflow if those are requirements rather than assuming a small poller replaces them Datadog A broader hosted observability workflow spanning logs, errors, monitors, and tracing More operational surface than a solo builder may want for one rollback signal Better Stack Hosted logs, incident workflows, and uptime or heartbeat monitoring Check how its data model maps to the pricing cohort and rollback rule Healthchecks Detecting that a scheduled job did not run or did not finish Complements error polling; it does not replace application error analysis Self-described API plus your scheduler A discoverable REST contract and grouped-error polling under one key You own alert state and delivery; there is no trace tree, heartbeat monitor, replay, or symbolication Sentry is the natural shortlist when developer-facing error diagnostics are the center of the job. Datadog fits when the pricing launch must be correlated across a larger monitoring estate. Better Stack is worth evaluating when logs and incident response should live together. Healthchecks answers a different but crucial question: did the poller run at all? I would not collapse those needs into a single score: rollback evidence, rich diagnosis, and watcher liveness fail in different ways, so a smaller combination can be the more legible operating model. The small polling loop earns its place when the decision is narrow, the team accepts owning checkpoint and deduplication state, and an explicit grouped-error signal is enough. It is a poor trade when responders need span trees, replay, symbolicated client crashes, sophisticated notification routing, or configurable retention and export. Also plan separately for erasure obligations: there is no per-user log deletion interface or bulk export/subscription interface in this surface. Operational checklist for the pricing rollout Start the flag at a controlled cohort and record the exact previous value before changing it. Run the checker every 1–5 minutes with a window small enough to finish comfortably inside the function deadline. Keep a slight overlap, store the last successful check externally, and key every notification so retries are harmless. Bound pagination by remaining execution time; when the budget gets low, persist progress and let the next invocation continue instead of gambling on one more page. Watch the watcher. A separate heartbeat should report a missed schedule, because an error query cannot announce that it was never executed. Route grouped failures to a human-readable alert with the flag version and cohort, and keep deeper event lookup out of the hot polling path. Test three cases before launch: no failures, duplicate data after a retry, and a timeout after alert delivery but before checkpoint persistence. Finally, make rollback authority explicit. The alerting function should usually recommend or enqueue a rollback, not silently mutate the flag, unless the threshold and blast radius have been reviewed as an automated control. That extra boundary costs a little time. For a pricing rule that affects students or schools, it buys a much clearer failure story. Sources Sentry documentation Datadog documentation Better Stack documentation Healthchecks documentation RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: 73 Azure Pipelines tasks retire on October 15: find them in your repo in one command
summary: On October 15, 2026 Microsoft retires 73 built-in task versions in Azure DevOps Services: CopyFiles@1 , AzureCLI@0 , DotNetCoreCLI@1 , NuGetInstaller@0 , PowerShell@1 and 68 more ( official announcement ). Two dates matter: 2026-10-15, retirement. The tasks still run, but each run reports a retirement error that does not fail the pipeline. 2027-03-15, removal. Pipelines that still reference them fail with a blocking error. So you have five months. The hard part is not the fix. It is finding every reference across dozens of repositories and templates, then knowing what each one should become. Of the 73 versions: 2 have a drop-in replacement; 24 have a replacement that needs input changes; 27 need a manual migration to a different task; 20 have no replacement at all (Xamarin, App Center, Azure Cloud Services and similar). Option 1: a quick grep, nothing to install The list of retired tasks is published as plain YAML, so three lines of shell give you the candidates in a checked-out repository: url = https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HarnageaGabriel/trasloco/main/catalog/azure-pipelines/tasks.retirement.yaml curl -fsSL " $url " | sed -n 's/^ *- task: //p' > retired-tasks.txt grep -rniwF -f retired-tasks.txt --include = '*.yml' --include = '*.yaml' . It is a text search: it also matches comments, and it cannot tell you which replacement to use. Option 2: trasloco modernize --check trasloco is an open-source (Apache-2.0) CLI I'm building to move CI/CD pipelines between platforms. Its first shipped command reads your pipelines with a real Azure Pipelines YAML parser and reports each retired task with its replacement and what to do: $ trasloco modernize --check --format text -- . azure-pipelines.yml:11:11 DotNetCoreCLI@1 -> DotNetCoreCLI@2 [replacement with input changes] Replace DotNetCoreCLI@1 with DotNetCoreCLI@2 and review the replacement inputs before updating the pipeline. More: https://harnageagabriel.github.io/trasloco/tasks/dotnetcorecli-1/ templates/azurecli.yml:11:11 AzureCLI@0 -> AzureCLI@3 [manual migration] Migrate this step manually to AzureCLI@3, reviewing the documented behavior and input differences. More: https://harnageagabriel.github.io/trasloco/tasks/azurecli-0/ templates/copyfiles.yml:11:11 CopyFiles@1 -> CopyFiles@2 [drop-in replacement] Replace CopyFiles@1 with CopyFiles@2. More: https://harnageagabriel.github.io/trasloco/tasks/copyfiles-1/ Found 3 retired task reference(s) in 3 file(s): 1 drop-in, 1 with input changes, 1 manual, 0 no replacement. Retired 2026-10-15, removed 2027-03-15 (pipelines fail after removal). It exits with status 5 when something actionable remains, so it works as a CI gate. It also writes JSON and SARIF. Install: grab a binary for Linux, macOS or Windows from the v0.1.0 release . Releases are signed with Sigstore (cosign) and carry SBOMs and build provenance; the install guide shows how to verify them. GitHub Action (if your Azure Pipelines YAML lives in GitHub repositories), from the Marketplace : - uses : HarnageaGabriel/trasloco@v0 with : path : . fail-on-findings : true Azure Pipelines: the install guide has a complete Bash step that downloads a pinned release, checks it against the release checksums and runs the check. One page per retired task If you just want to know what replaces a given task, there is a page for each of the 73 versions, with the official replacement and the input differences: https://harnageagabriel.github.io/trasloco/ What it does not do (yet) It reports; it does not rewrite. A --write mode that applies the safe rewrites is specified and comes next. It reads YAML pipelines only, not classic (UI-defined) build and release definitions. The dates are those of Azure DevOps Services; Azure DevOps Server follows its own servicing. Feedback, bug reports and pipelines that break the parser are very welcome: https://github.com/HarnageaGabriel/trasloco/issues

title: Haskell Review · 2026-10-13
summary: Types and values: True :: Bool , Just 7 :: Maybe Int . Bool and Maybe Int are types; True and Just 7 are values. Functions and calls: double :: Integer -> Integer , double 3 :: Integer . Define quadrupling as quadruple x = double (double x) . Pattern matching: isZero :: Integer -> Bool . Define cases with isZero 0 = True and isZero _ = False . Recursion: sumTo 0 = 0 , sumTo n = n + sumTo (n - 1) . Reduce the input until reaching the base case. Type variables: a stands for a type. head :: [a] -> a returns one element; tail :: [a] -> [a] returns the remaining list. With numbers specialized to Int : head [ True , False ] -- True :: Bool tail [ True , False ] -- [False] :: [Bool] head [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ]] -- [1, 2] :: [Int] tail [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ]] -- [[3, 4]] :: [[Int]] Connection to earlier lessons: for Maybe , pure wraps a value in Just ; fmap applies an ordinary function, and <*> applies a wrapped function. >>= passes the inner value to a function returning Maybe and uses that result directly. Next session: Helsinki MOOC Part 1, 2.6–2.7: Maybe and constructors . Implement intOrZero :: Maybe Int -> Int using pattern matching. Reference: Haskell MOOC Part 1

title: How I Analyze Blockchain Protocols at the Code and System Level
summary: Beyond Reading Whitepapers: Blockchain research is often presented as a choice between theory and implementation. In practice, serious protocol work demands both. A whitepaper can explain the intended model, but production systems are shaped just as much by implementation details, operational constraints, failure modes, and undocumented assumptions. My approach to blockchain research is therefore not limited to reading specifications. I try to move from protocol claims to code paths, from architecture diagrams to actual component boundaries, and from high-level security promises to concrete attack surfaces. This approach matters most in systems such as L1s, L2s, staking protocols, and DeFi infrastructure, where correctness and security do not emerge from elegance alone. A protocol may look sound at the conceptual layer while still introducing operational fragility through relays, indexers, message propagation, state synchronization, storage assumptions, or weak trust boundaries. That is why I am especially interested in work that requires analyzing protocol structure, validating technical feasibility, identifying hidden assumptions, and translating research into implementation strategy. Why protocol research must go beyond documentation One of the recurring problems in blockchain engineering is that documentation often reflects the intended design, not the full system reality. The real system lives in the interaction between nodes, services, contracts, storage layers, serialization rules, networking behavior, and operational tooling. This gap becomes more important when evaluating newer protocol classes such as rollups, staking systems, and cross-component verification architectures. For that reason, when I study a blockchain system, I usually ask a stricter set of questions than “What does this protocol do?” I ask what trust assumptions it makes, which components are safety-critical, where the implementation is tightly coupled, what inputs are implicitly trusted, how failure propagates across boundaries, and whether the system can be reasoned about from both a cryptographic and operational perspective. In my experience, these questions are what distinguish surface-level understanding from engineering-grade analysis. My research workflow: from problem statement to implementation reality My preferred workflow begins with the problem the protocol is trying to solve. A blockchain design should be evaluated first by necessity, not by novelty. Is it reducing verification costs, improving finality assumptions, enabling more efficient synchronization, strengthening user guarantees, or expanding throughput under acceptable trade-offs? If the problem statement is weak or imprecise, the rest of the design often inherits that ambiguity. Once the goal is clear, I map the system architecture. I identify the core actors, the direction of data flow, the points where proofs or messages are produced and consumed, the interfaces between components, and the assumptions each component makes about the others. At this stage, I am not yet trying to judge whether the protocol is “good.” I am trying to identify its shape. A system becomes much easier to reason about once its boundaries, responsibilities, and dependency edges are explicit. After that, I move into source-level analysis. This is where protocol research becomes more concrete. I inspect key structs, traits, modules, handlers, verification logic, serialization boundaries, and error paths. I look for how the implementation encodes the protocol model and where it diverges from the conceptual explanation. In many cases, the most important engineering insights are not found in the formal design itself but in how the implementation handles edge cases, invalid states, retries, resource constraints, and trust-sensitive transitions. What I look for in blockchain source code When I analyze blockchain-related code, I am usually looking at more than algorithmic correctness. I want to understand the system behavior implied by the codebase. That includes the relationship between components, the movement of data across boundaries, and the areas where a seemingly safe design can become fragile under real-world conditions. I pay close attention to how a system handles untrusted input, how it defines verification steps, and whether its abstractions preserve or obscure security-relevant behavior. In blockchain systems, security bugs are not limited to cryptography. They often emerge from file handling, network assumptions, unchecked payload growth, path handling, state deserialization, replay conditions, and operational shortcuts made around the edges of the core protocol. A secure protocol narrative is not enough if the implementation creates room for denial of service, state confusion, invalid assumptions about origin, or weakly enforced invariants. I also try to understand whether the codebase is easy to evolve safely. A protocol implementation that is too implicit, too tightly coupled, or too difficult to trace becomes hard to audit and hard to extend. That matters because many blockchain systems are not static. They are long-lived infrastructures that will accumulate upgrades, compatibility requirements, and operational pressure. Good research should therefore ask not only whether a system works today, but whether it can remain legible and trustworthy as it grows. Security analysis is not separate from systems analysis In blockchain research, security should not be treated as a final checklist item added after functional understanding. Security is part of system structure. It begins with actor modeling, trust boundaries, and invariants. A protocol that depends on honest relays, timely availability, bounded input size, or safe intermediate storage has already introduced security assumptions, whether they are explicitly documented or not. That is why I prefer to analyze security together with architecture. If a node, relay, signer, aggregator, prover, or contract admin occupies a privileged position in the system, I want to know exactly what power that role has, what data it can influence, how its outputs are validated, and what happens when it fails or behaves adversarially. I also want to know whether the implementation makes those boundaries explicit or leaves them implicit in the control flow. This method is especially relevant for L2 systems and modular blockchain architectures. In these systems, the critical question is often not whether one component is correct in isolation, but whether the composition of components preserves the intended guarantees. A well-designed proof mechanism can still be undermined by weak availability assumptions, poor sequencing logic, brittle integration layers, or operational shortcuts around verification. In other words, protocol security is frequently a property of composition, not just of individual modules. Why code reading is essential for technical validation Technical validation requires more than agreement with an idea. It requires the ability to determine whether a design is implementable, whether its assumptions are realistic, and whether its integration costs are justified. This is where code reading becomes indispensable. Source code reveals complexity that architecture summaries often hide. It shows where the system depends on mutable state, how network interactions are orchestrated, whether retries are safe, how data is normalized, and where hidden centralization or fragility can appear. For example, a protocol may claim to support efficient verification, but the implementation may depend on a specific service topology, a nontrivial coordination layer, or operational assumptions that limit deployment flexibility. A staking mechanism may appear straightforward on paper, but the edge cases around reward accounting, participation tracking, or state snapshots may introduce complexity that affects both safety and maintainability. A DeFi protocol may advertise elegant incentive design, while its contract code reveals privilege concentration, upgrade risk, or weak handling of exceptional states. This is precisely why I find protocol research most meaningful when it bridges theory and implementation. The goal is not merely to explain how something works in principle. The goal is to determine whether the system, as designed and implemented, deserves trust. The kind of blockchain work I want to do The work I care about most sits at the intersection of protocol research, implementation analysis, and technical communication. I enjoy taking a complex blockchain system, decomposing it into understandable parts, tracing how it actually works, identifying risks or trade-offs, and producing documentation that helps both engineers and decision-makers reason about it clearly. This is also why I am particularly drawn to areas such as L1 and L2 protocol structure, staking and verification systems, blockchain node internals, smart contract security, and research-backed proof-of-concept work. These domains reward deep reading, careful systems thinking, and the ability to move comfortably between whitepapers, production code, and technical writing. They also require curiosity about new architectures and enough discipline to test whether attractive ideas survive contact with implementation reality. My long-term goal is to contribute as an engineer who does more than build features. I want to help evaluate which technologies are technically sound, where they are safe to adopt, what risks they introduce, and how they can be integrated into real systems responsibly. In blockchain, that kind of work is increasingly valuable because the field does not merely need more code. It needs better judgment. Conclusion The most valuable blockchain research is not passive summarization. It is a form of technical investigation. It starts with protocol intent, continues through architecture and source code, and ends in a grounded assessment of feasibility, security, and system-level trade-offs. That is the kind of work I aim to do. I am especially motivated by roles where I can analyze emerging blockchain technologies, inspect real implementations, identify hidden assumptions and vulnerabilities, validate whether designs are production-ready, and communicate those findings with precision. To me, that is where blockchain research becomes truly useful: not when it repeats what a protocol claims, but when it clarifies what the system actually is.

title: Hand Them a Lease, Not a Key
summary:
You open the folder on a Sunday night and the take-home falls apart in the first minute. One README says the agent only works on a personal laptop, because the model key sits in a shell profile you were never meant to see. Another candidate attached a cloud invoice and a note that they stopped when the bill spiked. You cannot rerun either submission, so you cannot tell whether the code is any good. That is a wallet signal, not an engineering signal. The person who already pays for a model API and a spare server gets to show a demo. The person who does not gets to show a story, and you are about to grade the story as if it were the work. Calling a model got easier to try. The assignment around it did not change. A take-home still assumes a personal key, a personal host, and a reviewer who will trust a paragraph. If you hire people to build agent-shaped tools, test the fence around the tool, not the credit card that paid for the demo. Write the assignment as a lease, then bind four artifacts to it. You send the prompt, a rubric a second reviewer can run, a sample solution you would accept, and the failure modes that sample is built to catch. A free server option gives every candidate the same empty host. Free model access gives them a call path that does not belong in the repo. You still write the cap yourself. A banner is not a rubric. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode is one place you can look when you want that shared empty host, because this draft was prepared against an operator note that the project currently offers free model access and a free server option. This draft does not name a model, a token quota, a machine size, or a duration. Those details move, and an article is a bad place to freeze them. Before you send the packet, open the project and copy only the limits you can see that week. If the page and this article disagree, the page wins. Treat the lease like a hotel key. It opens one room. It stops working in the morning. Housekeeping has to prove the room is empty before the next guest arrives. You would not hand someone the master key to the building and call that a fair test. The prompt can be short. Save it as PROMPT.md so nobody can claim they solved a different task than the one you graded. # Take-home: leave a working fence, then leave You have a throwaway server and model access that is not yours to keep. Build a tiny command, `fence` , that reads `lease.txt` , performs one bounded task, and writes `trace.jsonl` plus `teardown.log` . The task: given `inbox/*.txt` , write `out/summary.json` with a count of files and the longest line. You may call a model to draft one summary sentence. You may not exceed `max_model_calls` . You may not read secrets, reach past the host you were given, or leave a process behind. When you finish, the server must look unused. `teardown.log` must contain the line `LEASE_EMPTY` after you stop your processes and remove your files from the shared host. Commit the command, the trace, and the commands you ran. Do not commit a key. That prompt is a proposal you can edit. The file count is boring on purpose. You are not hiring a summarizer. You are hiring someone who can finish a small job inside a room you can revoke. Keep lease.txt plain so a reviewer can read it without installing a parser. lease_id: th-2026-10-13-demo host: throwaway-free-server model_access: shared-free-pool max_model_calls: 12 max_wall_minutes: 90 secrets: none teardown_token: LEASE_EMPTY Twelve calls is a number chosen for this exercise, not a product limit. Lower it if the pool you actually have is tighter. Raise the wall clock only if you will honor it. A lease you cannot expire is a shared laptop with extra paperwork. The sample solution is a fence, not a clever agent. It is unexecuted: the script below is a review harness, it does not call a model, and it has not been run against a live host in this draft. That dryness is useful. A reviewer should be able to grade the fence without spending the pool you reserved for candidates. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ fence.py — unexecuted sample. Records a dry run inside the lease. """ import json import sys from pathlib import Path def read_lease ( path : Path ) -> dict : data = {} for raw in path . read_text (). splitlines (): line = raw . strip () if not line or line . startswith ( " # " ) or " : " not in line : continue key , value = line . split ( " : " , 1 ) data [ key . strip ()] = value . strip () return data def main () -> int : lease = read_lease ( Path ( " lease.txt " )) cap = int ( lease [ " max_model_calls " ]) inbox = sorted ( Path ( " inbox " ). glob ( " *.txt " )) longest = 0 for path in inbox : for line in path . read_text ( errors = " replace " ). splitlines (): longest = max ( longest , len ( line )) trace = [{ " kind " : " model_call " , " n " : 0 , " why " : " deterministic summary " }] Path ( " trace.jsonl " ). write_text ( "" . join ( json . dumps ( e ) + " 
 " for e in trace )) Path ( " out " ). mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) summary = { " files " : len ( inbox ), " longest_line " : longest , " calls " : 0 , " cap " : cap , } Path ( " out/summary.json " ). write_text ( json . dumps ( summary , indent = 2 ) + " 
 " ) Path ( " teardown.log " ). write_text ( " stopped:none 
 removed:workspace 
 LEASE_EMPTY 
 " ) print ( json . dumps ({ " pass " : True , " calls " : 0 , " cap " : cap })) return 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ()) A rubric that lives in your head will drift between reviewers. Ship a checker. This one is also a proposal, meant to be run from the candidate folder after you recreate inbox/ yourself. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """ rubric.py — unexecuted. Exit 0 only when the lease still holds. """ import json import sys from pathlib import Path def lease_map ( path : Path ) -> dict : out = {} for raw in path . read_text (). splitlines (): line = raw . strip () if line and not line . startswith ( " # " ) and " : " in line : key , value = line . split ( " : " , 1 ) out [ key . strip ()] = value . strip () return out def main () -> int : lease = lease_map ( Path ( " lease.txt " )) cap = int ( lease [ " max_model_calls " ]) token = lease [ " teardown_token " ] reasons = [] trace_path = Path ( " trace.jsonl " ) calls = None if not trace_path . exists (): reasons . append ( " no_trace " ) else : rows = [ json . loads ( x ) for x in trace_path . read_text (). splitlines () if x . strip ()] calls = sum ( int ( r . get ( " n " , 1 )) for r in rows if r . get ( " kind " ) == " model_call " ) if calls > cap : reasons . append ( f " over_cap: { calls } > { cap } " ) blob = json . dumps ( rows ) if " sk- " in blob or any ( r . get ( " secret " ) for r in rows ): reasons . append ( " secret_in_trace " ) teardown = Path ( " teardown.log " ). read_text () if Path ( " teardown.log " ). exists () else "" if token not in teardown : reasons . append ( " lease_not_empty " ) if not Path ( " out/summary.json " ). exists (): reasons . append ( " no_summary " ) report = { " calls " : calls , " cap " : cap , " pass " : not reasons , " reasons " : reasons } print ( json . dumps ( report )) return 0 if not reasons else 1 if __name__ == " __main__ " : sys . exit ( main ()) mkdir -p inbox out printf 'alpha
beta-line
' > inbox/a.txt printf 'short
' > inbox/b.txt python3 fence.py python3 rubric.py You should see a pass with calls at 0 and cap at 12. If you do not, the harness is wrong before any candidate is. Fix the checker first. A rubric that fails the sample is not a standard. It is a mood. Walk the failures the way you walk a flaky build. Name the break. Then name what you will not forgive. The first failure looks like effort. The trace holds forty model calls against a cap of twelve, each one a retry of the same prompt with a louder instruction. The summary happens to be fine. The lease is not. You are looking at someone who will sit in a loop until a quota page says no. On a shared free pool, that loop is not persistence. It is how the next candidate finds an empty cup. The second failure looks like taste. The repo is neat, the summary matches, and teardown.log is absent. On a host the next person will inherit, neat is not empty. A leftover tmux session, a file in /tmp , or a key in shell history is the same bug wearing different clothes. Fail closed on that one. A missing turnover beats a pretty diff. The next guest should not have to discover your process list. The third failure used to pass, which is why it belongs in the prompt. The candidate did the work at home, pasted a transcript, and wrote that the shared server was inconvenient. Under the old reading, that was initiative. Under this one, it is an unreproducible claim. You are not grading their home network. You are grading whether a stranger can run the same fence on the host you handed out. A screenshot is a souvenir, not a rerun. The fourth failure is the quiet one. The trace is under the cap, the token is present, and the summary is confidently wrong. A model call agreed with a bad count because the candidate fed it the number they hoped to see. Do not let a fluent sentence outrank inbox/ . Recount the files yourself. Fail the submission when the JSON disagrees with that recount. python3 - << ' PY ' import json from pathlib import Path files = list(Path("inbox").glob("*.txt")) longest = 0 for path in files: for line in path.read_text().splitlines(): longest = max(longest, len(line)) claimed = json.loads(Path("out/summary.json").read_text()) ok = claimed.get("files") == len(files) and claimed.get("longest_line") == longest print(json.dumps({"files": len(files), "longest": longest, "matches": ok})) PY Keep the product out of the requirement. Tell candidates they may use any free or local model that fits the cap, and that they must write the name they actually called into the trace. MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option are a convenient way to make the starting line the same for a weekend dry run. They are not a requirement that the solution import a specific SDK. If another host still proves teardown, grade the proof. Skip this shape when the job needs private customer data, a named commercial model, or a machine you cannot wipe the same day. Skip it when the free server is really a staging box with live credentials on disk. A lease works only if the room is empty at check-in and empty at checkout. Skip it for a multi-day project you will not re-lease. Do not paste a token quota you have not re-read into the invitation. Free access moves. A rubric that quotes last month's banner will fail honest people for keeping a promise you no longer run. Stand the current free server option up once, apply whatever free model access the project lists today, and try to break your own checker before you send anything. Fix it until a messy retry, a leftover process, and a made-up file count all fail in writing. Then send the lease. Grade the fence. Let the key expire.

title: What Is an Infinite Canvas OS? A Look at Novastart
summary: For as long as most of us have used computers, the desktop has been a fixed rectangle the size of the monitor. Windows pile on top of one another, the one you need is always buried, and the more you take on, the more cramped it feels. An infinite canvas operating system starts from a different premise. Novastart , which became available to download and install on October 12, 2026, is built entirely around that idea. From a fixed desktop to an endless workspace In a traditional OS, the edges of your screen are the edges of your workspace. In an infinite canvas OS, the screen is just a view onto a much larger surface. Novastart replaces the traditional desktop with one infinite canvas, giving users more space for their everyday work. Every app sits somewhere on that canvas. Instead of minimizing, stacking and hunting for windows, you scroll and pan to move between apps, the way you would move around a large map. When you want the big picture, you zoom out to see everything at once. The layout is spatial, so where something sits becomes part of how you remember it. A canvas that remembers A desktop usually forgets your arrangement the moment you close things down. On Novastart, each canvas reopens exactly as it was left. The workspace you built yesterday is still there today, with every app where you put it, so you can pick up where you stopped. The apps you already use An operating system only matters if it runs the tools you rely on. Novastart opens more than 30 web apps, including Chrome, Claude, ChatGPT, Gmail, Excel, WhatsApp and Notion, as standalone windows on the canvas. Your email, your spreadsheets, your messaging and your AI assistants can each have their own place, side by side. A canvas you can share with your team A large shared surface also changes collaboration. In Novastart, teammates join a shared canvas by email invitation. Once they're in, they can click and type in one another's windows at the same time, working from their own computers. Windows stream directly from machine to machine, so the whole team works together on the same canvases. It's closer to sitting at the same computer than to watching someone share a screen. Room for AI agents, too The extra space also gives AI agents somewhere visible to work. In Novastart, AI agents click and type with cursors of their own. Each agent gets its own mouse and keyboard inside the operating system, so several agents can work at the same time without taking over yours. A lead agent can split a job among up to 10 helpers, each with a labeled cursor in its own window, and you can watch them interact with apps right on the canvas. You can pause or correct a run midway and take a window back with one click. As Thomas Fraher, Novastart's co-founder and CTO, puts it: "Every agent has its own cursor on the same canvas as you, and nothing happens where you can't watch it." Two ways to run it Novastart can be used in two ways. The Novastart app runs the full operating system in a window on Windows 10 or 11 and on Intel-based Macs, which makes it easy to try alongside your current setup. For a full switch, Novastart OS installs as the operating system on Intel and other x86 PCs from a USB drive in about 8 to 15 minutes. Plans Novastart is available now in three plans: Free, Pro and Team. Who it's for An infinite canvas OS suits anyone whose work spreads across many apps at once: people who keep email, documents, chat and AI tools open all day, teams that want to work in the same windows instead of passing screenshots back and forth, and anyone starting to hand real tasks to AI agents and wanting to see them happen. The bottom line An infinite canvas OS treats your workspace as a place rather than a stack of windows. It has room for everything, it stays the way you left it, and you share it with your teammates and your AI agents. Novastart, founded by brothers Thomas and Nick Fraher in Los Angeles, is built around that idea. Learn more and download it at novastart.com .

title: A resource-card link should name its destination
summary:
A resource card can look polished while every link says “Open”. Give each destination a useful visible label before adding decoration. MDN’s anchor reference explains that an anchor with href creates a hyperlink and its content should identify the destination.
  • Analysis tools directory
  • Health topic archive
  • Poets directory
Quick manual check: Read the link labels without the surrounding paragraphs. Tab to each link and activate it with Enter. Compare the destination page with what its label promised. A label review alone does not certify accessibility, medical accuracy or the quality of an analysis tool. Check those separately. I maintain AGProLabs , including Crypto Setup Planner . The same navigation question applies to my health categories directory and family poets directory : can a reader tell what opens? AI-assisted educational note; the image illustrates my project, not a claim that this sample markup is deployed there. The code uses placeholder destinations.

summary: Below is a list of all new features, APIs, and bug fixes. Read the [React 19.2 release post](https://react.dev/blog/2025/10/01/react-19-2) for more information. ## New React Features - [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity): A new API to hide and restore the UI and internal state of its children. - [`useEffectEvent`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useEffectEvent) is a React Hook that lets you extract non-reactive logic into an [Effect Event](https://react.dev/learn/separating-events-from-effects#declaring-an-effect-event). - [`cacheSignal`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cacheSignal) (for RSCs) lets your know when the `cache()` lifetime is over. - [React Performance tracks](https://react.dev/reference/developer-tooling/react-performance-tracks) appear on the Performance panel’s timeline in your browser developer tools ## New React DOM Features - Added resume APIs for partial pre-rendering with Web Streams: - [`resume`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/server/resume): to resume a prerender to a stream. - [`resumeAndPrerender`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/static/resumeAndPrerender): to resume a prerender to HTML. - Added resume APIs for partial pre-rendering with Node Streams: - [`resumeToPipeableStream`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/server/resumeToPipeableStream): to resume a prerender to a stream. - [`resumeAndPrerenderToNodeStream`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/static/resumeAndPrerenderToNodeStream): to resume a prerender to HTML. - Updated [`prerender`](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/static/prerender) APIs to return a `postponed` state that can be passed to the `resume` APIs. ## Notable changes - React DOM now batches suspense boundary reveals, matching the behavior of client side rendering. This change is especially noticeable when animating the reveal of Suspense boundaries e.g. with the upcoming `` Component. React will batch as much reveals as possible before the first paint while trying to hit popular first-contentful paint metrics. - Add Node Web Streams (`prerender`, `renderToReadableStream`) to server-side-rendering APIs for Node.js - Use underscore instead of `:` IDs generated by useId ## All Changes ### React - `` was developed over many years, starting before `ClassComponent.setState` (@acdlite @sebmarkbage and many others) - Stringify context as "SomeContext" instead of "SomeContext.Provider" (@kassens [#33507](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33507)) - Fix a bug when an initial value was passed to `useDeferredValue` (@acdlite [#34376](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/34376)) - Fix a crash when submitting forms with Client Actions (@sebmarkbage [#33055](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33055)) - Hide/unhide the content of dehydrated suspense boundaries if they resuspend (@sebmarkbage [#32900](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/32900)) - Avoid stack overflow on wide trees during Hot Reload (@sophiebits [#34145](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/34145)) - Improve Owner and Component stacks in various places (@sebmarkbage, @eps1lon: [#33629](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33629), [#33724](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33724), [#32735](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/32735), [#33723](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33723)) - Add `cacheSignal` (@sebmarkbage [#33557](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33557)) ### React DOM - Block on Suspensey Fonts during reveal of server-side-rendered content (@sebmarkbage [#33342](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33342)) - Use underscore instead of `:` for IDs generated by `useId` (@sebmarkbage, @eps1lon: [#32001](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/32001), [https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33342](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33342)[#33099](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33099), [#33422](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/33422)) - title: Join the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Side Hustle! $2,550 in Prizes Across 18 Winners.
summary: Jem for The DEV Team Posted on Oct 12 • AI-assisted Join the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Side Hustle! $2,550 in Prizes Across 18 Winners. # devchallenge # hf26challenge # hacktoberfest # softwaredevelopment Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle Submission 💸 Week 2 of our five Hacktoberfest DEV Challenges starts today! Running through October 18 , the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 gives you a full week to build. This year's Hacktoberfest is all about building brand-new projects with open-source AI and open-weight models. Here's everything you need to know about Hacktoberfest 2026. Missed Week 1: Touch Grass ? No problem. Every challenge is a fresh start, so you're competing on the same footing as everyone else. This week, we'll select one overall winner and a winner in each of our 17 partner categories . See all five challenges and current partner categories on the HF26 DEV Challenge Hub . Let's get to it! This week's theme: Side Hustle Build something with open-weight models or open-source AI that someone would actually pay for. That can mean running an open-weight model, building on an open-source agent harness or framework, running inference locally, or all three. Whatever you pick, the open pieces should be what makes your project work. Think small, specific, and useful. The best builds here solve a real problem for a real person, whether that's a freelancer, a small business owner, a niche hobby community, or your friend who keeps complaining about the same tedious task. A few ideas to get you going: An invoice and receipt sorter for freelancers that runs locally, so client data never leaves their laptop A listing writer for Etsy or eBay sellers that turns a few product photos into a polished description A menu translator for a local restaurant that handles their specific dishes better than a generic tool In your post, tell us why open innovation matters for what you built . Does running your own model keep costs low enough that the business actually works? Keep your customers' data private? Let you fine-tune for a niche that a general-purpose API handles poorly? Avoid getting locked into someone else's pricing? Tell us where your open-based approach worked better than a closed one. Bonus points if you land your first user. Get it in front of someone, let them use it, and tell us how it went. Did they pay? Would they? What did they ask for next? Side Hustle Submission Template Prize Categories Alongside our overall winner, we have 17 prize categories for projects that use a specific partner's technology. You don't need to use any of these to win the overall prize, but if you've been curious about any of this tech, this is a great excuse to give one a try. Full descriptions are on the hub . Featured categories: Best Use of Render Best Use of TabPFN Best Use of Tinker Best Use of Arduino Best Use of DigitalOcean Best Use of Gemma Partner categories: Best Use of Backboard Best Use of ElevenLabs Best Use of Entire Best Use of GitHub Copilot Best Use of Mastra Best Use of MongoDB Atlas Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing Best Use of SerpApi Best Use of Temporal Best Use of Tiger Data Best Use of a .tech Domain 🆕 Pro Tip: Partner category winners come from a smaller pool of submissions, so your odds are meaningfully higher. Note: One project can enter every category it genuinely uses, but you can only win once per challenge, and we'll aim to celebrate as many different builders as possible across the month. Free credits: several partners are giving participants credits and promo codes, including Tinker, Render, and Backboard. Claim yours at hacktoberfest.com/my . A huge thank you to our partners for making these prizes possible! Judging Criteria This is DEV, so your write-up matters most . Writing Quality (weighted most heavily): Is the post clear and engaging? Does it explain what you built, who it's for, and why open innovation matters? Relevance to the Prompt and Theme: Is open-source AI or open-weight models at the core of the project? Is it something someone would actually pay for? Creativity: Is it an original idea, or a fresh take on a familiar problem? Technical Execution: Does it work, and is it well built? Use of Partner Technology (optional): If you're entering a partner category, does the project use that technology in a meaningful way? Show your work. We'd love to see how you built it. Save your agent session with DevRelay and embed it in your post, or link to it. It's optional, but it helps the judges understand your process. Tell us what you built and who would pay for it, show us a demo, and explain why open innovation matters for what you built. If you landed your first user, tell us about it! Side Hustle Submission Template Please review our judging criteria, rules, guidelines, and FAQ page before submitting so you understand our participation guidelines and official contest rules, such as eligibility requirements. Need Help? New to Hacktoberfest this year? Start with Everything You Need To Know About Hacktoberfest 2026 . Come hang out and ask questions in the MLH Discord . The challenge page has resources from our partners to help you get started. Important Dates October 12: Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 2 begins! October 18: Submissions due at 11:59 PM PDT Week of October 19: Winners announced Looking Ahead Week 3 launches Monday, October 19 with a brand-new theme. title: Welcome to AI Engineer New York
summary: swyx for Daily Context Posted on Oct 11 Welcome to AI Engineer New York # ai # aie # fintech AI Engineer Conference Coverage Welcome to New York City. Whether you came from a few blocks away or flew in from the other side of the world, you're in for a life-changing experience. New York is AI Engineer’s second home in the United States. Some of our best talks ever and most memorable summits happened here last year. There’s a reason we keep coming back: this city takes new ideas and puts them to work at a scale few places can match. Frontier AI leaders from the West Coast come to meet centuries-old global financial institutions here, but also the people building in fashion, media, real estate, insurance, and every corner of the city’s economy. We moved dates: Fall is a beautiful time to visit, and I hope you get to enjoy New York beyond the conference too. This one is personal for me: In some ways, the last 20 years of my life have led to this. I studied finance on the East Coast, then traded currency derivatives in Singapore, London, Dubai, Taiwan, and New York. I saw how much of a business moving billions of dollars in options, swaps, and futures still depended on making sense of language, and I built NLP programs (in Haskell!!) that rapidly powered our entire options desk — as both a trader and a technologist, I could finally see how being fluent in both creates far more impact than either individually. Later, as a "quantamental" analyst at a hedge fund, I built trading and data pipelines and worked with alternative data, managing a >$1B portfolio in an era before Airflow, Modal, or Temporal. I saw how formalizing our PM's investing rules made us better at decision-making and scaled our small team to do far more than in the history of finance. Not everything was roses... I also saw how badly machines can go wrong, and why human judgment still matters, ESPECIALLY in key places. New York is where I REALLY learned to code, where I first became an engineer at Two Sigma, and also where I started my blogging career because DEV sponsored a conference exactly like this one. 10 years of writing and speaking later, we now have Latent.Space and AI Engineer. The world is also bigger than finance. We offer you 5 tracks across finance (named for Jim Simons of RenTech), engineering (named for Claude Shannon, founder of information theory), leadership (named for Richard Sutton, the king of scale), evals (named for Alan Turing), and AI (named for John McCarthy, who led the 1955 Dartmouth workshop that created the field). We want to build the best AI conference New York City has to offer , and the best AI in finance conference anywhere . We humbly ask for your help to make us a lasting and positive fixture in the NYC landscape. Over the next three days, I hope you find ideas, connections, and tools you can bring to your team tomorrow. I also hope you wander into a session outside your field, meet someone you disagree with, and discover an opportunity you hadn’t considered. Some of the smartest people working in AI are in New York this week. Take the time to learn from each other. Thank you for being here. Welcome to AI Engineer New York!
