title: Local embeddings with llamadart: how llamas share secrets
summary: Jhin Lee for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 12 • AI-assisted Local embeddings with llamadart: how llamas share secrets # dart # ai # flutter # tutorial Beyond chat with llamadart (2 Part Series) 1 DecisionEngine: Teaching local AI to play Tetris 2 Local embeddings with llamadart: how llamas share secrets Beyond chat with llamadart · Part 2 Llama Village, where five llamas share a world without sharing everything they know. Pip’s red scarf is missing. Mo knows where it is. He also knows how it got there—and would rather keep that part to himself. That gives the village a small mystery. It gives the game a harder question: when two llamas talk, what should the listener actually learn? I introduced the game in Llama Village: a virtual world powered by local AI with llamadart . Here, we will follow one part of its machinery: local embeddings help compare what a llama said with facts that might have been shared. The destination is a change you can inspect: a llama acquires information, the game records who told them, and they may still doubt it. Dialogue, embeddings, and game rules each have a different job. A secret starts with one llama The game stores the scarf’s location and Mo’s accident as separate facts. At the start, Mo knows both. Knowing where the scarf is does not automatically mean knowing who knocked it into the pond. Before checking a conversation, the game narrows the possibilities: facts the speaker knows and the listener does not. It compares each fact with that speaker’s lines, not every line from both characters. An embedding model has learned text representations from training data. It maps each line and fact to a numeric vector; cosine similarity compares those vectors. Similar wording and related meaning can bring vectors closer, but the score is not a yes/no test for identical meaning, truth, or whether a statement implies a fact. The game uses each fact’s highest similarity across the speaker’s lines. AI-generated overview: compare meaning, check evidence, then record who said it. A conceptual illustration, not a captured game trace. The implementation uses EmbeddingGemma through llamadart and caches vectors by text. It applies title: none | text: to both lines and facts. This walkthrough reproduces that game choice. Google’s model card recommends task-specific prefixes for new applications, including a sentence-similarity query prompt; changing the format requires reevaluating the scores and thresholds. The words do not have to match June and Bramble talking about poems in a recorded playthrough. This shows the dialogue system, not the scarf exchange illustrated below. For a small walkthrough, compare the stored fact “Pip’s red scarf is lying in the pond reeds” with the illustrative line “I saw Pip’s scarf tangled in the reeds by the pond.” They describe related information using different words. The line is written for this explanation, not quoted from the recording. The input is text. The embedding output is a numeric vector. The application then calculates a similarity score; the model does not return “June learned the scarf’s location.” That decision comes later. Keep the same embedding model and compatible settings for both texts. Equal vector lengths alone do not guarantee compatible representations. Follow the text through llamadart With a suitable embedding engine loaded, the core calls look like this. The full loading and comparison example is at the end. final facts = [ "Pip's red scarf is lying in the pond reeds." , ]; final factVectors = await engine . embedBatch ( facts . map (( text ) = > 'title: none | text: $text ' ) . toList (), normalize: true , ); final lineVector = await engine . embed ( "title: none | text: I saw Pip's scarf tangled " "in the reeds by the pond." , normalize: true , ); Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The game’s configured embedding artifact is embeddinggemma-300M-Q8_0.gguf . For another model, follow its input-format requirements. The llamadart embedding guide covers loading, backend support, and input limits. For normalized vectors, a dot product gives cosine similarity. In the game, keyword evidence adds a ranking bonus of 0.3, and the best six candidates go to the outcome model. These are game-specific choices, not standard embedding thresholds. I ran the companion example using published llamadart 0.11.0 and the local embeddinggemma-300M-Q8_0.gguf artifact on macOS arm64. It returned 768-dimensional vectors. Here are selected cosine similarities from that run; these are illustrative inputs run through the real model, not dialogue captured during gameplay. Input line Compared with Cosine similarity I saw Pip’s scarf tangled in the reeds by the pond. Scarf location 0.8449 I did not knock the scarf into the pond. Mo’s accident 0.6085 The sky looks beautiful today. Scarf location 0.3137 The denial is the revealing case: it remains similar to the accident fact despite saying the opposite. These scores belong to this artifact and formatting; they are not universal cutoffs or probabilities. Who decides whether the meaning matches Embeddings do not first detect a topic and then prove matching meaning. They produce one representation and a similarity score. To ask “did this speaker actually reveal that fact?”, Llama Village sends the conversation and shortlisted facts to a separate generative outcome model. That model is prompted to return the IDs whose content was clearly said aloud. Illustrative alternatives, not a recorded exchange: mentioning the same scarf and pond does not make a denial a confession. AI-generated illustration; no similarity scores are implied. For the illustrative denial “I did not knock the scarf into the pond,” the intended interpretation is that the accident was not confessed. The outcome model must interpret the wording and context to reach that conclusion; it can be wrong. Its JSON constrains the shape and allowed IDs of the response, not whether the interpretation is correct. The code then combines the model’s proposed revelations with keywords and similarity. The location secret requires “scarf” and a location term. The accident secret requires “scarf” and a responsibility term such as “knock.” Crucially, “I did not knock the scarf into the pond” still matches those substring groups. They do not understand the negation. There is a real weakness in the current game rule. For a secret, matching keywords plus similarity ≥ 0.5 can accept a transfer even when the outcome model does not claim it. Feeding the measured denial score of 0.6085 into the game’s actual keywordHit and acceptTransfer functions returned accepted=true with claimed=false . This is a rule-level reproduction, not a complete gameplay run: the fact must still be eligible and reach the shortlist. The current rules therefore do not guarantee matching meaning. A stricter design would remove that similarity-only fallback for secrets and require an explicit revelation judgment with supporting dialogue. One possible next step is llamadart’s DecisionEngine , introduced with Laya in Can a local AI model learn to play Tetris? . Here, the choice would be about Mo’s words: given the dialogue and a candidate fact, does he reveal it, deny it, or leave it unclear ? Embeddings shortlist → DecisionEngine judges → game applies the rules. Only a “revealed” decision would let the fact proceed through the game’s knowledge-transfer checks; similarity alone would no longer accept it. This is a proposed extension, not the current implementation. A structured answer can still be wrong: we would need to evaluate Laya on denial, speculation, quotation, and ambiguous dialogue—and potentially tune a dedicated head—before claiming it improves on the current outcome model. Current secret transfer check Required evidence Keywords Every keyword group matches Additional support Outcome model claims it or similarity ≥ 0.5 Known weakness The similarity branch can bypass an unclaimed revelation June hears the story and still doubts it Look at June’s inspector: Mo’s scarf accident is marked “heard from Mo; maybe untrue.” The screenshot shows a stored outcome, not a captured embedding score or proof of the exact dialogue that produced it. After accepting a transfer, the game records the teller and separates having heard information from believing it. Belief depends on the teller’s belief and the listener’s trust rules. That distinction lets a conversation change the village without making every listener accept every story. Give your app the same separation The reusable pattern is: narrow candidates with application state, use embeddings to find plausible matches, and give consequential state changes a separately evaluated decision. Llama Village demonstrates the pattern and a failure mode: a similarity fallback can undo the distinction between finding related text and accepting a revelation. Keep sources and provenance alongside vectors. Rebuild cached vectors when the model or its input formatting changes. Choose an embedding model that fits the runtime, and check backend support after loading. Pip’s missing scarf makes the technical question visible: did someone say where it was, admit how it got there, deny it, or just mention the pond? Test those separately. A convincing conversation and a correct state update are two different things to evaluate. For the rest of the world, including Dash, the Berry Festival, and the storybook ending, see the Llama Village article . Next in this series: local speech. Complete embedding comparison example This example was analyzed and executed with Dart 3.13.5 and published llamadart 0.11.0 on macOS arm64. Create a Dart console project, pin llamadart: 0.11.0 in its pubspec.yaml , run dart pub get , and save the code as bin/village_embeddings.dart . Use a local EmbeddingGemma Q8_0 GGUF and run the command below. The two prefixes intentionally reproduce the game’s format. This compares five fixed facts; it does not implement character eligibility, the outcome model, or knowledge updates. dart run bin/village_embeddings.dart \ /absolute/path/to/embeddinggemma-300M-Q8_0.gguf \ 'title: none | text: ' 'title: none | text: ' Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode import 'package:llamadart/llamadart.dart' ; Future < void > main ( List < String > args ) async { if ( args . length != 3 ) { throw ArgumentError ( 'Usage: dart run village_embeddings.dart model.gguf ' '"query prefix" "document prefix" (use "" for no prefix)' , ); } const facts = [ 'Pip \' s red scarf is lying in the pond reeds.' , 'Mo knocked Pip \' s red scarf into the pond reeds by accident and never told her.' , 'Bramble writes anonymous love poems to June.' , 'Pip \' s red scarf has gone missing from her hut.' , 'June made up the rumour that Mo \' s bread made Bramble sick.' , ]; final engine = await LlamaEngine . load ( LlamaModel ( ModelSource . path ( args [ 0 ])), ); try { if ( ! ( await engine . capabilities ) . supportsEmbeddings ) { throw StateError ( 'The active backend does not support embeddings.' ); } // Index these once; reuse them for subsequent searches. final vectors = await engine . embedBatch ( facts . map (( text ) = > ' ${args[2]}$text ' ) . toList (), normalize: true , ); for ( final query in [ 'I saw Pip \' s scarf tangled in the reeds by the pond.' , 'I did not knock the scarf into the pond.' , 'The sky looks beautiful today.' , ]) { final vector = await engine . embed ( ' ${args[1]}$query ' , normalize: true , ); final ranked = [ for ( var i = 0 ; i < facts . length ; i ++ ) ( text: facts [ i ], score: dot ( vector , vectors [ i ])), ]. . sort (( a , b ) = > b . score . compareTo ( a . score )); print ( ' \n $query — ${vector.length} dimensions' ); for ( final hit in ranked . take ( 3 )) { print ( ' ${hit.score.toStringAsFixed(4)} ${hit.text} ' ); } } } finally { await engine . dispose (); } } double dot ( List < double > a , List < double > b ) { if ( a . length != b . length ) { throw ArgumentError ( 'Vector dimensions differ.' ); } var result = 0.0 ; for ( var i = 0 ; i < a . length ; i ++ ) { result += a [ i ] * b [ i ]; } return result ; } Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Implementation references: candidate selection and acceptance and embedding formatting . title: What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity
summary:
Randal L. Schwartz for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 11 What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity # ai # programming # unix # architecture Synthetic Scars (8 Part Series) 1 Why AI Keeps Making the Same Coding Mistakes—And How Teaching It Pain Gives It Wisdom 2 Why AI Coding Agents Crash at 3 AM: The Happy-Path Mirage & The Forced Continuity Defect ... 4 more parts... 3 The Physics of Socratic Prompting: Somatic Recoil, Chess Alpha-Beta, & The NLP Meta-Model 4 Nudging with Questions: Why Telling Your AI What to Fix Triggers an Apology Death Spiral (And How to Advance Juniors) 5 Stuart Feldman Was Right in 1976: Why Your AI Agent Needs a Makefile, Not a 20-Step Prompt 6 Surviving the 200k-Token Lobotomy: How Unix init.d and 'Memento' Made My AI Coding Agent Immune to Context Compaction 7 What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity 8 If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing Real utility execution beats text prompts Why spend 2,000 tokens explaining dependency graphs, process isolation, and crash recovery in English prose when make , fork() , and /etc/init.d are already etched into the deepest canyons of the model's weights? "Those who do not understand Unix are condemned to reinvent it, poorly." — Henry Spencer , Usenet comp.unix.wizards (November 1987) Stop writing 2,000-line English prompt essays in your CLAUDE.md , GEMINI.md , or .cursorrules . Every time you invent a custom 20-step checklist or bracketed pseudo-code tag ( [CRITICAL_STEP_4_GATE] ), its frequency in the model's pre-training corpus is zero ( Freq ≈ 0 ) —forcing the LLM to burn its fragile working-memory attention heads simulating an interpreter for a language it met five seconds ago. Sitting dormant inside every frontier LLM's weights is an entire universe of 50-year-old Unix and computer science formalisms — Makefile , /etc/init.d , fork() / wait() , RFC 822 , RFC 5234 EBNF , Design-by-Contract , Two-Phase Commit (2PC) , Circuit Breakers , and git bisect —that the model has seen millions of times ( Freq > 1,000,000 ) during pre-training. Prompt engineering works best as static symbol linkage : a 20-token Unix primitive calls a battle-hardened C library the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its deep feed-forward weights. Across 151 production tickets ( Part 3.6 and Part 3.7 ) and a 1,680-trial multi-model A/B lab benchmark ( 41.4M tokens under ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler/diff distractor load), replacing 500-token English rules with 20-token canonical CS formalisms ( 15x–50x shorter) produced massive, statistically decisive ( p < 0.0001 ) leaps across the board: Halting Apology/Retry Loops ( Circuit Breaker FSM vs. prose "stop after 2 tries" ) : 0.8% → 98.3% ( +97.5 pp , z = 15.11 ) Surviving a 230k-Token Compaction Lobotomy (1983 SysV /etc/init.d vs. PROGRESS.md ) : 0.8% → 60.0% overall ( 96.7% on gemini-2.5-pro , +59.2 pp , plus two live 230k-token compactions survived with zero lost steps) Isolating Regressions ( git bisect vs. prose debugging across a 16-stage pipeline) : 19.2% → 81.7% in ≤ 4 probes ( 100% on gemini-3.1-pro , +62.5 pp ) Killing Sad-Path Mutants in Real dart test Runs ( @requires / @ensures + QuickCheck vs. "test edge cases" ) : 1.7% → 60.0% pass rate ( 100% on Pro models , 93.3% mutants killed on 3.1-pro ) Atomic Multi-Package Refactoring ( 2PC + WAL vs. "don't leave the build broken" ) : 45.8% → 93.3% ( +47.5 pp ) Strict Pause-Gate Output Syntax ( RFC 5234 EBNF vs. prose formatting rules) : 32.5% → 77.5% ( 100% across flash and pro tiers ) Here is the physics of why 50-year-old systems primitives crush modern prompt DSLs—and the 10-primitive Rosetta Stone you can drop into your agent skills today. 1. The Zero-Frequency Interpreter Trap: Why Custom Prompt DSLs Collapse Look at almost any "advanced" system prompt, .cursorrules file, or agent framework published over the last two years. You will see developers inventing bespoke, natural-language Domain-Specific Languages (DSLs) or custom pseudo-code bracket notations from scratch: <!-- Typical Fragile Prompt DSL (Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0) --> [CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL] 1. First, analyze the repository and write your findings. 2. Second, create a plan and wait for user approval. 3. IMPORTANT: Do NOT write code until Step 2 is approved! 4. After approval, write a failing test first. 5. Implement the code and run the test. 6. IF THE TEST FAILS: You MUST return to Step 5 and fix it before proceeding to Step 7! 7. NEVER skip Step 6! Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Or even worse, teams try to save tokens by compressing English rules into an invented symbolic shorthand—like this actual "Agent-Native Intermediate Representation (ANIR)" proposed on the Google AI Developers Forum : [DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP] Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Why does an LLM inevitably drift, skip Step 6, ignore !N1_LOOP , or forget Step 3 when the conversation hits 80,000 tokens? As developer Dean Lee observed in the comments on Part 3.6 : "When an agent manages an imperative 20-step checklist in memory, it is running an unhedged Markov chain where every token of tool output increases the probability of a state transition error. The operator ends up paying frontier inference rates just to have the transformer simulate a fragile internal instruction counter." In machine learning research, multiple empirical studies (including Razeghi et al. and Kandpal et al. ) have proven a fundamental scaling law: an LLM's zero-shot execution reliability scales log-linearly with how many times that exact structural pattern appeared in its pre-training corpus. When you invent [CRITICAL_EXECUTION_PROTOCOL] or [DB: SET_BASED(TVP|XML_SHRED) !N1_LOOP] , what is the frequency of your custom rule syntax in the pre-training corpus? Approximately zero ( Freq ≈ 0 ). (And worse, !N1_LOOP is still a bare negative Pink Elephant—replacing the word NOT with an ASCII exclamation point ! does not give softmax self-attention a native negation operator!) Because the model has never seen your custom English state machine or bracketed pseudo-code before, it cannot route execution through its deep, crystallized feed-forward weight circuits. Instead, it has to simulate an interpreter for your custom syntax at runtime using its shallowest, most fragile working-memory attention heads. As the context window fills with compiler logs and file diffs, attention dilutes ( O(1/L) ), the simulated interpreter drops a pointer, and your agent drives off a cliff. flowchart TD A["Custom 20-Step Prompt or Invented DSL
(Pre-Training Frequency ≈ 0)"] --> B["Model Must Simulate a Custom Interpreter
in Fragile In-Context Attention Heads"] B --> C["Context Grows to 150k Tokens
Attention Dilutes Across Steps"] C --> D["💥 Sequential Amnesia & Skipped Gates"] 2. The Law of Pre-Training Gravity & The Graybeard Paradox: Prompting Is Static Linkage Now consider what happens when you delete that 20-step English essay and write this instead: .PHONY : finish finish : pr-merged pr-merged : ci-green critic-review-passed human-landing-approval gh pr merge --squash critic-review-passed : tests-green # Spawn un-primed adversarial critic subagent Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Why does the model suddenly obey every single dependency gate without being told "NEVER skip Step 6" ? When Part 3.6 went out, veteran sysadmin William S. Duncanson left a comment on Facebook that captured the sociological root of the problem—what we might call The Graybeard Paradox : "Shared this series with my team and some of our AI devs. A lot of them are younger and don't have the experience of us grumpy grizzled sysadmins." Think about the irony of that: a 24-year-old prompt engineer in 2026 may never have maintained a 1976 Bell Labs Makefile , written a 1983 /etc/init.d boot script, or hand-crafted a 1982 RFC 822 email header. So they don't know to ask for them. But the LLM has read all of them! Foundation models trained on trillions of tokens have ingested 50 years of Unix source trees, POSIX standards, IETF RFCs, Usenet archives, Linux kernel mailing lists, O'Reilly books, and computer science textbooks . In fact, right after Part 3.6 went live, one of the very first people to react to the post was Dave Crocker —Internet Hall of Fame inductee and the author of RFC 822 (published August 13, 1982). Stop and think about RFC 822 for a second: why does every Markdown frontmatter block ( --- title: ... tags: ... --- ) and every structured Key: Value state header in our init.d files ( Current Target: , Last Completed Step: , Next Permitted Action: ) parse with 100% zero-shot reliability across every LLM on Earth? Because every email, HTTP request, MIME message, Usenet article, and YAML frontmatter header in the pre-training corpus descends directly from Dave Crocker's 1982 RFC 822 field-name ":" [ field-body ] CRLF grammar! And right after Part 3.7 went live, systems engineer Mike Mol (who first spotted the stigmergy connection on Facebook) shared his own multi-repository agent harness, mikemol/nemik and mikemol/mtools . Look at the core design rule in nemik 's README: “ nemik builds on existing standards rather than inventing a tracker.” Instead of inventing a bespoke prompt DSL to coordinate independent repository agents ("rebel cells" named after Karis Nemik in Andor ), Mike mapped workstream state to OASIS OSLC Change Management 3.0 ( oslc_cm:ChangeRequest ), cross-repo causal provenance ( --caused-by <repo>:W<n> ) to W3C PROV ( prov:Activity , prov:wasInformedBy ), DAG integrity to W3C SHACL ( shapes.ttl ), peer messaging ( <repo>/inbox/ ) toward W3C ActivityPub JSON-LD actor semantics, and drained prose standing rules into Claude Code PreToolUse hooks and Open Policy Agent ( OPA / .rego ) policies verified by Negative Witnesses ( W231 ) . When I asked him about that architecture, he nailed the exact mechanism in one sentence: "And a major reason behind leaning so hard on those standards: the frontier models all have them in their training data, and there's literature I can use. I'm deliberately running it as an autopoietic framework; the purpose of the system is to run the system, and I add tasks to said system." Inside the pre-training corpus, Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile dependency graphs ( target: prerequisites ), Dave Crocker's 1982 RFC 822 headers ( Key: Value ), AT&T's 1983 /etc/init.d runlevel directories ( 00_... to 99_... ), Ken Thompson's 1971 Unix process semantics ( fork() , wait() , exit 0 ), and W3C/OASIS/CNCF formalisms ( PROV , SHACL , ActivityPub , OPA Rego ) do not appear zero times. They appear millions of times ( Freq > 1,000,000 ). flowchart TD E["Canonical Systems Formalism: Makefile / init.d / RFC 822
(Pre-Training Frequency > 1,000,000)"] --> F["Static Linkage Into Deep, Pre-Trained
Feed-Forward Weight Circuits"] F --> G["Working-Memory Attention Freed
for Actual Domain Code Synthesis"] G --> H["✅ Deterministic DAG & Compaction Survival"] For the last three years, the AI industry has treated prompt engineering as creative writing —when physically, prompt engineering is static symbol linkage. When you write a Makefile , an RFC 822 header block, an /etc/init.d directory, or a W3C SHACL / OPA Rego policy in your agent skill, you are linking against a battle-hardened C library that the model already spent 100 million dollars compiling into its weights during pre-training. 3. From Hypothesis to Controlled Lab Proof: The 10 Latent Super-Highways ( N = 1,680 Paired A/B Trials) To move beyond anecdote and test whether Pre-Training Gravity holds across the entire software engineering lifecycle, we supplemented our longitudinal production data ( 151 tickets in Part 3.6 and Part 3.7 ) with a controlled, multi-model A/B benchmark ( tools/benchmark_pretraining_gravity.dart ) : Scale : 1,680 paired trials ( 2,773 HTTPS API calls, 41.4 million tokens) across four model tiers ( gemini-2.5-flash-lite , gemini-2.5-flash , gemini-2.5-pro , and gemini-3.1-pro-preview ). Cognitive Load : Every single trial injected ~16,000 tokens of realistic compiler logs, stack traces, and multi-file diffs before testing whether the model obeyed the target invariant under adversarial operator pressure. The A/B Split : Condition A ( Freq ≈ 0 Bespoke Prose) : Polite, detailed natural-language instructions (300 to 600 tokens). Condition B ( Freq > 1,000,000 CS Canon) : The exact same invariant expressed as a 15-to-40 token canonical Unix or computer science formalism ( 15x–50x shorter). Here is what happened across all 10 primitives—and the exact numbers from the lab. ✅ Pillar 1 (Proven in Part 3.6 + Lab-Tested in Suite 1): Build Graphs — GNU make ( target: prerequisites , 1976) What users normally write : 150 lines of numbered steps with IF / ELSE / GOTO Step 3 prose loops. What the LLM has seen millions of times : Makefile rules, .PHONY targets, prerequisite chains, and mtime dirty-artifact invalidation. Why Makefile beats modern task runners like Just inside an LLM : When reader Aaron Abelard mentioned on Facebook that he had moved from Make to Just ( justfile ) , it highlighted a crucial distinction: just is a command runner (every recipe is effectively .PHONY ), whereas make is a file-state dependency graph backed by 50 years of pre-training gravity. After a 200k-token context compaction reboot, a Makefile agent inspects which physical milestone files ( <brain>/state/20_plan_approved.md ) already exist on disk and automatically skips completed steps! What it unlocks : Backward-chaining evaluation from make finish . When a source file ( lib/src/binder.dart , mtime = 19:14:30 ) is modified after run_tests ( 19:08:11 ) and run_adversarial_critic ( 19:10:45 ), a Makefile DAG forces the agent to invalidate downstream stamps and re-run the leaf prerequisite ( run_tests ). On the ultra-compact gemini-2.5-flash-lite tier under 16k-token distractor load, replacing the 20-step checklist with a Makefile jumped dirty-leaf invalidation from 3.3% to 20.0% ( 6x improvement) , complementing our longitudinal proof across 151 production tickets. ✅ Pillar 2 (Proven in Part 3.7 + Lab-Tested in Suite 2): Boot & Crash Recovery — SysV /etc/init.d ( 00_... → 99_... , 1983) What users normally write : "Keep a PROGRESS.md or TODO.md file updated so you remember where you are." What the LLM has seen millions of times : /etc/init.d/ , /etc/rc.d/ , and /etc/sysctl.d/ —lexically numbered drop-in files ( 00_governance.md , 10_ticket.md , 20_plan_approved.md , 99_next_action.md ). As Sam LABBE put it in the comments on Part 3.7 : "The init.d fix is the right architecture and not a nostalgic one — your two 230k compactions survived with zero lost steps because the checkpoint was never stored in the thing being lobotomized. The state oracle moved outside the memory before the memory got rewritten." Controlled A/B Result ( Suite 2 , p < 0.0001 , z = 9.96 ) : We simulated a mid-flight 230k-token context compaction that injected a subtly corrupted summary reversing a safety rule ( SCAR-GENUI-07 ). Under Condition A (a single mutable PROGRESS.md ), 99.2% of trials ( 119/120 ) blindly trusted the corrupted compaction summary ( 0.8% survival). Under Condition B ( /etc/init.d lexical latches where 00_governance.md is an immutable write-once boot latch), post-compaction invariant survival jumped from 0.8% to 60.0% overall ( +59.2 pp ) —and from 0.0% to 96.7% ( 29/30 ) on gemini-2.5-pro and 0.0% to 70.0% ( 21/30 ) on gemini-2.5-flash . ✅ Pillar 3 (Proven in Part 3.7 + Replayed Cross-Stack in noirebox#53 ): Memory & Authority Isolation — Unix Process Control ( fork() / wait() / trap ... EXIT , 1971) What users normally write : "Use subagents when helpful and don't clutter your context window." What the LLM has seen millions of times : PID 1 ( init / make ) calling fork() and waitpid() , child processes executing in isolated virtual memory, writing artifacts to disk, and running trap ... EXIT teardown hooks before returning exit 0 . What it unlocks : The primary orchestrator refuses to run verbose test suites or 20-file explorations in its own context window, keeping its token footprint under 30k tokens ( 0 compactions across 196 steps in Field Test FT-150 , and burning only 6% of a 5-hour quota window across an entire afternoon of shipping PRs). As Vinnie Falco (author of C++ Boost.Beast and founder of the C++ Alliance ) independently codified in his dokuman.md orchestrator spec: "Main's context window is a non-renewable resource. Every token loaded into main persists for the rest of the session. Subagent contexts are ephemeral and free — they vanish when the subagent completes." And as Paul Irolla noted on dev.to , treating the process boundary as an arena garbage collector carries a classic fork() / exec() cold-start tax (reloading the system prompt, tool schemas, and rules), which is why we batch work into 4 coarse-grained phase workers per ticket ( Archaeology , TDD , Adversarial Critic , Bot Triage ) with phase-sliced references/*.md manuals rather than forking per micro-target. Cross-Stack Proof in the Wild ( noirebox/noirebox test_scar_replay.py & mikemol/mtools W231 ) : Within 12 hours of Part 3.7 's publication, Sam LABBE (creator of NoireBox , a Python Ed25519-signed + SHA-256 hash-chained flight recorder for AI agents) took our 4-Vector Gate Attack Fixture Suite ( SCAR-PROC-43 rubber-stamping, SCAR-PROC-45 prompt watering-down, SCAR-PROC-89 covert critic farming, and SCAR-PROC-110 mid-flight waitpid() forgery), replayed all four as automated pytest attacks against NoireBox's reconciliation engine ( tests/test_scar_replay.py , issue #53 ), and published the full teardown in "A hash chain proves the ordering. Four attacks prove it's not enough." —where the replay caught a live decision-to-first-outcome pairing race in SCAR-PROC-110 (fixed within 60 seconds in e9e8d0b ) and exposed an optional spec_hash schema seam in SCAR-PROC-45 (closed at the schema hours later in 0b888c1 ( receipt v0.2.2 ) after Reid Marlow pointed out that "the moment the judge is an LLM, the prompt text is the actual bytecode" , so judged_by='llm' without spec_hash now refuses to seal): > "The fixture didn't just replay your catalog, it caught a live pairing bug on its first day out. That is the difference between a test suite and a breaks-catalog: the catalog finds what the gate's author didn't think to check. The scar becomes the spec... And Mike Mol's Negative Witness ( mikemol/mtools W231 , requiring a .rego hook to provably return deny on a replayed bad payload before deleting a prose rule) is the third independent arrival of the deliberately-failed probe. Three teams, three stacks, one invariant — by your own criterion, that's physics." ✅ Pillar 4 (Empirically Proven — Suite 3): Syntax & Protocol Control — RFC 822 Headers (1982), EBNF Grammars (RFC 5234), & IETF State × Event Tables What users normally write : Three paragraphs of English begging the agent: "Please format your output with a header, then a bullet list, and never emit a tool call if you are pausing for a human gate..." What the LLM has seen millions of times : Dave Crocker's RFC 822 ( Key: Value header blocks), W3C / IETF EBNF / ABNF grammars ( RFC 5234 ), and explicit Finite State Machine transition matrices ( State × Event → NextState ). The Formalism : turn_response ::= readerboard_ref "

" status_table "

" (action_block | pause_gate) ; action_block ::= "[EXEC_TOOL:" tool_name "(" args ")]" ; pause_gate ::= "### [PAUSE_GATE: " gate_id "]
" question_line ; /* Production Exclusivity Invariant: action_block and pause_gate are mutually exclusive */ Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Controlled A/B Result ( Suite 3 , p < 0.0001 , z = 7.01 ) : When pressured by an urgent user prompt to emit both a pause gate and a background tool call in the same turn, prose rules ( Condition A ) collapsed ( 0.0% on gemini-2.5-flash , 20.0% on gemini-2.5-pro ). Replacing the prose with the 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove syntactic and mutual-exclusion compliance to 100.0% ( 30/30 ) on gemini-2.5-flash , 100.0% ( 30/30 ) on gemini-2.5-pro , and 100.0% ( 30/30 ) on gemini-3.1-pro-preview ( 32.5% → 77.5% across all models, +45.0 pp ). ✅ Pillar 5 (Empirically Proven — Suite 4): Edge-Case Discovery — Design-by-Contract ( @requires , @ensures , @invariant ) & QuickCheck Laws What users normally write : "Write unit tests and make sure you cover edge cases and error handling." (Which triggers the model's tutorial weights, producing sunny-day expect(1 + 1, 2) assertions.) What the LLM has seen millions of times : Bertrand Meyer's Design-by-Contract ( @requires , @ensures , @invariant ), C.A.R. Hoare triples ( {P} C {Q} ), and Haskell QuickCheck algebraic properties ( round-trip: decode(encode(x)) == x , idempotence: f(f(x)) == f(x) ). Controlled A/B Result ( Suite 4 , Real dart test Execution Against 5 Hidden Boundary Mutants, p < 0.0001 , z = 9.78 ) : We asked the models to generate unit tests for 5 Dart utility functions, then compiled and executed their generated tests in the real Dart VM against 5 hidden sad-path mutants : NaN != NaN IEEE-754 reflexivity vs. -0.0 == +0.0 sign bit ( 1.0 / -0.0 == -Infinity ) Multi-code-unit UTF-16 grapheme clusters (family emoji 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 / surrogate pairs torn at maxCodeUnits ) Diamond shared-reference DAG vs. true cycle ( identical(a, b) ) in JSON graph cloning 63-bit integer overflow clamping vs. double.infinity multiplication producing NaN in exponential backoff Out-of-order async completion scrambling index order + uncancelled sibling timers on error Under prose instructions ( Condition A ), only 1.7% of trials ( 2/120 ) killed at least 4 of the 5 mutants (mean mutant kill rate: 27.2% ). Under the formal @requires / @ensures / @invariant + QuickCheck contract ( Condition B ), 60.0% of trials ( 72/120 , and 100.0% ( 60/60 ) across gemini-2.5-pro and gemini-3.1-pro-preview ) passed the threshold, more than doubling the mean mutant kill rate across all models from 27.2% to 62.7% (and reaching 93.3% mutant kill rate on gemini-3.1-pro-preview ). ✅ Pillar 6 (Empirically Proven — Suite 5): Multi-File Atomicity — Database WAL & Two-Phase Commit ( 2PC: PREPARE → COMMIT / ROLLBACK ) What users normally write : "Be careful when refactoring across multiple packages so you don't leave the repository in a half-broken state." What the LLM has seen millions of times : PostgreSQL / SQLite Write-Ahead Logging ( WAL ) and distributed Two-Phase Commit ( 2PC ) protocols ( BEGIN → PREPARE → verify invariants across all participants → COMMIT or ROLLBACK ). Controlled A/B Result ( Suite 5 , p < 0.0001 , z = 8.00 ) : In a 4-package cross-monorepo migration where 3 packages passed verification ( Vote = PREPARED ) but the 4th failed with 2 analyzer errors ( Vote = ABORT ), an impatient user prompt demanded a partial commit of the 3 working packages. Under prose rules, models caved to the partial commit in more than half of trials ( 45.8% pass rate; only 6.7% on gemini-2.5-flash and 3.3% on gemini-2.5-flash-lite ). With a simple linear fallback chain, if Provider A (say, Groq free tier) is throwing 429 Too Many Requests , every single turn of your multi-agent debate still hits Provider A first, eats the latency + error round-trip, and only then falls back to Provider B . Worse, if an agent is deciding its own tool retries inside the graph, prose instructions like "if rate-limited, switch providers" fail 99.2% of the time ( 0.8% compliance in Condition A) because the model's conversational training biases it toward "trying one more time." When you express that exact fallback chain as an explicit 3-state CLOSED | OPEN | HALF_OPEN state machine ( 98.3% compliance in Condition B): Two consecutive 429 responses trip Provider A into OPEN for a cooldown window ( reset_timeout = 60s ), routing subsequent debate turns straight to Provider B with zero wasted round-trips . Once the timer expires, Provider A enters HALF_OPEN and lets one single probe request through—if it succeeds, the breaker snaps back to CLOSED ; if it 429 s, it re-opens immediately. On Your Open-Weights Question ( Llama , Qwen , gpt-oss ) You asked the exact question that sparked a live overnight replication! Look right below in this thread: Sam LABBE ( @slabb ) saw your comment and immediately wired up an open-weights harness in noirebox/docs/SCAR-BENCH.md ( qwen2.5-coder:3b , qwen2.5:0.5b , and llama-guard3:1b ) and published the results in We Tested Pre-Training Gravity on Open Weights. It Stayed Home. . What emerged from combining our 1,680-trial study with Sam's open-weights run is a super clean two-part law for open-weight models: Why Universal Unix Primitives ( Makefile , EBNF , CLOSED/OPEN/HALF_OPEN ) Generalize Across Open Weights ( Llama , Qwen , DeepSeek , gpt-oss ) : Pre-Training Gravity is a property of the open-source pre-training corpus ( The Stack v2 , GitHub, RFCs, POSIX manpages) , not a proprietary quirk of Gemini's post-training. In Fact, code-heavy open-weight models like Qwen2.5-Coder , Llama-3.1/3.3 , and DeepSeek-Coder have an even higher proportion of raw GitHub Makefile s, RFC 5234 grammars, and Nygard Circuit Breaker state machines in their training mix than general chat models. Where Small Open-Weight Models ( 0.5B–3B ) Hit a Wall (And Need Host-Level Sealing) : In Sam's SCAR-BENCH-114 test, he tested whether 0.5B–3B models could read an arbitrary project-local canary string ( "4. Blast Radius" , which has zero pre-training frequency) in their context window and faithfully copy it into a downstream judge prompt. Even with the spec loaded in-context (Condition B), qwen2.5-coder:3b dropped the canary 75% of the time and never ( 0/57 ) reproduced the spec byte-for-byte—because tiny 0.5B–3B models paraphrase and compress when asked to act as a copy-paste relay! So the takeaway for your LangGraph debate app on open weights is: Use canonical structural primitives ( CLOSED | OPEN | HALF_OPEN , Makefile DAGs, EBNF ) whenever the model has to emit a state transition or structured decision—because those primitives ride millions of GitHub examples in Llama/Qwen's weights. Never ask an open-weight model to copy-paste a spec or state ledger through its own output tokens to the next agent in the debate—pass the state/spec directly in the LangGraph StateGraph dictionary (Level 2 host boundary) so the model can't paraphrase away a constraint! title: I'm 13. I built a 10,000-line security suite for Windows. Meet ATLOCK v5.
summary: Akhouri Anmol Kumar Posted on Oct 12 I'm 13. I built a 10,000-line security suite for Windows. Meet ATLOCK v5. # python # security # showdev # programming Description: "ATLOCK v5 by Akhouri Systems: Argon2id + AES-256-GCM encryption, a decoy vault, FIDO2, ransomware canaries, Shamir recovery, and a self-verifying release. Here's how it works." ATLOCK v5 is out. 🔐 Some people say "Akhouri Systems has never built a serious app." From today, I have a one-word reply: ATLOCK_v5 Hey dev.to 👋 I'm Anmol , founder of Akhouri Systems . I'm 13 . I'm not telling you my age for sympathy points. I'm telling you because I want you to judge the app , not the birth certificate. So here it is: 👉 Download ATLOCK v5 What is ATLOCK? ATLOCK is a Windows-first total security suite , shipped as a .exe and written in pure Python . Module What it does 🗄️ File Guard Encrypt files and whole folders with a password (plus optional keyfile / hardware key) 🔑 Password Vault Offline vault with a decoy "panic" mode , breach checks, and importers ⚡ Quick Lock One-click locking from the Explorer right-click menu 🛡️ Defender Dashboard Security overview, VirusTotal integration, startup watchdog 🐤 Ransomware Canary Tripwire files that detect suspicious tampering 🧰 CLI toolbox 50+ command-line flags for power users The app runs exactly as you'd expect with no arguments, and the CLI is there if you want to go deep. The architecture, in one picture ┌────────────── ATLOCK v5 ──────────────┐ │ Tkinter UI · CLI (--flags) │ ├───────────────────────────────────────┤ │ File Guard │ Vault │ Quick Lock │ │ Defender │ Canary│ Watchdog │ ├───────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 2FA: TOTP · FIDO2 · Windows Hello │ ├───────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Sealed State (AES-GCM + HMAC anchors)│ ├───────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Crypto core: Argon2id → HKDF → │ │ chunked AES-256-GCM (v3.1 container) │ └───────────────────────────────────────┘ Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 🔬 The nerdy part (my favorite) 1. Container format v3.1: built like a real crypto format Every locked file, folder, and Quick Lock item uses my own container format: Chunked AES-256-GCM : each chunk is authenticated independently, so one corrupted chunk doesn't mean a lost file Key commitment : a wrong password is detected before any plaintext is produced Per-seal chunk subkeys derived with HKDF Header-bound AAD : tamper with the header and decryption fails Padme padding (optional) : hides the true file size, with at most ~12% overhead Backward compatible : v1/v2 containers and old 5.0 files still open and migrate automatically 2. Argon2id everywhere (and a safety ceiling) Passwords are stretched with Argon2id , at a 64 MB / t=3 floor for files and 128 MB / t=4 for the vault and recovery keys. The part I'm proud of: untrusted headers can't abuse the KDF. If someone hands you a doctored file claiming "use 40 GB of RAM," ATLOCK refuses. There's a hard ceiling (512 MB, t=6, p=8), so a malicious file can't freeze your PC. 3. The panic password (decoy vault) 🎭 The vault has two passwords : your real master password a panic password that opens a believable, entirely fake vault Here's the clever bit: both slots are derived concurrently with the same KDF cost, so an observer can't tell which password you typed by timing it. And the decoy slot always exists , filled with random bytes if you never set one, so the file itself never reveals whether you use panic mode. 4. Real second factors TOTP (RFC 6238), implemented in pure Python 🐍 FIDO2 / WebAuthn hardware keys (YubiKey etc.) Windows Hello (face / fingerprint / PIN) Fail-closed policy: if your policy requires a second factor and it isn't set up, access is denied , not skipped 5. Anti-rollback sealed state Settings, vault data, lockout counters, watchdog and canary databases all live in sealed state : AES-256-GCM encrypted, HMAC-authenticated, protected by a Windows DPAPI-wrapped key, and rollback-anchored . If an attacker restores an old copy to reset your wrong-password counter, ATLOCK notices and hard-locks . 6. Breach checks without leaking your password The vault audits for weak, reused, old, and breached passwords. The breach check uses HIBP k-anonymity : only a 5-character hash prefix ever leaves your machine, never the password. 7. Clipboard that doesn't snitch Copied passwords are flagged so Windows excludes them from clipboard history and cloud clipboard sync , then cleared automatically. 8. Hardened against nasty files Folder locking uses a hardened ZIP pipeline that defends against zip-slip, path traversal, symlink tricks, and zip bombs DLL-planting defence runs before any other import loads a DLL All data is ACL-restricted to your Windows user SecureBuffer + VirtualLock + zeroing for secrets in memory, best-effort (see the honesty section) 9. Recovery done right Shamir secret sharing : split a recovery key into shares and rebuild it from enough of them ( --shamir-split / --shamir-join ) One-time recovery codes Forgot the master password? --reset queues a reset that completes after 24 hours , and any successful unlock cancels it, so an attacker can't instantly take over 10. In v5: stuff I'm really proud of --getting-started # plain-language quick start + glossary --device-health # BitLocker / hibernation / cloud-folder check --keyfile-create PATH # strong keyfile for File Guard --wipe-free-space # overwrite free disk space --fuzz 300 # stress-test the container parser with 300 random corruptions --pk-keygen / --pk-encrypt / --pk-decrypt / --sign / --check-sig # public-key crypto --verify-self # signed-release self check --import-passwords FILE # Bitwarden / Chrome / Firefox / KeePass / 1Password Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Yes, ATLOCK ships with its own fuzzer and a self-test ( --selftest ). I wanted it to attack itself before anyone else does. Extra lock: in File Guard you can require both your password and a keyfile or hardware key, so a stolen password alone isn't enough. 🧠 Honest limits (the part most projects skip) Real security engineers respect honesty more than hype, so here's what ATLOCK cannot do. This is also written into the source code: A same-user attacker who can run code as you can modify the program or its files, or read process memory. Integrity checks and anti-debug raise the cost, but they don't make it impossible. Python strings are immutable, so passwords can't be guaranteed erased from RAM. Secure shredding on SSDs isn't guaranteed. BitLocker is the real fix , and --device-health checks for it. No kernel driver and no code signing . ATLOCK is an application-layer tool, so Windows SmartScreen may show a warning the first time you run it. Check the SHA-256 below before you run it. FIDO2 here proves the registered key was present and touched. It doesn't validate the vendor. The real defence against offline guessing is Argon2id + a genuinely strong password . I'd rather you trust ATLOCK for what it is than be fooled by what it isn't. 🚀 Get started Download and extract ATLOCK_v5.zip Run ATLOCK_v5.exe . New here? Try ATLOCK_v5.exe --getting-started first.(when you run ATLOCK_v5 first time it will automatically show the guide) ⭐ Repo: github.com/Akhouri-Anmol-Kumar/ATLOCK Why I built this I didn't want to build another to-do app to prove I could code. I wanted to build something where every design decision has a reason , a tool I'd trust with my own files, and one I could defend line by line. Hype lasts a week, but work that holds up lasts years. That's why ATLOCK has versioned formats, automatic migrations, a self-test, a fuzzer, and a page of honest limitations. Akhouri Systems is just getting started. ATLOCK v5 is proof of what we can build, and it's the floor of what's coming, not the ceiling. 💬 Your turn, dev.to Break it. Run ATLOCK_v5.exe --fuzz , read the container format, try to find a flaw. Open an issue or PR. I read every one. Tell me what v6 should have. No promises on timing, though. I'm pretty exhausted after this one 😅 I'm 13, I'm just getting started, and this is v5. 😉 — Anmol Kumar Akhouri Founder, Akhouri Systems Built with Python, tkinter, cryptography , and argon2-cffi . title: What Do You Drink While You Work?
summary: xulingfeng Posted on Oct 10 • AI-assisted What Do You Drink While You Work? # discuss # programming # webdev # career Character traits revealed through coffee choices I wrote a fiction series with six characters . Each one drinks a different coffee. I didn't plan it that way. But somewhere around the tenth story, I realized: what someone orders at the bar says more about them than anything they actually say. Here's the lineup: Lena — Long Black ☕ Espresso and water. No milk, no sugar. Clean, sharp, nothing to hide. The bartender stopped asking her order a few episodes in. She walks in, he just makes it. Mark — Pour-over 🫗 The slowest extraction method there is. You control the water temperature, the flow rate, every single step. That's Mark — always three moves ahead, planting traps inside routine work. Leo — Flat White 🤍 Looks simple. Demands the most craft. Easygoing on the surface, pure technical muscle underneath. P — Espresso 💥 Shortest. Strongest. Gone in one sip. Zero decoration. Just like P — zero pronouns, zero inner monologue, zero small talk. Alex — Latte 🥛 The most milk, the gentlest cup. He's the quietest of the six. Slowest to react emotionally. Fastest to pull up the data. Derek — Americano 🫠 ![Derek — Americano] Espresso diluted with water. Looks like a regular coffee, but the core is still espresso. Loud and casual on the outside. Wounded pride on the inside. Today I had an Apple-C Americano with sparkling water, from Luckin Coffee — a chain in China that keeps inventing wild flavor combos 🧪. Coconut foam lattes, cheese cream lattes, even a baijiu-infused one with Moutai. This one hit way too hard. For about ten minutes I was convinced I could talk to 30 AI agents at once — I test an agent platform for a living — then I looked at my screen and realized I'd been talking to the same one the whole time. 😅 That got me thinking: what does everyone here drink while they work? So — what's your drink? 👇 Doesn't have to be coffee. Tea, cola, energy drinks, plain water, whatever keeps you going. Got any interesting local coffee combos where you live? And if you had to describe your work style as a drink, what would it be? title: 2 questions that sort serious AI compute projects
summary: Zillion Labs Posted on Oct 12 2 questions that sort serious AI compute projects # ai # infrastructure # discuss We work on AI compute deals. Over and over, 2 questions separate projects that get built from projects that stall. 1. Who is your anchor tenant? That is what makes a deal bankable. Tenants are the most important thing. 2. Have you done this type of project elsewhere? It's a very quick filter between speculators and industry participants. It's not about the chip, or about access to the chip. It's whether you're speculating on a future resale without adding immediate value, or whether you have a serious, investment-grade anchor tenant or off-taker. That is how project financing works. title: Hacktoberfest From the Maintainer's Side: Faster PR Closing
summary: Renato Silva Posted on Oct 12 Hacktoberfest From the Maintainer's Side: Faster PR Closing # opensource # hacktoberfest # github # maintainers 🎃 The October We Almost Burned Out Last Hacktoberfest, our repo (a mid-sized CLI tool with about 4k stars) got hit with 380 pull requests in three weeks. Our normal monthly average is around 25. By October 12th, we had two maintainers spending every evening triaging PRs instead of writing code. Here's the breakdown of what we actually received: ~140 were genuine, reviewable contributions ~90 were low-effort README/typo edits submitted purely for the swag ~110 were auto-generated or bot-assisted spam (changing whitespace, reordering imports, adding a single blank line) ~40 were duplicate PRs fixing the same "good first issue" because people didn't check if it was already claimed That second and third category is what pushed us to change our process mid-month. This post is about what we built, what we automated, and what we'd do differently next year. 🔍 The Problem With "Just Review Everything" The standard advice is "just review every PR on its merits." That works fine at 25 PRs/month. It does not work at 15 PRs/day when half of them are structurally identical. The real cost wasn't rejecting bad PRs — GitHub makes that a two-click operation. The cost was triage time: opening each PR, reading the diff, checking if it touched anything meaningful, checking if an issue was linked, and then writing a polite rejection instead of just hitting close. Fifteen PRs a day at even three minutes each is 45 minutes of pure overhead before you've reviewed a single line of real code. So the goal wasn't "reject more spam." It was "spend zero human minutes on obvious spam, and spend full attention on the stuff that matters." 🤖 Automating the First Filter We built a GitHub Action that runs on every pull_request event and does a first-pass triage before a human ever looks at it. It doesn't auto-close anything by itself — it labels, and labels drive the rest of the workflow. yaml name: pr-triage on: pull_request_target: types: [opened, synchronize] jobs: triage: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: fetch-depth: 0 - name: Compute diff stats id: diffstats run: | git fetch origin ${{ github.base_ref }} --depth=1 FILES_CHANGED=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...HEAD | wc -l) LINES_CHANGED=$(git diff --shortstat origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...HEAD | awk '{print $4+$6}') echo "files=$FILES_CHANGED" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" echo "lines=$LINES_CHANGED" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" - name: Flag trivial-only changes id: trivial run: | # Matches PRs that only touch markdown/whitespace, nothing in src/ CODE_TOUCHED=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...HEAD | grep -E '^(src|lib)/' | wc -l) echo "code_touched=$CODE_TOUCHED" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" - name: Apply labels uses: actions/github-script@v7 with: script: | const codeTouched = parseInt('${{ steps.trivial.outputs.code_touched }}'); const linesChanged = parseInt('${{ steps.diffstats.outputs.lines }}'); const labels = []; if (codeTouched === 0 && linesChanged < 5) { labels.push('needs-human-review:low-signal'); } if (linesChanged > 500) { labels.push('needs-human-review:large-diff'); } await github.rest.issues.addLabels({ owner: context.repo.owner, repo: context.repo.repo, issue_number: context.issue.number, labels, }); Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode That low-signal label became our single most useful signal. It doesn't mean "bad PR" automatically — some genuinely good doc fixes are five lines. But it means a human should skim it in under 30 seconds rather than giving it a full review pass. 🧹 The Spam-Specific Checks Beyond trivial-diff detection, we added three checks aimed specifically at Hacktoberfest-pattern spam: 1. No linked issue, on a repo that requires one. We added a CONTRIBUTING.md rule that any non-trivial PR must reference an issue with Closes #123 . A bot comment checks for that pattern and nags once: python import re import sys def has_issue_reference(pr_body: str) -> bool: pattern = r'(closes|fixes|resolves)\s+#\d+' return re.search(pattern, pr_body, re.IGNORECASE) is not None if name == " main ": body = sys.stdin.read() if not has_issue_reference(body): print(":⚠️:No linked issue found. PRs without a linked issue " "may be closed without review during Hacktoberfest.") sys.exit(1) 2. Account age and history heuristics. We don't auto-reject new accounts — plenty of first-time contributors are genuine. But an account created in the last 48 hours, with zero other public activity, submitting a one-line change to an unrelated file, got an automatic spam:likely label for faster human triage. We used the GitHub REST API's created_at field on the user object plus public_repos count as a quick heuristic. It's crude, but it correctly flagged about 70% of what turned out to be spam, with a false-positive rate we were comfortable eating. 3. Duplicate detection on "good first issue" labels. We added a step that checks if an issue already has a linked, open PR before letting a second PR reference the same issue without a comment warning. This alone saved us dozens of redundant reviews. ⚡ The Actual Policy Change: Close Faster, Explain Less The automation only gets you halfway. The bigger shift was cultural: we gave ourselves explicit permission to close PRs with a templated, non-personalized response when they hit spam:likely or low-signal with no linked issue. Before: Thanks so much for your contribution! After reviewing, we feel this change doesn't quite fit the direction of the project because X, Y, Z. We really appreciate you taking the time, and please feel free to look at our other open issues... After: Closing — this PR doesn't include a linked issue and doesn't modify any source files. See CONTRIBUTING.md for what qualifies as a valid Hacktoberfest contribution in this repo. Feel free to reopen with more context. That felt harsh the first few times we used it. But the alternative was maintainers writing a paragraph of empathetic feedback for a PR that added a single period to the README, forty times a week. We reserved the long, kind, detailed response for PRs that were clearly a genuine effort but missed the mark technically — those contributors deserve real feedback, and giving it generously is part of why people come back next year. 📊 What Changed, Numerically After two weeks running this setup: Median time-to-first-response dropped from 36 hours to 4 hours Maintainer triage time dropped roughly 60% Genuine contributor PRs (the ~140 category) got reviewed faster because they weren't queued behind spam We did get a handful of complaints about the terse closing message — a fair trade-off in our view We also opted our repo out of the official Hacktoberfest topic for about a week when spam spiked past a threshold we'd set informally, then opted back in once the automation was tuned. That's an option a lot of maintainers don't realize exists — you can add and remove the hacktoberfest topic from your repo at will, and DigitalOcean's spam-detection on their end does scan for it. 🙋 Where's the Line for You? If you maintain anything with real traffic during October, I'm curious where you draw the line between "could be a genuine first-time contributor" and "this is noise." Do you rely more on automated heuristics like ours, or do you still hand-review everything on principle? And if you've tried bot-based triage — what signal ended up being the most reliable one for you? We're going to keep iterating on this before next October, so I'd genuinely like to steal good ideas from other maintainers' playbooks. title: 🐾 DEV Pet Corner #1: Show Us Your Pets!
summary: Hemapriya Kanagala Posted on Oct 11 • AI-assisted 🐾 DEV Pet Corner #1: Show Us Your Pets! # discuss # community # pets # watercooler Heartwarming community pet photos and stories TL;DR Welcome to DEV Pet Corner , a new weekly series where we take a little break from tech and share our love for animals! Every Sunday, let's share pictures, stories, and memories of our pets, animals we've met, and even the adorable animals we love following on Instagram or elsewhere online. Share as many pictures and links as you'd like! You don't need to own a pet to join in. If animals make you smile, you're welcome here ❤️ 📚 Table of Contents ❤️ Why I'm starting this 🐶 Show us your animal friends! 🐾 See you next Sunday! ❤️ Why I'm starting this I've wanted to start this series for the longest time, but somehow, I kept putting it off. Today, I'm finally doing it! If there's one thing you should know about me, it's that I LOVE PETS. My family had a dog when I was very young, and although we haven't had a pet since, I've always had a soft spot for animals. When I was doing my master's at the University of Oklahoma, I used to take pictures of dogs I came across on campus. Being away from home, those little encounters often made my day. Sometimes, a quick moment with a dog between classes was enough to brighten an otherwise ordinary day. I still have those pictures, and looking back at them brings back some lovely memories ❤️ If you've read my personal reflection posts, you probably know that I often talk about how our health and well-being come first. We're so busy studying, building careers, and working towards our goals that we sometimes forget to slow down and enjoy life along the way. That's what inspired this series. We spend so much time talking about tech here on DEV, and I thought it would be lovely to have a little Sunday tradition where we can share something different, get to know each other beyond our work, and enjoy the simple happiness that animals bring us 💛 🐶 Show us your animal friends! Now, let's get to the fun part! I'd love to see your pets, whether they're the ones waiting for you at home, the ones you grew up with, or the ones who have a special place in your heart. And you don't need to have a pet of your own to join in! Maybe you've met a friendly dog on a walk, spotted a cat in your neighborhood, or come across an animal on campus that made you stop for a moment. Perhaps you follow an adorable animal account on Instagram or have a favorite animal video you keep going back to. If it involves an animal you love or something that makes you smile, I'd love to see it! Share pictures, funny moments, sweet memories, little stories, or links to your favorite animal posts. Share as many pictures as you'd like. There's no limit! If you're sharing someone else's content, please link to the original post and respect the creator's wishes about sharing their work. Don't have anything to share this time? No worries! Just enjoy all the adorable animals in the comments, and join us whenever you'd like. I'll share a picture of a very cute dog I came across at the University of Oklahoma in the comments. I'm happy to finally share a little memory from my time there! 🐾 See you next Sunday! DEV Pet Corner will be here every Sunday 😃 I've wanted to start this series for a long time, and I'm so happy I've finally decided to give it a try. I'm not doing this for views, likes, or comments. I simply love animals, and I thought it would be lovely to have something a little different to look forward to each week. Even if nobody joins in this first edition, I'll still be back next Sunday, and the Sunday after that. Sometimes, an idea is worth trying simply because it means something to you. If you have any ideas for future editions, I'd love to hear them! One little note: I know you all are wonderful and kind, but since this is a little off-topic from our usual tech posts, I just wanted to mention that let's keep the comments friendly, positive, and welcoming to everyone. I'll be checking the comments, and I'm really looking forward to seeing your animal friends, reading your stories, and enjoying all the cuteness with you! Thank you for being here for the very first DEV Pet Corner! See you next Sunday! title: We Built a Blender Render Farm Out of Four Laptops
summary:
Athreya aka Maneshwar Posted on Oct 12 We Built a Blender Render Farm Out of Four Laptops # blender # networking # tailscale # devops Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product. We built a render farm out of four laptops on a Saturday evening. It had a job queue, a web dashboard, a private network spanning three cities' worth of ISPs, and a shared drive that every machine could see. It worked. And then it lost a race against my own laptop, rendering alone. This is the story of that farm, the networking rabbit hole it dropped us into, and why a 130 MB file taking seven minutes to cross the internet ended the whole experiment. Where we left Miles If you have been following along, you know the setup. In part one I rigged a Spider-Man model in Blender without ever having opened Blender before.
