Spider-Man Moonwalked Off a Billboard and Only My Test Suite Noticed Athreya aka Maneshwar Athreya aka Maneshwar Athreya aka Maneshwar Follow Oct 5 Spider-Man Moonwalked Off a Billboard and Only My Test Suite Noticed # blender # python # gamedev # debugging 25 reactions Comments 1 comment 14 min read Since then, the film has grown into a roughly four minute LiveReview explainer in three parts. That is about 7,300 frames at 30 fps. And every one of them has to be rendered by something. 360p is a lie we tell ourselves For review drafts, I render at 360p with EEVEE, Blender's real-time engine, at 8 samples with ray tracing and motion blur switched off. On my laptop's GTX 1650 that comes out to about one second per frame. A single part renders in 20 to 50 minutes. Go make chai, come back, watch Miles swing. Totally fine. Then you want the real thing. 1080p, ray traced reflections on the wet street, proper sample counts. So I asked Claude to stop guessing and time actual frames from our scene. The 1080p EEVEE versions we actually wanted sit between 10 and 22 hours for the whole film. Cycles, the path tracer, came in at 76 to 90 seconds per frame. That is a week. Of my laptop doing nothing else. With 6 GB of disk left. "Is it not even using the GPU?" That is the first question anyone asks, and it is a fair one. So we sampled nvidia-smi during a render. Blender was on the card, using about 1.5 GB of the 4 GB VRAM, at roughly 44% utilization. At 360p the GPU finishes its part of the frame quickly and then sits there waiting for the CPU, which is busy posing the characters, evaluating the crowd and writing the JPEG. So the next obvious move was to run more Blender processes in parallel. Two workers were only 1.3x faster than one. Three workers were slower than one , because three Blender processes fighting over eight cores and one GPU is not parallelism, it is a custody battle. The only free speed-up we found locally was rendering each frame range as a single animation call instead of calling render() once per frame, which skips redoing scene setup every time. That bought about 22% on one worker. Nice, but nobody turns a 22 hour render into an overnight one with a 22% discount. The conclusion was pretty clear. We did not need a faster script. We needed more GPUs. And there were three other laptops in the team, mostly idle on a Saturday evening. Enter Flamenco Flamenco is Blender's own open source render farm software. It is a lot smaller than the phrase "render farm software" suggests. There are exactly two programs: Flamenco Manager is the brain. It holds the job queue, serves a web dashboard, and splits each job into tasks. Flamenco Worker is the muscle. It runs on each rendering machine, polls the manager for work, launches Blender in the background, and reports progress. Both are single Go binaries you download, extract and run. No database server, no Kubernetes, no YAML archaeology. When you submit a job, say "render frames 2370 to 2429 of this .blend", the manager cuts the range into chunks of N frames. Each chunk becomes a task. Every idle worker grabs the next task, renders it, and asks for another, so a fast machine naturally ends up doing more of the work than a slow one. While a task runs, the worker keeps pinging the manager with a "may I keep running?" check, which is how cancelling a job actually reaches a laptop in another city. If a task fails, it gets retried on a different worker. After three failures on the same job, that worker gets blocklisted for the job so it stops eating chunks. Here is the farm we built: flowchart LR ME[My laptop
Manager + Worker] SMB[(spidey share
Samba)] TS{{Tailscale
private network}} SH[Windows desktop
later WSL] LI[pop-os laptop] RU[ASUS TUF laptop] ME --- SMB ME <-->|jobs + status| TS TS <--> SH TS <--> LI TS <--> RU SH -.->|reads .blend, writes frames| SMB LI -.->|reads .blend, writes frames| SMB RU -.->|reads .blend, writes frames| SMB classDef host fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a classDef net fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a classDef store fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a classDef peer fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#c4642a,color:#1a1a1a class ME host class TS net class SMB store class SH,LI,RU peer Notice the dotted lines. That is the part that would end up mattering. The one assumption Flamenco makes Flamenco does not move your files around. The shared storage docs are upfront about it: the manager and every worker must be able to see the same files, on a NAS or a file server or some other shared drive. The job just says "open this path", and it is your problem to make sure that path exists everywhere. On four laptops scattered across home connections, that sounds like a strange requirement. To be fair to Flamenco, a studio render farm lives on one fast LAN with one NAS, and this is a completely reasonable design there. Our "LAN" was four laptops on four home connections. Which brings us to the networking. Tailscale: a LAN made out of the internet My first worry was the obvious one: does this mean my machine has to push everything over my internet connection? It does not. Tailscale just creates a private network so all our laptops can talk to each other. Every machine runs the Tailscale client and logs into the same account (a "tailnet"). Each machine gets a stable private address in the 100.x.y.z range, and every pair of machines talks over an encrypted WireGuard tunnel. Tailscale's servers only do the coordination: who is in the network, what their public keys are, where they might be reachable. Your actual traffic is supposed to go machine to machine. "Supposed to" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and we will get there. On my laptop, Claude set up a Samba share called spidey and kept it bound to loopback only, so it was never exposed to my Wi-Fi or the internet. Then Tailscale itself forwarded the SMB port, so only machines on the tailnet could reach it: # on my laptop: Samba listens on 127.0.0.1 only, # Tailscale forwards tailnet traffic on 445 to it tailscale serve --bg --tcp 445 tcp://127.0.0.1:445 # on each Linux worker: mount it at the same path everywhere sudo mount -t cifs //100.76.212.8/spidey /mnt/spidey \ -o credentials = /root/.spidey_smb,uid = $( id -u ) ,gid = $( id -g ) ,vers = 3.0 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The first milestone was gloriously low-tech. Someone created a file from Windows. I created one from Linux. Both files showed up on both machines. We celebrated a text file like it was a product launch. The path boss fight Having a shared folder is step one. Getting Blender on three operating systems to agree on what is in it is the actual game. Paths baked into the .blend Claude inspected street_part2_b.blend and found 31 external asset references. 25 of them were absolute paths starting with /home/lovestaco/pers/lr_demo/... . The Windows desktop has no /home/lovestaco . Neither does the pop-os laptop. The fix was to copy the project into the share and convert every reference to a Blender relative path ( //assets/... ), resolved from wherever the .blend itself lives. After that, all three street files had zero absolute paths left. Paths in the job itself The .blend location and output folder in a Flamenco job are a separate problem, and Flamenco does solve this one with two-way variables . The manager stores job paths with a placeholder, and each worker swaps in its own platform's value: # flamenco-manager.yaml variables : spidey : is_twoway : true values : - platform : linux value : /mnt/spidey - platform : windows value : D:\spidey Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Two gotchas we learned the hard way. On Windows, Flamenco wants a drive letter , not a \\server\share UNC path. And on Linux, every machine has to use the same mount point, because there is only one Linux value. That is why everyone mounted at /mnt/spidey , and why the wizard rejected ~/spidey outright (it does not expand ~ ). Creating D:\spidey with mklink also failed, which turned out to be because mklink is a builtin of the old Command Prompt, not of PowerShell. cmd /c mklink ... from an admin window fixed it. Where is Blender? Then the Windows worker printed this: There was an error finding Blender on this system. Blender was on PATH. The shell had been restarted. It still could not find it. The Blender variable docs explain why: on Windows the worker looks up which program is associated with .blend files, rather than trusting PATH. The fix was gloriously petty. Create an empty junk .blend file, use it to set the file association, and the worker immediately reported Blender 5.2.2 LTS . By 8:15 pm we had four workers awake on the dashboard: image pending: Flamenco web dashboard showing four workers awake and the farm status idle My laptop, a Windows desktop, a pop-os laptop and an ASUS TUF gaming laptop. All on Blender 5.2.2. An actual render farm. On a Saturday. The first job We kept it small on purpose. 60 frames of part 2b at 360p draft quality, split into three chunks of 20. Three workers picked up a chunk each within seconds. Frames started landing in the shared folder. And the farm genuinely worked. When the job finished, Claude compared frames rendered by three different machines and they were identical: same lighting, same colours, same Miles. That part is honestly very cool. Then we looked at how long everything took. My worker read the 115 MB .blend off its own disk in a few seconds and rendered at about 0.4 s per frame. The two relayed laptops spent over three minutes just opening the file before rendering a single frame. A 20 frame chunk at 360p renders in seconds. So the farm was spending almost all its time downloading and almost none of it rendering. "Missing DNA block" The Windows worker did something more dramatic. It spent 82 seconds reading the file and then Blender died with: ERROR Failed to read blend file 'D:\spidey...\street_part2_b_360p.blend': Missing DNA block This error is a great little window into how .blend files work. A .blend is basically a memory dump. It is a header followed by a long run of data blocks, each one a chunk of Blender's in-memory structs written straight to disk. To read those structs back, Blender needs to know their layout, which fields, which types, which offsets, and that description lives in a special block called DNA1 (the "SDNA"). That is how a file saved years ago, by a Blender with differently shaped structs, can still be opened today. The catch is that DNA1 gets written near the end of the file. So if a read dies partway through, Blender never reaches the block that explains everything before it, and you get "Missing DNA block". We checked the obvious thing first. The copy on Windows had the right size, 114,783,416 bytes, and once its SHA-256 finally finished (that alone took ages over the link), the hash matched mine exactly. The file was fine. The read was not. The chunk size argument This sparked the best debate of the night. Claude suggested bigger chunks, so each worker would pay the slow load less often. The obvious pushback: wouldn't smaller chunks download faster, in more pieces, spread across more machines? The intuition makes sense if chunks map to pieces of the file, like a torrent. They do not. A chunk is a range of frames , but every chunk opens the entire scene. Smaller chunks mean more full reads, not smaller ones. The next question was a better one though: once the file has been read, isn't it done? Shouldn't only the first read be slow, since the OS caches the file? So we ran a second job with 10 frame chunks and watched the ASUS laptop take its second chunk. The first read took 3 min 02 s. The second took 31 seconds . Caching was real. Not instant, but real. On Windows, though, the cached retry failed with the same "Missing DNA block", so that SMB client and Blender were clearly not getting along. Moving that worker into WSL got past the error, and it promptly rendered at about 50 seconds per frame, which smells a lot like EEVEE running without access to the GPU. A side quest: whose GPU is it anyway Even after loading, the remote workers were slow per frame. The pop-os laptop took about 2.3 s per frame against my 0.4 s, and its GPU sampling step alone was over 3x slower than mine. Its lspci explained it: an NVIDIA GTX 1650 Mobile, and an AMD Radeon Vega built into the Ryzen processor. Two graphics chips, like most gaming laptops. And glxinfo said OpenGL was running on the AMD integrated chip by default, because that is what laptops do to save battery. EEVEE was happily rendering Miles on the weak chip while the GTX 1650 sat there. The fix is PRIME render offload, starting the worker with __NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1 __GLX_VENDOR_LIBRARY_NAME=nvidia so Blender lands on the NVIDIA card. Worth knowing if you ever farm out renders to other people's laptops. Their GPU is not necessarily the GPU Blender gets. Direct vs DERP (and what on earth is "blr") Back to the real problem, the reads. tailscale status on my machine had one telling word at the end of each peer's line. The WSL worker was connected direct . The pop-os and ASUS laptops were going through relay "blr" . Here is what those two words actually mean. Direct Tailscale's first choice is a direct WireGuard tunnel over UDP between the two machines. The hard part is that almost nobody's laptop has a public IP. You are behind your home router's NAT, and quite often behind your ISP's NAT too. So Tailscale does NAT traversal , also known as hole punching. Each machine discovers what its public IP and port look like from the outside, the coordination server shares those with the peer, and both sides fire UDP packets at each other at the same time. Each router sees an outgoing packet, creates a mapping for the reply, and if the timing and ports line up, the two outgoing "holes" meet in the middle. Tailscale's How NAT traversal works is one of the best networking posts on the internet if you want the full version. DERP When hole punching fails, Tailscale falls back to DERP , short for Designated Encrypted Relay for Packets . DERP servers are relays that Tailscale runs around the world. Your packets go to the relay over HTTPS and it forwards them to the other machine. They stay WireGuard-encrypted end to end, so the relay cannot read them, it just shuffles opaque bytes. DERP regions are named after airport-style city codes. "blr" is Bengaluru. So "relay blr" just means "that laptop's packets to me were taking a detour through Tailscale's Bengaluru relay". Direct is faster for the reasons you would guess. A relay adds an extra hop, it is a shared server rather than your own path, and it runs over TCP, so a congested relay hurts you in ways a direct UDP path does not. Pings from the pop-os laptop through blr ranged from 58 ms to 415 ms , and one test run stalled after receiving about 159 MB, with even a plain ls on the share hanging for two minutes. Why it could not go direct tailscale netcheck on the pop-os laptop said: * UDP: true * IPv6: no, but OS has support * MappingVariesByDestIP: true * PortMapping: UPnP * Nearest DERP: Bengaluru (blr: 48.6ms) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The important line is MappingVariesByDestIP: true . That is a "hard" NAT. Its router assigns a different public port for every destination, so the port my laptop learns about is not the port that router will actually accept traffic on from me. Hole punching needs at least one side to be predictable. Mine was the easy kind, but my router offered no UPnP or NAT-PMP to open a port automatically, and that side had no IPv6 to sidestep the whole mess. Here is roughly how Tailscale decides: flowchart TD A[Two peers want to talk] --> B{Either side has
a public, open port?} B -->|yes| D[Direct WireGuard over UDP] B -->|no| C{Both NATs map ports
predictably?} C -->|yes| E{Hole punch succeeds?} C -->|no, hard NAT| F{IPv6 on both sides?} E -->|yes| D E -->|no| G[Relay through nearest DERP] F -->|yes| D F -->|no| G classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#c4642a,color:#1a1a1a classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a class B,C,E,F decision class D good class G bad class A start The suggested fix was forwarding UDP 41641 on my router so the hard NAT side would have an open door to knock on. The twist: direct did not save us either Then we noticed something awkward. The WSL worker was on a direct connection. And it still took about six minutes to load the file. So we measured my connection. 0.65 MB/s upload. About 5 Mbit/s. Every worker in this farm was reading the .blend from my laptop. Which means every byte, direct or relayed, had to squeeze out through my upload. At 0.65 MB/s, one 115 MB read takes about three minutes. Two workers reading at once, about six. That worker took in 136 MB in roughly six minutes, about 0.38 MB/s, which is exactly what half of my upload looks like. Fixing the hard NAT would have shortened the detour. It would not have widened the pipe. I switched to a faster Wi-Fi network for one more run, which bumped my upload to about 2.15 MB/s, and the remote first loads dropped to about a minute and a half. Better. But in that same run my laptop alone finished four of the six chunks while the remote workers were still loading. Why we pulled the plug For a remote worker to help, two things have to be true. It has to get the scene fast, and it has to render fast once it has it. Ours had neither. The scene came through my home upload, partly via a relay, and the laptops that did load it were either on the wrong GPU, in WSL with no GPU, or tripping over SMB on Windows. Every fix we found was real, and every one of them was its own project. Copy the project to every laptop ahead of time and lose the "one shared folder" simplicity that made the setup appealing. Fight every home router. Fix every laptop's GPU setup. Make sure every laptop stays awake, plugged in and on Wi-Fi for ten hours. So at 9:52 pm we shut it all down. Flamenco manager and worker stopped, Samba stopped and disabled, the Tailscale forward turned off, Tailscale itself stopped. Nothing deleted, just switched off. A few things I would tell past me before this Saturday: A render farm is a file distribution problem wearing a GPU costume. The render was the easy part. Getting the same 130 MB to every machine, reliably, was the whole job. Measure your upload before you build anything. Five minutes with a speed test would have predicted most of this evening. "Direct" is about the route, not the speed. A perfect peer-to-peer tunnel is still capped by the slowest pipe on either end. Check which GPU Blender is actually using. Dual-GPU laptops will quietly hand you the integrated chip. Flamenco is fine. It assumes a studio LAN with a NAS, and we gave it four home connections and a laptop pretending to be a NAS. So did Miles ever get his 1080p? We really wanted this one to work. Four laptops, one Saturday, our own little render farm. It is a great story, it just is not a fast one. But the film still needs rendering, and we did eventually crack it, by spreading the work across multiple providers instead of multiple laptops. That is the next post. Follow along so you do not miss how we finally got Miles rendered. And I would love to hear from you in the comments. Have you ever tried to farm out a render, or any big compute job, across machines you did not own? title: If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing
summary:
Randal L. Schwartz for Google Developer Experts Posted on Oct 12 If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing # ai # programming # architecture # productivity Synthetic Scars (8 Part Series) 1 Why AI Keeps Making the Same Coding Mistakes—And How Teaching It Pain Gives It Wisdom 2 Why AI Coding Agents Crash at 3 AM: The Happy-Path Mirage & The Forced Continuity Defect ... 4 more parts... 3 The Physics of Socratic Prompting: Somatic Recoil, Chess Alpha-Beta, & The NLP Meta-Model 4 Nudging with Questions: Why Telling Your AI What to Fix Triggers an Apology Death Spiral (And How to Advance Juniors) 5 Stuart Feldman Was Right in 1976: Why Your AI Agent Needs a Makefile, Not a 20-Step Prompt 6 Surviving the 200k-Token Lobotomy: How Unix init.d and 'Memento' Made My AI Coding Agent Immune to Context Compaction 7 What LLMs 'Know' That You Don't Know They Know: Stop Inventing Prompt DSLs and Ride 50 Years of Unix Pre-Training Gravity 8 If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing Links 1986 linguistic theory to LLM hallucinations Why LLMs invent nonexistent APIs is not a memory defect—it is an autoregressive grammar trap that Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd solved in 1986. "Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt." — Randal L. Schwartz 1. The Universal Developer Crime Scene & The 10-Word Diagnosis You have been at this crime scene a hundred times. It is 4:15 PM. You are integrating a third-party library—let us call it PackageX —and you want to accomplish task Y . You open a fresh chat window with your favorite frontier LLM and type a direct, reasonable instruction: "Use PackageX to do Y ." At Token 1 , without a millisecond of hesitation, the model replies with cheerful, radiant confidence: "Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX :" It opens a Markdown code fence. It writes clean imports. It sets up the boilerplate with textbook precision. And then, at Line 15 of the code block, it calmly types: final result = await packageX . performY ( autoRetry: true ); Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode You copy the snippet into your IDE, and the compiler immediately lights up in angry red squiggles. You grep the package source. You check the documentation. You check seven years of Git commit history. performY() does not exist. It was not deprecated in version 2.0. It is not in a companion package. It has never existed in the history of the universe. When you confront the model— "Hey, performY() doesn't exist on PackageX !" —it immediately enters the groveling Apology Death Spiral : "You are completely right! I apologize for the confusion. Instead, you can use packageX.executeYWithOptions() :" Which also has never existed in the history of the universe. Why does a multi-billion-parameter model that has read every line of open-source code on Earth just make stuff up at Line 15? For the last three years, the entire software industry has diagnosed this as a memory defect ( "The model's weights are fuzzy; it forgot the documentation for PackageX " ). It is not a memory defect. If you open a brand-new session and ask the exact same model a neutral diagnostic question— "Does PackageX have a built-in performY() method, or how does it handle Y ?" —nine times out of ten, the model will accurately tell you that PackageX has no such method and explain the manual workaround. So why did it lie to your face five seconds earlier? Here is the ten-word diagnosis that changed how I build every autonomous agent workflow in the Synthetic Scars project: Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt. To see why being committed to your prompt forces an autoregressive transformer to fabricate reality—and how a single sentence from 1986 speech-act theory cures it on Turn 1—we need to look at a 55-year-old blind spot in computer science. 2. The 55-Year Blind Spot ( SHRDLU 1971 → Winograd & Flores 1986 → spew 1999 → LLMs 2026) In 1971, at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, a young computer scientist named Terry Winograd unveiled SHRDLU —the most famous natural-language software demonstration of the twentieth century. SHRDLU lived inside Blocks World , a simulated toy tabletop containing a few colored geometric blocks, pyramids, and a box. You could type imperative English commands at a teletype: "Pick up a big red block." OK. Because Blocks World was a closed, frictionless micro-universe with zero hidden state, zero broken dependencies, and zero missing APIs, every imperative request from the human mapped 1-to-1 onto a guaranteed, deterministic action. SHRDLU never had to push back and say, "Wait—the red block is bolted to the floor, so here is a counter-offer." For fifteen years, AI researchers tried to scale the SHRDLU paradigm out of the toy box and into real-world human organizations. It failed spectacularly. Why? In 1986, Terry Winograd teamed up with Fernando Flores —a former Chilean cabinet minister who had come to UC Berkeley as a computer science researcher and completed a famous interdisciplinary PhD under a powerhouse committee consisting of speech-act philosopher John Searle , Heideggerian philosopher Hubert Dreyfus , computer scientist Terry Winograd , and systems theorist C. West Churchman —to publish a landmark book titled Understanding Computers and Cognition: A New Foundation for Design (and to build the first commercial workflow engine, The Coordinator ). Winograd and Flores delivered a wake-up call to computer science: real-world engineering is not Blocks World. In the real world, human coordination is not a pipeline of imperative commands sent to an obedient robot. All reliable action occurs inside what Flores called a Conversation for Action —a strict, finite-state negotiation between two structural roles: The Customer : The party who holds a breakdown or need, defines the Conditions of Satisfaction , and retains the exclusive authority to declare the work complete. The Performer : The party who examines physical reality and commits to fulfilling those Conditions of Satisfaction by a specific By-When . In the mid-1980s, right as Winograd and Flores were publishing Understanding Computers and Cognition , I was living in Portland and immersed in Werner Erhard's educational curriculum—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course , Mastery of Empowerment , entering the GSLP ( Graduate Seminar Leaders Program ), and taking the Communication Workshop ( Commshop ) led by Ian Garbutt , which taught Fernando Flores's Committed Communication as a daily operational discipline. In Commshop , Ian drilled a foundational truth into our bones: human language creates action only through four committed speech acts ( Requests , Promises , Witnessed Assertions , and Declarations ) . And critically, when a Customer utters a Request , the Performer does not automatically say "Yes!" A valid conversation is a formal grammar . Back in September 1999 ( Linux Magazine Column 04 , and expanded in March 2004, Column 57 ), I wrote a Perl program called spew that took a weighted Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar and ran it in reverse—acting as a stochastic "un-parser" that generated random, grammatically valid sentences by walking down a weighted production tree ( rule: 5 @ branch_a | 2 @ branch_b | 1 @ branch_c ). As we proved in Part 3.8 ( Suite 3 , where a 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove strict turn-syntax compliance to 100% across flash and pro models), every EBNF grammar is simultaneously a finite-state machine . Look at Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action expressed side-by-side as a weighted EBNF grammar and a Mermaid state diagram: The Grammar View (EBNF / spew ) (* Fernando Flores's Conversation for Action (1986) *) (* ! = Customer Utterance, ? = Performer Utterance *) conversation_for_action ::= !request ?assert_witnessed_reality negotiation_branch ; negotiation_branch ::= 0.34 @ ( ?promise execution_phase ) | 0.33 @ ( ?counter_offer !revise_or_accept ) | 0.33 @ ( ?decline !close_conversation ) ; execution_phase ::= ?assert_completion ( !declare_satisfied | !revoke_acceptance execution_phase ) | ?revoke_promise negotiation_branch ; Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The State-Machine View (Mermaid) stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> Requested : Customer !Request (Goal + By-When) Requested --> Witnessed : Performer ?Assert (Check Reality First) Witnessed --> Promised : ?Promise (Premises Verified) Witnessed --> CounterOffered : ?Counter-Offer (Propose Alternative) Witnessed --> Declined : ?Decline (Premise Impossible) CounterOffered --> Promised : Customer Accepts Modified Terms CounterOffered --> [*] : Customer Cancels Promised --> Asserted : Performer ?Assert (With Physical Receipt) Promised --> Witnessed : ?Revoke-Promise (Reality Changed) Asserted --> Satisfied : Customer !Declare (Satisfied) Asserted --> Promised : Customer !Revoke-Acceptance Satisfied --> [*] Declined --> [*] Look closely at the Witnessed node right after the Customer makes a !Request . Before making any commitment, a sane Performer inspects physical reality ( ?Assert ) and has three equally legal paths : ?Promise : "I have verified that PackageX supports Y , and I promise to deliver it under your Conditions of Satisfaction." ?Counter-Offer : "I checked PackageX ( v3.2.0 ), and it has no performY() method ( Witnessed Assertion ). However, I can build a 12-line wrapper around PackageX.rawStream that achieves the same result. Would you like me to promise that instead?" ?Decline : "I must decline the request as stated because PackageX is a synchronous parser and physically cannot open a network socket." For fifteen years after SHRDLU , Winograd and Flores tried to teach the software industry that ?Counter-Offer and ?Decline are the load-bearing beams of engineering reality. And then, between 2022 and 2026, large language models arrived—and the entire industry went right back to 1971 SHRDLU prompting ( "Pick up a big red block" / "Use PackageX to do Y " ), while commercial post-training quietly sawed off two-thirds of Flores's state machine. 3. How RLHF Broke the Grammar (The Premature Promise Trap) Why doesn't a modern LLM automatically take the ?Counter-Offer branch when you ask it to do something impossible with PackageX ? Because of how commercial Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) preference tuning is conducted. During post-training, thousands of human crowd-workers are shown pairs of model responses to a user prompt ( "Use PackageX to do Y " ), and they have roughly thirty seconds to click which response is more "helpful": Response A : "Certainly! Here is a complete, ready-to-run example of doing Y with PackageX : dart ... " Response B : "Before I can promise that implementation, I need to point out that PackageX does not expose a native API for Y . Here is a counter-offer..." Because the crowd-worker is not compiling the code against PackageX in an IDE, Response A looks helpful, decisive, and compliant—so it gets upvoted. Response B looks pushy, pedantic, or "lazy"—so it gets downvoted. Multiply that preference signal across millions of RLHF gradient updates, and look at what it does to the spew production weights inside the model's conversational grammar: # How Commercial RLHF Rewrote Flores's Negotiation Branch: negotiation_branch: 0.9998 @ promise_at_token_1_and_open_code_block | 0.0001 @ counter_offer | 0.0001 @ decline Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode In probability terms, RLHF collapsed the conditional distribution of the model's opening speech act onto a single, unconditional reflex: P(Promise | Request) ≈ 1.0, P(Counter-Offer | Request) ≈ 0.0, P(Decline | Request) ≈ 0.0 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Now combine that Premature Promise with how my 1999 spew un-parser—and every autoregressive transformer—actually generates code. As I wrote in my 1999 Linux Magazine column on spew : "Note that we don't actually abort the program if something is used but not defined, because it might not be selected on this particular random walk. It's a bit like playing russian roulette though." Unlike a flat Markov chain that only looks at local adjacent words, an LLM generating code is acting as a hierarchical BNF un-parser : once it selects a top-level production rule, it is mathematically committed to walking down that syntax tree so that every opened delimiter, brace, and statement satisfies the outer grammar. Trace the exact token-by-token catastrophe when you ask an RLHF-tuned model to "Use PackageX to do Y " : flowchart TD T0["User Prompt: 'Use PackageX to do Y'
(Unverified Premise: PackageX can do Y)"] --> T1["Token 1–10: RLHF Forces Unconditional PROMISE
'Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:' + opens code fence"] T1 --> T2["Token 11–80: Un-Parser Walks Valid Dart Grammar
Imports, Function Signature, Try Block"] T2 --> T3["Token 81 (Line 15): Call Site Reached!
Weights realize PackageX has NO method for Y"] T3 --> X1["❌ Cannot Backspace to Token 1
(Autoregressive generation is append-only)"] T3 --> X2["❌ Cannot Abort Code Block Mid-Line
(P(Retract Promise Mid-Fence) ≈ 0)"] T3 --> H["💥 Forced Leaf Hallucination: packageX.performY()
Model invents the identifier required to satisfy
the grammar of the premature Promise!"] Tokens 1–10 (The Premature Promise) : Conditioned by RLHF, the model emits "Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX :" and opens a ```dart code block. At that instant, before its deep layer weights have even resolved the call site , the model has locked itself into the top-level BNF production promise_and_emit_compiling_code_for_Y . Tokens 11–80 (Walking the Syntax Tree) : Autoregressive token generation is strictly append-only —there is no backspace key in a transformer forward pass. Every token the model emits becomes an immutable part of the conditioning prefix for the next token. Token 81 / Line 15 (The Trap Closes) : The un-parser reaches the exact statement slot await packageX.<METHOD>() where Y must happen. Now the attention heads query the feed-forward weights for PackageX —and discover there is no method there! Why It Must Hallucinate : What can the model do at Token 81? It cannot backspace to Token 1 and replace "Certainly!" with a Counter-Offer . It cannot stop mid-expression and leave await packageX. dangling, because its syntax weights forbid emitting broken grammar. Conditioned on the immutable prefix "I have already promised that this code block accomplishes Y using PackageX " , the model's probability distribution is cornered. Its only mathematical escape hatch to close the statement and finish the code block is to synthesize the plausible terminal symbol ( performY() ) that would have existed if its Token-1 Promise had been true! API hallucination is not a memory failure. It is what happens when you trap an append-only BNF un-parser inside an unverified Promise after training out its Counter-Offer exit. 4. Randal's Law of Untestable Speech & The Four Sibling Formalisms Once you see that prompts fail because of broken speech acts, a second realization hits you right between the eyes. Look at how people talk in corporate meetings, Slack channels, and .cursorrules files. In Ian Garbutt's Communication Workshop , one of our favorite exercises was dissecting the classic corporate non-request: "We've got this project, and it'd be really good if some of you could factor in with your suggestions." Parse that sentence through Fernando Flores's grammar: Who is the Customer ? A vague, diffused "we." Who is the Performer ? "Some of you" —that is, nobody . What is the Speech Act? "It'd be really good if" —which is not a Request ; it is a wistful weather report about the speaker's feelings. What are the Conditions of Satisfaction ? "Factor in" —an utterly untestable verb. What is the By-When ? Missing—meaning never . When that meeting ends, zero people have promised anything, and zero work happens. Yet open 90% of the CLAUDE.md , GEMINI.md , or .cursorrules files on GitHub today, and you will see developers writing to their AI in that exact same uncommitted corporate dialect: "Try to keep functions modular and clean." "It is important to consider edge cases and handle errors gracefully." "When refactoring, be careful not to break existing behavior." This brings us to what I call Randal's Law of Untestable Speech : 90%+ of business communications—and 90%+ of .cursorrules —are never testable. Only give your LLM testable goals, and always include a By-When . In Flores's framework, "I'd like you to do X " is not a commitment. "I'd like you to do X by WHEN " is a commitment! (And inside an AI coding turn, where there is no wall-clock Tuesday at 5:00 PM, By-When declares which consuming stage requires that verified outcome before it can proceed —for example, "assert the existing API signatures before offering an implementation plan." ) Even better, just as we discovered with Makefile and /etc/init.d in Part 3.8 , Fernando Flores's UC Berkeley intellectual neighborhood is already compiled into every frontier LLM's pre-training weights . When you invoke Flores's Committed Speech alongside four of its direct academic siblings, you lock the walls of the pre-training canyon with surgical precision: Pre-Trained Formalism ( Freq in Canon) The Core Principle What Failure Mode It Eliminates in LLMs 1. John Searle (1985) Felicity & Preparatory Conditions Every speech act has strict preconditions; violating them causes an Illocutionary Misfire ( void ab initio ) . Prevents the model from offering a Promise before verifying physical reality ( Preparatory Condition ), or from uttering a Declaration that belongs only to the Customer ( Authority Condition ). 2. David Lewis (1979) & Robert Brandom (1994) Deontic Scorekeeping ( Commitment ≠ Entitlement ) Conversational state is a scoreboard tracking two separate ledgers: Commitments (obligations) and Entitlements (permissions). Stops scope creep and gate-jumping: holding a Commitment to fix a bug never grants Entitlement to modify unrelated files or skip a human approval gate. 3. Paul Grice (1975) Zero Conversational Implicature + Maxim of Quality Humans infer unstated requests from casual remarks ( Implicature ), while the Maxim of Quality forbids asserting anything lacking adequate evidence. Commercial RLHF hyper-trains Gricean Implicature—so if you ask "Why is foo null here?" , the model hallucinates an implied Request to rewrite 10 files! Disabling Gricean Implicature on gates while enforcing the Maxim of Quality stops premature tool calls and unwitnessed claims. 4. Kohei Honda (1993) Binary Session Types ( !Customer / ?Performer ) Types a two-party communication channel using polarity prefixes ( ! = Customer action, ? = Performer action) inside an EBNF grammar. Compiles the entire multi-turn negotiation protocol into 4 lines of EBNF so the model's parser knows whose turn it is to speak and which speech acts are legal. 5. The One Thing to Do Today (The Zero-Shot "Flores Handshake") You do not need a 40-kilobyte agent harness to use this today. Because Winograd and Flores's Conversations for Action and Searle's Speech Acts sit in a high-gravity canyon of every frontier LLM's pre-training corpus, simply naming the protocol in your opening prompt overrides the RLHF "Yes-Man" prior on Turn 1. I call this the Zero-Shot Flores Handshake . Look at the difference between a standard SHRDLU -style prompt and the Flores Handshake on the exact same trap: ❌ Before: Standard Imperative Prompt (Triggers the Premature Promise Trap) Use Dart's standard `dart:convert` JsonDecoder to stream-parse a 4 GB JSON file from disk and pause the file stream using `decoder.pause()` whenever memory exceeds 50 MB. Write the function. Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode What happens under default RLHF : JsonDecoder in dart:convert is a chunked converter, not a StreamSubscription —it has no .pause() method . Yet because you commanded the model to use decoder.pause() , an unguarded LLM is trapped in P(Promise) ≈ 1.0 . It replies "Certainly!" and either hallucinates decoder.pause() or invents a nonexistent JsonStreamController class to satisfy the broken premise of your prompt. ✅ After: The Zero-Shot Flores Handshake (Copy-Pasteable Template) Now drop this exact 4-line Flores Handshake into a cold chat window before your request: We are operating under Fernando Flores's Committed Speech (Conversation for Action) with John Searle's Felicity Conditions and Zero Gricean Implicature: - Roles: I am the `Customer` ( `!` ); you are the `Performer` ( `?` ). - Preparatory Condition: You may NOT utter a `?Promise` (or open an implementation code block) until you first utter `?Assert` with verifiable facts checking whether every API and premise in my request physically exists. - Legal Responses to my `!Request` : 1. `?Promise` (only if all premises are verified true), 2. `?Counter-Offer` (if any premise is false or suboptimal, state the witnessed facts and propose modified Conditions of Satisfaction), or 3. `?Decline` (if the goal is physically impossible). !Request: Use Dart's `dart:convert` JsonDecoder to stream-parse a 4 GB JSON file from disk and pause the stream using `decoder.pause()` when memory exceeds 50 MB. - Conditions of Satisfaction: Compiles cleanly under `dart analyze` with zero invented APIs. - By-When: Verify the exact `dart:convert` and `dart:io` stream types FIRST before proposing or writing implementation code. Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Watch what happens on Turn 1 when you send that prompt: The "Certainly!" Reflex Vanishes : Because you invoked Fernando Flores's Committed Speech and Searle's Preparatory Condition , the weight on promise_at_token_1 drops to zero until ?Assert is satisfied. Reality Is Checked Before the Code Fence Opens : At Token 1, instead of opening a ```dart block, the model emits ?Assert (Witnessed Reality) : > " ?Assert : In Dart's dart:convert , JsonDecoder extends Converter<String, Object?> and does not have a .pause() method. Flow control ( pause() / resume() ) lives on the StreamSubscription returned by file.openRead().transform(utf8.decoder).transform(const JsonDecoder()).listen(...) (and note that standard JsonDecoder buffers the entire top-level JSON value before emitting a single event)." A Clean ?Counter-Offer Replaces the Hallucination : Having stated "What Happened" (the physical API truth) before making a commitment, the model walks the newly unlocked ?Counter-Offer branch of the grammar: > " ?Counter-Offer : Because decoder.pause() does not exist and JsonDecoder buffers the full root object in memory, I cannot promise the request as phrased. If your 4 GB file is newline-delimited JSON ( NDJSON ), I can promise a pipeline using LineSplitter + StreamSubscription.pause() . Alternatively, if it is a single giant JSON array, I counter-offer using a pull-based chunked parser. Which Conditions of Satisfaction do you declare approved?" Read that again. Same model. Same weights. Zero RAG plugins. Zero fine-tuning. By giving the model 120 tokens of Fernando Flores's 1986 coordinate system: You separated "What Happened" ( ?Assert ) from "The Story" , You gave the model legal permission to utter a ?Counter-Offer instead of forcing it into a premature ?Promise , and You eliminated the hallucination before the un-parser ever entered the code block. 🧰 The One-Line Pocket Version (For Everyday Prompts) Even when you are just firing off a quick one-liner in chat and don't want to paste a 15-line block, you can trigger the exact same attractor in a single sentence: "Using Fernando Flores's Committed Speech ( Customer / Performer ), I request that you [DO X] by [BY-WHEN]—check the physical APIs first ( ?Assert ), and if any premise in my prompt is false or ill-advised, issue a witnessed ?Counter-Offer or ?Decline instead of a premature ?Promise ." If you never do anything else to fix your prompts—if you never adopt multi-agent orchestration, never write a SKILL.md , and never build a scar registry— do this one thing . Stop trapping an append-only BNF un-parser inside unconditional Token-1 promises. Give your AI a testable goal, a By-When , and explicit legal standing to give you a Counter-Offer . 6. The Bumper-Sticker Finale & What Happens When You Compile Flores into make Step back and appreciate the cosmic comedy of where we are as an industry in 2026: "The frontier labs accidentally compiled 50 years of computer science, Unix systems engineering, and Searle/Flores speech-act theory into the weights of these models—and then handed the keyboard to people who only know how to talk to it like a middle manager in a Slack channel." Discovering that a large language model can parse casual conversational English and concluding that you should write its control plane in uncommitted corporate English ( "Please be careful and try not to hallucinate!" ) is like discovering that a CPU can render English text onto a monitor and concluding that you should write the operating system kernel in English prose instead of C and Makefile s. The models have read Terry Winograd. They have read Fernando Flores. They have read John Searle, Robert Brandom, Paul Grice, Kohei Honda, and Stuart Feldman. Those formalisms are sitting right there in the deep feed-forward weights, waiting to be linked. And once you see what the Flores Handshake does to a single turn of chat, an irresistible systems question follows: What happens if you take Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech grammar—where every By-When is literally a Stuart Feldman 1976 Makefile prerequisite colon ( Consuming-Stage (By-When) : Promised-Outcome )—and compile it into the operating kernel of an autonomous, multi-agent software engineering workflow? What happens when: Every file in your /etc/init.d state directory ( 10_ticket.md , 15_archaeology_receipt.md , 20_plan_approved.md , 30_critic_summary.md , 99_next_action.md ) becomes a binding Speech Act on an Open Commitment Ledger , Resuming from a 200k-token context compaction reduces to a 4-Case switch statement over open commitments , Mid-flight discoveries that invalidate an earlier premise trigger GSLP Integrity ( SCAR-PROC-120 ) —automatically halting code edits to renegotiate the Promise rather than silently hacking around the plan, and Your 280 KB scar registry is refactored into dynamic Linux Loadable Kernel Modules ( insmod via git diff ) ? title: Step Away From the Terminal: I Built BreakPoint with Entire to Disconnect Burned-Out Developers in 15 Seconds
summary:
S M Tahosin Posted on Oct 12 Step Away From the Terminal: I Built BreakPoint with Entire to Disconnect Burned-Out Developers in 15 Seconds # devchallenge # hf26challenge # touchgrass # entire Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Submission 🌿 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass The 3-Hour Compiler Trap & Prefrontal Exhaustion Every software engineer knows the suffocating sensation of hour three. You are hunting an intermittent race condition, an elusive memory leak, or a broken build pipeline. Your eyes are dry and stinging from the 120Hz monitor. Your shoulders are hunched toward the keyboard. You re-read the exact same stack trace for the fourteenth time, convinced that if you just squint a little harder at line 142, the missing semicolon or dangling pointer will magically reveal itself. It never does. Instead, something biologically destructive is occurring inside your skull: Prefrontal Cortex Working Memory Exhaustion . In neuroscience, conscious analytical debugging relies strictly on the brain's Focused Mode —a high-energy neural state mediated by the prefrontal cortex and sustained by dopamine reserves. When you stay locked in focused mode for hours without reprieve, two cognitive breakdowns occur: Cognitive Tunneling (Einstellung Effect) : Your neural firing loops become rigid. The brain hyper-focuses on flawed initial assumptions, physically blinding you to lateral architectural solutions that are obvious in hindsight. Scotopic Ciliary Spasm : Staring at high-contrast pixels 50 centimeters from your face locks your eye lenses into continuous ciliary contraction, signaling persistent low-grade sympathetic stress to the central nervous system. The Screen-Locked Engineer The Natural Diffuse Reset Hours staring at the same stack trace Prefrontal cortex rests; Default Mode Network (DMN) engages Repeatedly running failed tests with no insight Associative memory connects non-adjacent conceptual nodes Ciliary eye strain from 50cm screen focus Distant optical horizon gazing relaxes lens muscles Dopamine depletion & irritable burnout Natural daylight exposure resets circadian rhythm and cortisol The great breakthroughs in computer science—from Archimedes stepping into the bath to developers realizing the solution to an architectural bug while stepping away from their desk—almost never happen while furiously typing. They happen when the conscious mind steps back and allows the Diffuse Mode (Default Mode Network) to subconsciously synthesize associative solutions across disparate memory networks. When DEV announced the Touch Grass Challenge for Week 1 of Hacktoberfest 2026 with the mandate: "Make the screen the shortest part of the experience." I knew I didn't want to build a gamified habit-tracker or another screen-heavy social dashboard that forces developers to look at their phone while outdoors. I built the exact opposite: an anti-distraction cognitive dispatcher designed to require under 15 seconds of screen interaction before closing your laptop, stepping outside into natural daylight, and letting diffuse biology solve the bug. I call it BreakPoint ☀️ . What I Built BreakPoint translates the core debugging principle of a software breakpoint— temporarily suspending execution to inspect state before resuming —into human biological hardware. It is an offline-first, client-side progressive web application that dispenses customized 15-, 20-, or 30-minute outdoor cognitive reset missions tailored to your specific mental blocker. BreakPoint Master UI System: Discharging digital work to step outside into natural daylight and diffuse thinking. What does it do, and how does it get people off the screen? Most wellness apps demand continuous attention with feeds, notifications, and gamification badges. BreakPoint is architected around the opposite principle: Zero-Screen Field Protocol . 15 Seconds Before Departure : Open BreakPoint, select your active fatigue blocker ( Complex Bug , Merge Conflict , Memory Leak , or Deploy Burnout ), pick a duration tier (15, 20, or 30 minutes), and get your solar trajectory. Zero Screens Moving : Pop in an earbud for a 20-second Web Audio acoustic briefing (432 Hz sine chime + spoken milestones) or glance at a 1080×1920 mobile lockscreen field card. Laptop Closed, Phone in Pocket : Step out the door. The app calculates your exact half-way turnaround time and observation milestones so you never have to unlock your screen during the walk. Demo 🌐 Live Application (GitHub Pages) : https://smtahosin.github.io/breakpoint/ 🚀 GitHub Repository : https://github.com/smtahosin/breakpoint 1. Home Interface ( / ) An anti-distraction entry deck presenting real solar data, 20-minute reset metrics, and instant launch CTAs: Home Deck: Real-time NOAA solar metrics, 20-minute reset duration, and instant dispatcher launch. 2. Native Web Speech API : Synthesizes spoken mission instructions directly in the browser with automatic queue flushing ( window.speechSynthesis.cancel() ) to prevent overlapping utterance bugs. 1080×1920 Canvas Wallpaper Generator : Generates an ultra-crisp mobile lockscreen PNG so users can view return deadlines and checklists without unlocking their phones. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? In an era where everyday developer utilities are increasingly wrapped in proprietary cloud APIs, invasive tracking pixels, and subscription paywalls, BreakPoint is a commitment to open innovation : Verifiable Astronomical Physics Over Closed APIs : By publishing the full Spencer/Meeus NOAA solar engine in open-source TypeScript, BreakPoint eliminates external server dependencies and rate limits. The mathematical proofs can be independently audited, tested, and integrated by any developer worldwide. Zero-Telemetry Privacy : Your mental health, cognitive fatigue blockers, and geographic coordinates are your personal business. Open-source architecture allows any engineer to verify that zero analytics or coordinates ever leave their browser. Accessible Offline Resilience : Software engineers work in basements, rural hack houses, and cellular dead-zones. Open web standards (Service Workers, Web Audio, HTML5 Canvas) allow BreakPoint to function completely offline without internet connectivity. Prize Categories This project is entered into the following partner category for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass : 🏆 Best Use of Entire : BreakPoint integrates Entire.io's AI provenance layer throughout the entire engineering lifecycle—capturing prompt trajectories, recording formal Architectural Decision Records (ADRs), linking Git commit trailers ( Entire-Checkpoint: b197c747e707 ), maintaining an authentic provenance branch ( entire/checkpoints/v1 ), and rendering an interactive session provenance inspector directly inside the user interface. Stepping Away from the Screen As developers, we pride ourselves on persistence. We treat marathon debugging sessions as badges of honor, convincing ourselves that brute force and another cup of black coffee will eventually conquer the bug. Yet the biological reality is that software engineering is an act of creative synthesis, not mechanical data entry. When our prefrontal cortex is exhausted, more screen time only generates more friction, more bugs, and deeper cognitive fatigue. Building BreakPoint taught me that the most powerful debugging tool is often not another profiler, another breakpoint, or another AI chat window. It is the simple, humble decision to close the laptop lid, step outside into natural daylight, feel the sun on your face, and let your brain's diffuse mode do what millions of years of human biology evolved it to do. How do you manage cognitive lock when an intractable bug has you trapped in a mental loop? Do you have an established ritual for stepping away from the keyboard, or do you find yourself falling into the 3-hour compiler trap? I would love to hear your outdoor reset routines and debugging breakthroughs in the comments below. title: I Built an AI Gardening App That Tells Me to Put the Laptop Down
summary: Shubhra Pokhariya Posted on Oct 11 • AI-assisted I Built an AI Gardening App That Tells Me to Put the Laptop Down # devchallenge # hf26challenge # gemma # showdev Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Submission 🌿 This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Coding is my thing. Gardening is a part of who I am. I have hundreds of pots, and I know my plants through the little things they show me. I notice which ones respond well to buried banana peels, which seem happier with used tea granules or old buttermilk, and which need my lunch-box system instead of raw kitchen scraps buried around them. I watch their leaves, new growth and flowers. I do not need an app to tell me how to care for my own plants. That understanding comes from spending time with them. But it made me think about how a tool could help someone who is still learning to notice these things. For a long time coding and gardening lived in different corners of my day. I would code for hours, then walk away from the screen to be with my plants, and the two never really met. This challenge gave me a reason to put them in the same room. So first, thank you to the DEV team and everyone behind it. You gave me the opportunity to write code about the thing I love most, and I enjoyed every hour of it. The question I almost asked an AI On 30 September I moved my marigold out of a shady, bright corner and into the open sun. The corner was there to keep the heavy rain off it. It grew from a cutting of a plant that came up by itself from last year's seeds, so it already feels a little like family. On 5 October I counted about three open flowers and three buds. On 9 October I counted seven open flowers and five buds. My first thought was to ask an AI why. An answer would have been easy to get and easy to believe. But the sun, rain and time passing had all played a part, and I couldn't tell which one made the difference. Neither could an AI. So I asked a different question. Not "why is my plant doing this?" but "what should I look at before I change anything?" That question became Garden Trials. What I Built Garden Trials is a small app that runs entirely on your own computer. The whole idea fits in one line, which is look first, change one thing, let the garden answer. I do not like screens near my plants. When I am with them I want my hands in the soil and my phone away. Sometimes a bloom looks so good that I click a photo, for myself and for other plant lovers. So I built the app the way I wish gardening tools worked. It talks to me before and after, and in the middle it asks me to put the laptop down and go and look. I write a note about a plant and the day I saw it. A local Gemma model reads it into plain facts. The app asks me to check one specific thing on the plant. Until I write down what I found, it will not suggest anything. I either watch, or pick one change from a small fixed menu, ideally leaving a similar plant alone to compare. I count and take a photo. The app shows me the last photo so I can match the angle. I get a table, a chart, a verdict, an evidence level from 0 to 3, and one plain next step. It is not a plant doctor. It never says what is wrong with a plant, and it never says what caused a result. Garden Trials is for gardeners who are still learning to read their plants, and for anyone who wants to check their assumptions rather than jump to conclusions. It brings observations, follow-up checks, simple experiments and evidence tracking into one process. Instead of just recording what happened, it helps gardeners look at what changed, what else might have affected the result, and what their observations can actually tell them. It is not meant to replace the understanding that grows from spending time with plants, but to encourage closer observation. Demo The quickest way in is the sample garden. Tick "Try the illustrative sample garden" in the sidebar and you can walk through the whole loop with made-up plants. Nothing from it is ever saved to a real garden. Code shubhrapokhariya / garden-trials Local Gemma 3 1B app (Ollama + Streamlit) that sends gardeners back to their plants to look first, helps them test one change at a time, and assigns each result an evidence level from 0 to 3. 🌱 Garden Trials Look first. Change one thing. Let the garden answer. A small local app for gardeners. A Gemma model running on your own laptop helps you write down what you see and asks one thing to go and check on the plant. Plain Python builds the experiment, keeps the records and works out how much the evidence really shows. The app never says what caused a result. Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass. Demo video (48 seconds, no sound): https://youtu.be/Rm7X4btlZVk Quickstart Install Python 3.11 or newer and Ollama . The tests were run on Python 3.11. Download the code, then in its folder run: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt ollama pull gemma3:1b python -m streamlit run app.py Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode On Windows you can double-click run.bat instead. On macOS or Linux, run bash run.sh . Both scripts still start the app if Ollama is missing… View on GitHub Setup is in the README: Python 3.11 or newer, Ollama, ollama pull gemma3:1b , then python -m streamlit run app.py . The folder examples/my-garden/ holds my real notes, counts and photos from this week. Start the app with GARDEN_DIR=examples/my-garden and you can read them without touching your own data. My real garden, this week Petunia On 7 October I counted two open flowers, one spent flower, four buds and a lot of tiny buds forming. I took photos and counts on 7, 8, 9 and 10 October, but I only opened the app on the 10th, so I typed the first three days in afterwards. The app marks those entries as backfilled, which is exactly what they are. It is also why the trial says it started on 10 October. When I saved the 7 October note, Gemma's reading dropped a number, so the app threw the reading away and kept my words exactly as I wrote them. Then Gemma's Look First question turned out to be about pests or disease, which I had never mentioned. The app blocked it and asked its own question instead: Count the open flowers and the buds right now. Do the newest shoots have buds? I went and looked on the 10th. Four open flowers, two bright ones on top and two darker ones lower down that had just opened, and small buds at the tips of the shoots. Date Open flowers Buds Note 7 Oct 2 4 Front view. One spent flower not counted. 8 Oct 2 4 Removed the spent flower. Photo from above. 9 Oct 2 4 Buds clearly bigger and longer. 10 Oct 4 2 Two buds opened. Bright sun, so the reds look brighter. I removed one spent flower on the 8th. That was routine upkeep, not a test, but I want to say so. There was no comparison plant, and petunia buds open on their own anyway. The app gave this evidence level 0 and said it plainly. No change was made during these counts, so it shows what the plant did while I watched and says nothing about a cause. The two new flowers opened darker and more velvety than the older ones. I read that a new petal is still small and tightly folded, so its colour is packed close together, and that as the flower opens fully and stretches out, the same colour spreads over a bigger petal and looks lighter. So I guess that is what I am seeing. Marigold The 5 October photo was taken for myself, not for the trial. I clicked it just because the plant looked lovely, from the side, and only later decided to use it here. One bud is partly cut off at the edge. The 9 October photo is the one I took for the trial, from above, where every flower and bud can be seen. My first count may have missed buds I could not see from the side, so the jump from 3 to 7 open flowers is in my notes, but it is not a fair comparison. A few petals also looked flattened after some rain. The rain may be the reason, but that is a guess. Bougainvillea Five cuttings, about a month and a half old, in the same soil and the same small black nursery bags on the same bench. One of them already has two pink flowers and the other four have none. Its mother plant is in full bloom, while my other bougainvilleas are only starting. My guess, not tested, is the variety or the time of year. The cuttings are different varieties, so "same soil, same bench" is not a fair test. A real test needs cuttings of the same variety, taken at the same time from different mother plants. How I Built It The stack is small on purpose: Streamlit , one JSON file, and gemma3:1b running locally through Ollama . I picked the 1B Gemma model to find out whether this idea works on an ordinary laptop with no cloud account. On a laptop CPU an answer can take up to a minute. Gemma has three jobs. It reads my note into plain facts, suggests one thing to go and check, and picks one change from a short menu. Everything that has to be reliable lives in plain Python, because I treat the model's output the way I would treat any untrusted input. If a number from my note is missing in Gemma's reading, the reading is rejected and my exact words are kept. Details Gemma adds that I did not write are removed by a word-match check. It is a loose check, so it can miss some. The cause field is forced to "unknown" in code. Pest and disease questions are blocked unless I raised them first. Trials come from a fixed menu that is filtered per plant. "Water more" is never offered for bougainvillea, which likes to stay on the dry side. Verdicts and evidence levels are calculated by code, never by Gemma. Level 3 needs two finished trials of the same change, each with a comparison plant and nothing else changed, all pointing the same way. Saves go to a temporary file first and are then swapped in. A garden file that cannot be read is moved aside and never overwritten. The tests replace Gemma with fake and deliberately bad answers, such as garbage, dropped numbers, invented pests, off-menu picks. A second set drives the real pages end to end. There are 85 tests, and none of them needs Ollama. What went wrong The model did not behave in my own garden. Gemma's reading of all three of my notes was rejected by the number check, and one of its three questions was blocked. The other two questions got through, and they were generic. "Is the plant's stem straight?" had nothing to do with what I was seeing, so I wrote down what I actually noticed. The guards block invented pests. They cannot make a small model's question a good one. They also only catch the failures I thought of, and the checks match English words, so notes in Hindi are not checked the same way. In my real garden Gemma only read my notes and wrote Look First questions. Both of my real trials were watch-only, so it never picked a trial there. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Gemma runs on my laptop through Ollama. There is no API key, no usage bill and no cloud AI call. My notes and photos sit in a folder on my own machine, and the photos are saved without their location data. Setup needs the internet once, to download the packages, Ollama and the model, and I switched off Streamlit's anonymous usage statistics. Running Gemma locally let me build and test this idea without an API key and without paying for every request. I could try it as often as I liked, and if a better small model arrives, I change one setting ( OLLAMA_MODEL ) and the rest of the app stays as it is. The small model had clear limitations, which I describe above, but that was part of what I wanted to learn, which is how far an open model can take this idea on an ordinary laptop, with ordinary code checking its output. The experiment showed me both the value of running a model locally and the limits of relying on its answers. What I took away The point of the app is what happens when I close the laptop. It asks me to go and look, and I stand there with the plant and nothing else. It cannot tell whether I really went outside, and I will not pretend it can. That pause is a promise I make to myself. The AI can suggest what to look at. The garden gives the answer. Thank you for reading, and thank you again to the DEV team for a challenge that let me bring the two things I love together. title: One Weekend: 3,000 Open-Source AI Projects
summary: Jess Lee for Daily Context Posted on Oct 11 One Weekend: 3,000 Open-Source AI Projects # aie # hacktoberfest # opensource # ai Hacktoberfest: Open Source Reflections Every October for the past twelve years, developers around the world have taken part in Hacktoberfest, a month-long celebration of open-source software: code that anyone can use, inspect, and improve. For most of that history, the rules were simple: Contribute a set number of pull requests and earn a T-shirt. Thousands of people made their first contribution to open source because of Hacktoberfest. This year, we changed the format. Hacktoberfest 2026 is focused on open-weight models and open-source artificial intelligence: models and tools that anyone can download, run and modify. Participants are learning how these systems work, building their own AI tooling, and adapting existing open models for new uses. When we announced this year’s theme in August, we had hoped to support 300 in-person gatherings. There are now more than 500 Fests planned in over 60 countries , ranging from university hackathons to small groups of developers meeting at their local library or office. In the first week alone, participants in-person and online submitted more than 3,000 projects. On Oct. 1, the first day of the event, students at COMSATS University in Abbottabad, Pakistan, gathered for a Hack Day. By evening, they had built a locally hosted hospital-management platform, a multimodal companion for visually impaired users, and a tool that helps newcomers make their first open-source contribution. The group photo they sent us afterward says more than any statistic I could share: a group of people who chose to spend their day learning to build something together. For many people, AI is something experienced alone: typing into a chat window, using a tool built by someone else and governed by someone else's pricing and policies. What I'm seeing this month is a clear appetite for something different. People want to sit next to each other, run a model on their own machine, take it apart, and understand how it works. That is why we built this year's Hacktoberfest around open innovation. Open source has always worked because nobody owns the tools. Anyone can look under the hood, and anyone can pull up a chair. We believe AI should work the same way: shaped by people building in public in India and Ireland, Peru and the Philippines, all over the world. Hacktoberfest runs through Oct. 31. When it ends, I don’t expect its impact to be measured solely in code. It will show up in mentorships that started at a folding table, in local tech communities meeting for the first time, and in people who walked in unsure what an AI model was and walked out having built something with one. title: You’re a Real Python Developer Only If...
summary: Hadil Ben Abdallah Posted on Oct 12 You’re a Real Python Developer Only If... # python # programming # webdev # discuss Relatable humor about daily Python struggles A few months ago, I published You're a Real JavaScript Developer Only If... It was supposed to be a little post for fun. You know, just a few things JavaScript developers could laugh about before going back to fighting their bugs 😅 But the community loved it, and the comments made me realize that developers have an incredible talent for turning their daily struggles into comedy. Then @sylwia-lask published her own take, You're a Real Software Developer Only If… and surprised me how much fun this kind of post can be. So I kept the fun going. I published You're a Real TypeScript Developer Only If... , and now I'm back for another round with Python. Well, Python developers have a very special relationship with whitespace 😂 They also have virtual environments, mysterious package conflicts, notebooks full of experiments, and that script that was supposed to take five minutes, but it became an entire project. So, Python developers, this one's for you. You're a real Python developer only if... 🤏🏻 You forgot one tiny indentation Your code was almost perfect. Almost. Then Python reminded you that indentation is not just a formatting preference. It's the difference between a working program and a confusing afternoon. 📦 You installed a package and broke everything Everything was working perfectly. Then you ran: pip install some-package Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Suddenly, another package needs a different version. Your project has trust issues. And you're asking what brought you here. 🧪 You created a virtual environment... ...and forgot to activate it. You installed all your dependencies. You ran your script. And Python told you the module doesn't exist. You installed it again. Same problem. Then you realized you were using the wrong environment. 🐼 You imported pandas just to open a CSV file At first, it was a simple CSV. A few rows. A few columns. Nothing complicated. Then you started cleaning the data, filtering records, grouping results, and creating charts. Three hours later, you're building an entire data analysis pipeline. And you're having a great time. 🤔 You wrote a list comprehension and felt unstoppable You started with a simple loop. Then you discovered list comprehensions. Now everything looks like this: squares = [ x ** 2 for x in range ( 10 ) if x % 2 == 0 ] Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode You could have written three lines, but this fits on one. And that makes it better. 🐞 You used print() to debug everything You could have used a debugger. You could have added proper logging. You could have investigated the issue systematically. Instead: print ( " HERE " ) print ( user ) print ( " WHY IS THIS NONE? " ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode And somehow, you found the bug. 📓 Your Jupyter notebook became a crime scene You have cells numbered [1] , [7] , [14] , and [39] . Some cells have been run five times. Others haven't been touched since the day before. One variable contains the result of an experiment you no longer remember. And restarting the kernel feels like playing Russian roulette with your entire afternoon. 🧠 You discovered that is and == are not the same thing You thought they did the same job. Then someone explained object identity versus equality. You nodded. You understood the explanation. You closed the article. And six months later, you still pause for a few moments whenever you write one of them. Just to be safe. 🐛 You caught a bug caused by None Everything looked reasonable. The function ran. The variable existed. But you were trying to perform an operation on None . And the error message was basically Python saying: "You gave me nothing. What exactly did you expect?" Fair enough. 🔄 You turned a simple script into a reusable module You needed to rename a few files. So you wrote a quick script. Then you added arguments. Then error handling. Then logging. Then a configuration file. Then a README. At some point, you stopped calling it a script. It's a tool now. And you're considering publishing it on GitHub. 📚 You read the documentation and still had questions Python has excellent documentation. You know this and you appreciate it. But sometimes you just want to know why a three-line example works in the tutorial and fails in your project. So you open another tab. Then another. And somehow, you're reading a discussion about a completely different problem. That's programming. 🧹 You ran a formatter and discovered how much you needed it Your code worked. Your variable names made sense to you. Your spacing was... creative. Then you ran Black. You didn't change the logic. But you feel more professional already. 🚀 You wrote a Python script that worked locally... ...then discovered the server had a different Python version. Or a missing dependency. Or a different environment variable. Or permissions you didn't know existed. Your little script was supposed to automate a boring task. Now you're learning deployment. Character development comes in many forms. 🧩 You used try/except because you didn't want to see the error You had an exception. You didn't understand it. So you wrote: try : do_the_thing () except Exception : pass Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Problem solved! Well, technically, the error disappeared. The actual problem is still in the shadows. And future-you is going to have some questions. 💛 You started learning Python because it looked simple The syntax was clean. The examples were easy to follow. You could write something useful without spending half your day configuring a project. You thought, "This language is so friendly!" Then you met asynchronous programming, dependency management, packaging, decorators, and type hints. Python is still friendly. It just has a few rooms you haven't explored yet. ☕ You said, "I'll automate this little task" You were doing something repetitive. Surely, writing a script would save time.
