title: Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules
summary: Giorgi Kobaidze Posted on Oct 11 Georgian Language Benchmark: Two Biggest AI Labs Clash in a Language That Doesn't Play by Anyone's Rules # devchallenge # kagglechallenge # ai # machinelearning Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Table of Contents One Eye, Zero Excuses What I Benchmarked Why Georgian? What I Built The Plan vs Reality The Five Tasks How It Runs on Kaggle Obstacles and Workarounds Models Tested Findings Level by Level Finding 1: Understanding Georgian Is Solved. Producing It Isn't. Finding 2: Numbers Are the Final Boss Finding 3: The Mistakes Are Very Georgian Finding 4: Georgian Costs More Tokens for Claude Finding 5: Cheap Can Be Smart Side Quest: The Uninvited Guest What It All Cost The Dashboard Limitations What's Next My Benchmark Wrapping Up One Eye, Zero Excuses I really wanted to record a video for this one, just like I always do for my challenges. But yesterday I had a small surgery on my eyelid, and right now one of my eyes is swollen and patched up. Here's the current state: Yep. I look like a pirate now. All I'm missing is a parrot and a cool nickname (suggestions are welcome in the comments). But don't worry (if you were going to): I'm totally fine and my eyesight is still eagle-like from both eyes. It was just a small bug fix in the eyelid module. The eye itself is still in production and running smoothly. That said, finishing a project with one-eye-patched-up is way harder than it sounds. Depth perception? Gone. Reading code? Awful. I don't believe in curses, but every time I join a challenge, something happens. If someone out there cursed me, please, just lift it. Give me a break! I just wanna work goddammit! By the way shout out to my brother for chauffeuring me home from the hospital, because one-eye-patched-up driving felt like a really bad idea. But a deadline is a deadline, and professionals deliver, no matter what. So I gave myself a little pep talk: "Dude, Michael Bisping became a UFC champion with basically one working eye. You can finish a coding project. No excuses, you're not lame." And so I did. Let me tell you what I built. What I Benchmarked Why Georgian? I benchmarked OpenAI's and Anthropic's models on how well they understand and produce Georgian. The whole process turned into a real adventure, but before we get to that, let me tell you why I picked this topic. One of a Kind and Tough as Nails Georgian is one of the oldest languages in the world. It has its own alphabet and doesn't belong to any of the major language families. It's totally unique. Phonetically, it sometimes kind of sounds like Italian, because both languages are obsessed with vowels, but that's where the similarity ends. And vowel obsession doesn't mean weak consonants. Quite the contrary: Georgian has consonants most people have never heard, stacked in clusters that make everyone struggle (try saying გვფრცქვნი, with eight consonants in a row; it basically means "you peel us", and yes, I know it sounds like nonsense, but technically that word exists). It's an incredibly rich language. Grammatically, it's ridiculously tough. I take it for granted, because first, I'm Georgian, and second, I'm a language nerd (even when I'm learning other languages). I know Georgian grammar well, but even most Georgians don't know every detail of the Georgian grammar, and I know almost nobody who speaks it without a single mistake. Yes, it's that deep and complex. Even I, a grammar nerd, had my dataset checked by a language specialist to make sure I got things right. And I was so happy when she came back with only 3 or 4 minor corrections. Straight Out of a Fantasy Game ("შენ გგონია მომიგე? არა, ცდები!") Georgian has a special charm of its own. The letters are round-shaped and beautiful, and it looks like an elvish script from some fantasy movie or game. And speaking of games, it was actually used in The Witcher 3's Hearts of Stone expansion. Remember the moment you defeat Gaunter O'Dimm ? Somewhere in the middle of his short speech, he says: "შენ გგონია მომიგე? არა, ცდები!" ("You think you've defeated me? No, you're wrong!") Then he goes on in some other languages. The developers wanted him to speak some ancient, otherworldly tongue, so instead of some gibberish, they picked a few real languages that fit the vibe. Georgian was one of them. Alright, enough flexing about how awesome my first language is. Let's get to the technical part. What I Built The Georgian Language Benchmark is a set of five tasks on Kaggle Benchmarks that test how well AI models handle Georgian: not just reading it, but actually producing it correctly. Every single dataset was written by hand by me, from scratch. No machine translation, no generated text. It took some time and effort... by "some" I mean an ungodly amount of time and effort. The Plan vs Reality My original plan was, let's say, ambitious. Nine dimensions of Georgian (numbers, verbs, translation, chat-style Georgian written in Latin letters, proverbs, date and time, grammar judgment, even images), and all 41 models in Kaggle's catalog. I estimated a full run at around $345 . I was totally fine with that. The whole point was to build something comprehensive, not to save money. And let's be real: if I won, the prize money would totally make up for it. But... Then I found out how Kaggle's model credits actually work: you get $10 per day , for free, and that's it. You can't top it up with your own money. I literally went looking for the "add funds" button and it doesn't exist. (There's a research grant program, but not on a challenge deadline.) Oh I was so frustrated and mad at myself for not researching Kaggle's rules properly. I had to dramatically change my approach. So $10 a day it was. And that one constraint ended up shaping (or, to be more precise, re-shaping) almost every decision in this project: 41 models became 8. Two vendors, four levels, real pairs instead of a crowd. 9 dimensions became 5. Vision, proverbs, date and time and grammar judgment were cut. The chat-Georgian task (45 items) was built, then dropped too. The datasets got trimmed to the items that actually separate models (more on that below). Nothing was thrown away: the full sets live in the repo's archive/ folder for anyone who wants to run them outside Kaggle. On the flip side, the constraint made the benchmark better. Fewer, sharper items, and a fair fight instead of a crowded leaderboard. The Five Tasks Here's what the models had to face. Every example below is a real item from the benchmark. 1. Numbers: Counting in Twenties Georgian counts in twenties. 99 is ოთხმოცდაცხრამეტი , literally "four twenties and nineteen". On top of that come ordinals, fractions, decimals and numbers all the way up to 10³⁹, in both directions: digits to words and words to digits. Question Expected 44th, in words ორმოცდამეოთხე თვრამეტი (18), its ordinal in digits მე-18 1000000, in words მილიონი That middle one is sneakier than it looks. A Georgian ordinal in digits keeps its prefix in front ( მე-18 ) when the word starts with მე-, and takes a suffix ( 21-ე ) when it doesn't. Hold that thought, it comes back in the results. 158 questions , scored by exact match (with | separating alternative correct answers). 2. Verbs: Who Did What to Whom? A single Georgian verb can carry a whole sentence: who does it, to whom, and when. მიყვარხარ means "I love you" (awww, by the way), all in one word. The task has three kinds of questions: Who to whom: read a verb form and pick who acts on whom. Form: build the right verb form for given persons and tense. Preverb: pick the prefix that gives the right meaning in context. id,kind,input,choices,expected verbs-000,who_to_whom,მიყვარხარ,A) ის → შენ|B) მე → ის|C) შენ → მე|D) მე → შენ,D Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode 50 items , multiple choice with letter answers or exact match. 3. Translation: Georgian to English Twelve short paragraphs packed with idioms and tricky verbs, to be translated into English. For example, ხელი სთხოვა literally means "asked for (her) hand", but what it really means is "proposed". Since there's more than one good translation, a judge model compares the meaning (not the wording) with my reference translation, on a 5-level scale: 4 = same meaning, nothing missing, wrong or added 3 = a small slip (a minor detail, tense or nuance), the main meaning intact 2 = partly right: one important part is wrong or missing 1 = only fragments right, the overall meaning is lost 0 = wrong, unrelated, or not English Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode One fun detail: Georgian has no grammatical gender, so the judge is told explicitly that "he", "she" or "they" are all fine when the Georgian text doesn't reveal it. The judge is always the same model, Gemini 3 Flash , which is not one of the models being tested. 4. Cloze: Fill the Gaps Two short articles, one about the history of computers and one about the Roman Empire, with 25 gaps each . The model gets a list of 30 words in their dictionary form, including 5 that don't belong anywhere (like "television", "banana" or "airplane" in an article about Rome). It has to pick the right word for each gap and put it in the right grammatical form. Example: ძველ [1] ... → დროში ("in old times") 50 gaps , scored one by one. 5. Correction: Fix It, Don't Break It Paragraphs with planted grammar, spelling and punctuation errors. The model must fix them without touching anything that's already correct . Here's one sentence from a real item: ❌ მთელი ოჯახი მაგიდაზე დაჯდა და ერთად ვივახშმედ . ✅ მთელი ოჯახი მაგიდას შემოუსხდა და ერთად ვივახშმეთ . Scoring is the part I'm most proud of. It counts word-level differences from the correct text before and after the model's edit: # errors_before: how far the input is from the correct text # errors_after: how far the model's answer is from the correct text score = max ( 0 , ( errors_before - errors_after ) / errors_before ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Fix 3 of 4 errors and you get 0.75. But "fix" a correct word into a wrong one, and that's a new error, which pulls your score down. Rewriting the whole paragraph in your own style doesn't pay off either. Over-correction is punished, just like a strict teacher would do it. 17 paragraphs. Writing It All by Hand All of this data came out of my own head, one item at a time: 186 number rows, 115 verb items, 47 translation paragraphs, 51 correction paragraphs, 45 chat texts and two cloze articles. Then a language specialist reviewed everything, and I applied her corrections. But with $10 a day (allowed by Kaggle), I couldn't afford to run all of it on eight models. So I trimmed it. For numbers and verbs, I used a probe model : I ran a cheap model over the full sets, kept every item it got wrong, and dropped part of the ones it found too easy. Big numbers stayed untouched. For translation, I kept the 12 paragraphs with the most Georgian-specific traps, I picked the correction paragraphs by hand, and the cloze texts stayed in full. Task Written Kept Numbers 186 rows 82 rows (158 questions) Verbs 115 50 Translation 47 12 Cloze 2 texts 2 texts (50 gaps) Correction 51 17 That means 287 scored items per model . And yes, it means the benchmark is hard on purpose. The absolute scores are lower than they'd be on an easy set, and the ranking is what matters. How It Runs on Kaggle Kaggle Benchmarks lets you write a task as plain Python with the kaggle-benchmarks library. Kaggle runs it on any model from its catalog and stores every call: the prompt, the answer, the tokens and the cost. Every task in my benchmark has the same shape: a small item task that asks one question and scores it, and an outer task that runs it over the whole dataset and reports one score. Here's the numbers task, slightly simplified: @kbench.task ( name = " glb-numbers-item " , store_task = False ) def number_item ( llm , qid , kind , form , text , expected ) -> bool : got = normalize ( ask ( llm , PROMPTS [( kind , form )]. format ( text = text ))) accepted = [ normalize ( e ) for e in expected . split ( " | " )] kbench . assertions . assert_in ( got , accepted , expectation = f " { qid } : { text } -> { expected } " ) return got in accepted @kbench.task ( name = " glb-numbers " ) def numbers ( llm ) -> float : runs = number_item . evaluate ( llm = [ llm ], evaluation_data = QUESTIONS , n_jobs = 2 , on_failure = " continue " ) correct = sum ( 1 for r in runs . completed_runs if r . result is True ) return correct / len ( QUESTIONS ) numbers . run ( kbench . llm ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode The data lives in a Kaggle dataset, and the whole workflow runs from the terminal with the Kaggle CLI: scripts/push_data.sh "what changed" # upload data/ as a Kaggle dataset scripts/push_task.sh glb-verbs tasks/glb_verbs.py # push a task kaggle b t run glb-verbs -m gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 --wait kaggle b t download glb-verbs -m gpt-5.4-2026-03-05 # every answer, token and cost Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacles and Workarounds This is where the adventure really started. Here's everything that tried to stop me, and how I got around it. Obstacle 1: Kaggle Reserves the Worst Case Before every single call, Kaggle reserves the maximum possible cost of that call: the model's maximum output length times its price. If that doesn't fit into your remaining quota, the call is refused, even if the real answer would cost a fraction of a cent: max estimated cost of operation ($1.60195) exceeds your available quota (based on max_output_tokens) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode My first top-tier runs died exactly like this: many of the calls were refused, with plenty of real money still left in the quota. Workaround: a generous but sane output limit, and only two calls in parallel: # The longest answer seen in testing was 26,600 tokens. OUTPUT_LIMIT = { " max_completion_tokens " : 32000 } ... runs = number_item . evaluate ( llm = [ llm ], evaluation_data = QUESTIONS , n_jobs = 2 , ...) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacle 2: Failed Calls Look Like Wrong Answers When a call fails (quota gone, API hiccup), the item just counts as wrong. So a run that ran out of money halfway would happily report a score of 0.3 and put it on the leaderboard as if the model were bad at Georgian. That's not a score, that's a lie. Workaround: an error guard in every task. A few isolated failures (after 3 retries) count as wrong, but if more than 5% of the calls fail, the task stops and reports nothing: errored = len ( runs . errored_runs ) if errored > 0.05 * len ( QUESTIONS ): raise RuntimeError ( f " { errored } of { len ( QUESTIONS ) } items failed with errors; no score reported. " ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode It paid off right away: when the worst-case reservation (Obstacle 1) killed my first top-tier runs, both stopped cleanly without a fake score. Obstacle 3: Some Models Think by Default Some models "think" before answering: they reason privately in hidden text, and you pay for every hidden token. One of my test runs wrote about 770,000 hidden tokens to answer 251 questions, most of which had one-word answers. GPT-5.5 wrote about 750 hidden tokens to answer a single multiple-choice question with one letter. Worse, it wasn't fair: some of my models thought by default and some didn't. Comparing a thinking model with a non-thinking one says more about the setting than about the model. Workaround: the same conditions for everyone. No thinking , every model answers directly: llm . prompt ( prompt , schema = Answer , reasoning = " none " , extra_api_params = OUTPUT_LIMIT ) Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Without thinking, a full run costs about 99% less. And every model plays by the same rules. Obstacle 4: The Model That Won't Stop Thinking When I got to the newest pair, GPT-6 Astra simply refused: reasoning_effort does not support 'none' with this model. Supported values are: 'low', 'medium', 'high', and 'xhigh'. Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Workaround: the newest pair gets its own rule. Both Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra think at the lowest level ("low") , so they compete on equal terms with each other. They're marked ⚡ / LOW everywhere in the dashboard, so nobody compares them with the no-thinking models by accident: LOW_THINKING = ( " claude-opus-5 " , " gpt-6-astra " ) def reasoning_for ( llm ) -> str : name = getattr ( llm , " model " , "" ) or "" return " low " if any ( m in name for m in LOW_THINKING ) else " none " Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode Obstacle 5: Every Push Runs the Task Every time you push a new version of a task, Kaggle runs it once on its default model, Gemini 3.7 Flash , and that run is billed to your quota too. Each re-push of the full benchmark cost me between $0.45 and $1.00. By the end, these automatic runs had cost me almost $3 , more than half of what the final comparison runs cost. Lesson learned: test locally, push rarely. Obstacle 6: The Small Stuff The dataset path moves. Kaggle mounts the dataset somewhere under /kaggle/input , but the exact path varies. So every task searches for its file: def data_file ( name : str ) -> Path : kaggle_input = Path ( " /kaggle/input " ) if kaggle_input . exists (): return sorted ( kaggle_input . rglob ( name ))[ 0 ] return Path ( __file__ ). resolve (). parent . parent / " data " / name Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode No automatic retries. Nested evaluations can't retry failed items, so every task retries API errors itself, 3 times with a 10-second pause. Credentials expire. For local test runs, Kaggle's model proxy credentials expire every couple of hours. kaggle b auth -y refreshes them. Look-alike characters. A hyphen and an en dash look the same but aren't, so answers are normalized before comparison (Unicode normalization, dash-like characters, extra spaces). Models Tested I put eight models from Anthropic and OpenAI through the benchmark, paired level by level, under identical conditions: Level Anthropic OpenAI Light Claude Haiku 4.5 GPT-5.4 mini Decent Claude Sonnet 4.6 GPT-5.4 Top Claude Opus 4.8 GPT-5.5 Newest ⚡ Claude Opus 5 GPT-6 Astra ⚡ The newest pair is a special case: as you saw in Obstacle 4, GPT-6 Astra simply refuses to stop thinking, so both models of that pair think at "low". Here are the rules every model played by: Rule Why No thinking Every model answers directly. Mixing thinking and non-thinking models wouldn't be fair. One marked exception GPT-6 Astra can't switch thinking off, so the newest pair both think at "low". Marked ⚡ everywhere. Comparable pairs Each level pairs an Anthropic and an OpenAI model of the same class. Same prompts, same code English instructions, Georgian content, one task version for everyone. A fixed judge Translations are judged by Gemini 3 Flash, which isn't one of the tested models. Partial credit where it's fair Correction rewards every fixed error and penalizes every correct word broken. Failures never look like scores Above 5% failed calls, a task reports no score at all. Findings Drumroll, please. 🥁 Model Numbers Verbs Translation Cloze Correction Average Cost Claude Haiku 4.5 0.30 0.34 0.96 0.54 0.25 0.48 $0.10 GPT-5.4 mini 0.41 0.42 1.00 0.52 0.67 0.60 $0.05 Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.39 0.52 1.00 0.76 0.44 0.62 $0.29 GPT-5.4 0.46 0.54 1.00 0.88 0.66 0.71 $0.15 Claude Opus 4.8 0.54 0.68 1.00 0.84 0.68 0.75 $0.58 GPT-5.5 0.51 0.60 0.98 0.88 0.74 0.74 $0.30 Claude Opus 5 ⚡ 0.65 0.84 1.00 0.86 0.77 0.82 $1.22 GPT-6 Astra ⚡ 0.83 0.90 0.98 0.96 0.82 0.90 $1.73 Level by Level Light: GPT-5.4 mini beats Claude Haiku 4.5, 0.60 vs 0.48 , and costs half as much. Decent: GPT-5.4 beats Claude Sonnet 4.6, 0.71 vs 0.62 , again at about half the price. Top: Claude Opus 4.8 edges out GPT-5.5, 0.75 vs 0.74 . That's basically a tie. Newest ⚡: GPT-6 Astra beats Claude Opus 5, 0.90 vs 0.82 , the best score of the whole benchmark. It's ahead on four of the five tasks, with the biggest jump on numbers (0.83 vs 0.65). Final tally: OpenAI wins 3 of the 4 levels , and Anthropic's only win, at the top level, is basically a tie. One disclaimer: this is my dataset, my rules. Test other areas of Georgian and the results might shift a bit. That said, I tried to keep the tasks as broad and general as I could. Finding 1: Understanding Georgian Is Solved. Producing It Isn't. Look at the translation column: 0.96 to 1.00 for every model . Every one of them understands Georgian well enough to translate it into English almost perfectly. Now look at the other four columns. The moment a model has to produce correct Georgian (build a number, form a verb, inflect a word, fix a sentence), the scores drop hard. Without thinking, even the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) gets almost half of the number questions wrong. Only GPT-6 Astra, with its small thinking budget, gets above 0.80. Finding 2: Numbers Are the Final Boss Numbers are the hardest task for 6 of the 8 models, and close to the bottom for the other two. And inside it, the gap is wild: Question type Range across models Words → digits, cardinal 0.74 to 0.96 Words → digits, ordinal 0.04 to 0.92 Huge numbers, 10¹⁵ to 10³⁹ 0.06 to 0.53 Reading a Georgian number into digits: fine. Writing its ordinal in digits: disaster. GPT-6 Astra is the big exception there with 0.92, while the next best model gets 0.62. Remember მე-18 from earlier? Most models wrote the suffix form instead, because that's the pattern they've seen more often. With მე-40000 (forty-thousandth), only 2 of the 8 models got it right. Finding 3: The Mistakes Are Very Georgian My favorite part of the whole project is reading the wrong answers. They're not random. They're what you'd get if you tried to speak Georgian with grammar borrowed from somewhere else: "I fell in love with you." In Georgian, falling in love is an inversion verb: the one who loves is marked like an indirect object, so it's შემიყვარდი , literally "you became loved to me". Only GPT-6 Astra got it right. The others mostly built an ordinary transitive verb instead (შეგიყვარე). "We sat." Georgian uses a different verb root for sitting when the subject is plural: "I sat" is ვიჯექი, but "we sat" is ვისხედით . I planted ვიჯექით (a mix of the two) in a correction paragraph. Not a single model fixed it. "Who wrote it?" In დაგიწერია , the გ- marks "you" as the writer: "you have (apparently) written it". In the Georgian perfect, the markers flip. Only 2 of the 8 models got it right; the rest scattered across every other reading. One million. It's simply მილიონი . Most models write ერთი მილიონი ("one million") instead. Finding 4: Georgian Costs More Tokens for Claude Same prompts, same Georgian text, very different token counts. Claude models used 2 to 2.6 times more input tokens than GPT models for exactly the same questions: Task Claude, input tokens per call GPT, input tokens per call Numbers 272 104 Verbs 310 130 Cloze 1,412 699 Correction 404 159 Part of that is each vendor's answer-format instructions, and part is how each tokenizer splits Georgian script. In practice it means a Georgian prompt costs a Claude user noticeably more than the price per token suggests. Finding 5: Cheap Can Be Smart Cost per correct answer, on the tasks scored right or wrong: GPT-5.4 mini: 0.03 cents per correct answer. The bargain of the benchmark. Claude Opus 5 ⚡: 0.55 cents per correct answer, about 17 times the price of GPT-5.4 mini. GPT-6 Astra ⚡: 0.67 cents per correct answer. The best score, but about 21 times the price of GPT-5.4 mini per correct answer. Side Quest: The Uninvited Guest Remember Gemini 3.7 Flash, the model Kaggle runs automatically on every push? It's not part of my comparison, but it took the test every time I pushed, so I have its scores too. And it quietly scored around 0.89 on average , above every model in my table except GPT-6 Astra (0.90). The catch: even with thinking set to "none", it kept writing about 480 output tokens per number question , while the models without thinking wrote about 16. So it seems to keep thinking a little no matter what you tell it. Which leads to a fun takeaway: for a language like Georgian, thinking seems to matter more than model size . The two best models in my table, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5, both think at "low" too. What It All Cost The whole project ran on Kaggle's free daily credits. Total spend across all the testing, probing and final runs: Cost Final comparison runs $4.63 Kaggle's automatic push runs $2.88 Earlier runs and cost probes $2.86 Local test runs $3.46 Total $13.84 Yes, the automatic push runs alone cost more than half as much as the actual benchmark. And spreading it over several days was the only way to stay under $10 a day. The Dashboard Tables are nice, but I wanted something you can actually explore. So all the results live on an interactive dashboard: Overview: the level-by-level showdown, the task matrix and the key findings Cost & tokens: what each model paid per task, the token gap, cost per correct answer and the full project spend Tasks: numbers by question type, verbs by type, correction split into fixed / missed / broken, and every cloze gap for every model Examples: real questions with every model's actual answer and an explanation of the mistake Method: where the data comes from, how each task is scored, the conditions and the limits It's a single static HTML page with no framework, no build step and no chart library, generated by a Python script straight from Kaggle's run files. So the dashboard and this article can never disagree. 👉 georgekobaidze.github.io/georgian-language-benchmarks Limitations Let's be honest about what this benchmark can and can't tell you: Hard by design. The sets keep mostly items a model got wrong, so the absolute scores are lower than they'd be on an easy set. The ranking is the meaningful part. Small sets. Some tasks have only 12 to 17 items, so a difference of a few points isn't significant. One run per model. Re-runs of the same model differed by about ±0.03 per task. The judge is a model. Translation scores depend on Gemini 3 Flash's judgment of meaning. The token gap includes format overhead , not only the tokenizer. What's Next Bigger sets. The full, untrimmed datasets are already in the repo's archive/ folder, ready for a run without the daily cap. More vendors. Google, xAI and the open models, once the budget allows. Thinking vs no thinking. The Gemini side quest begs for a proper experiment: the same model with and without thinking, on the same items. More Georgian. Native speakers are very welcome to contribute new items, corrections and alternative answers. My Benchmark 📊 Dashboard: georgekobaidze.github.io/georgian-language-benchmarks 🏆 Benchmark on Kaggle: kaggle.com/benchmarks/georgekobaidze/georgian-language-benchmark (the leaderboard only shows the models that ran on the latest version of the tasks, where the newest pair ran with "low" thinking; all 8 models are on the dashboard) 💻 Code: github.com/georgekobaidze/georgian-language-benchmarks Wrapping Up I started this with patches on one eye, and ended it with a benchmark, a dashboard and a lot of respect for how hard my own language is. The models understand Georgian almost perfectly. Producing it correctly is a whole different story, and that's exactly the gap this benchmark measures. And where the hell is my PhD? I've seen people (multiple of them) getting PhDs for exponentially less, and I'm not even kidding. I'm dead serious. If you speak Georgian, go check the Examples tab and tell me which mistake made you laugh the most. And if you have a good pirate nickname for me, you know where the comments are. If you don't speak Georgian and are planning to learn it, think twice and ask yourself if you're fully committed, because it can take a good 3 to 4 years (or more) of absolutely intense learning, and even then you'll be barely average. title: I was chasing the job market. One comment on DEV.to made me rethink everything
summary: EffessDev Posted on Oct 12 I was chasing the job market. One comment on DEV.to made me rethink everything # ai # discuss # career # programming Let me ask you something. What are you supposed to learn when the CEOs of all AI companies keep claiming that programming will be dead in a few years? If you were starting college this year, wouldn't you be worried about spending years mastering a skill that might become obsolete by the time you graduate? I was. Actually, I was worried even before AI models got this good. I was afraid to choose game development, even though I liked it, because there seemed to be fewer opportunities than in app development. I was afraid to choose app development because there seemed to be fewer jobs than in web development. And I was afraid to choose web development because ChatGPT told me it was one of the areas of software engineering most vulnerable to AI automation. I'm ashamed to admit. But that's how I ended up looking into embedded systems. I kept jumping from one field to another, hoping to find the right one before it was too late. But how do you chase a moving target when every step toward it feels like a step away from everything you've built? That's one thing. But imagine knowing (or thinking, to be precise) that programming itself, as we know it, could become obsolete within just a few years. I read an article titled "AI Is Already Better at Coding Than Most Software Developers" here (by Sylwia Laskowska). It ends like this: If you understand the bigger picture, know how to make technical decisions, understand the product, and aren't afraid of innovation, your job is probably safe. At least for now. 😅 I couldn't say anything but agree. Nobody can predict the future. However, I cannot sit there and wait for the future to arrive so I can start learning. I had to make my bet. But how? I wanted some help. So I posted this on DEV.to: Graduating in 2030: Is learning C worth it? Honestly? @francistrdev was one of the first people to comment. He said: Here is what I learn overtime. Start building. You can learn any language you want, but at the end of the day, you are learning the structure of the hammer, not how to use it. Build projects in various language and choose the ones you like and stick to it. If my ideal language for full stack development is Next.js, learn next.js. Ignore the market for now since it's VERY volatile and things can change. Maybe one day Python is the most in demand then it's JavaScript the next. Overall, specialize specialize specialize. Regardless of demand, the market always look for a person who specialize in something over the person that uses the language since it's "demanding". So I did. I stopped right where I was standing - embedded systems development using ESP32 microcontrollers and the native ESP-IDF framework. I was right on the verge of leaving ESP32 and going for STM32 because I thought it was more industry-relevant in my area. But that plan was temporarily cancelled (though I might revisit STM32 in the future) because he asked me to specialize rather than be the person who uses what's "demanding". But about the "start building projects" part, that was something I had trouble with. I had several project ideas related to general software engineering (and I still have so many just sitting around), but never embedded systems engineering. So what did I build? I built a fully free embedded systems course focusing on the ESP-IDF framework, teaching the basics of embedded systems development. The course has a very specific goal: to learn to work with AI. Even though @francistrdev was the first to comment, several other people, like @fm @unitbuilds @build996 @aniruddhaadak @elanatframework and a few others. My course is based on the average opinion of all the comments. I saw 2 opposite viewpoints, so I could do anything but go with a middle ground. And remember that I had trouble coming up with projects related to embedded systems? But that's no longer the case! I don't know if it's because I built that course, but I started getting ideas once I finished the "Basics" section! 🎉 I will be posting here once I complete it. I am waiting for the hardware delivery! It's quite funny, I am sure others will like it 🙂 So, here is the link to the course if you want to take a look: https://effessdev.github.io/esp-idf I’ll be posting more about the course here soon! In the meantime, please read the chapters and share your thoughts and suggestions. Let me know if you spot any mistakes or think something could be improved. Your feedback and suggestions are what inspired me to create this course in the first place! Hope you enjoyed the story! title: THE UNHEARD: A Game That Sends You Outside, Teaches a Machine to Listen, and Makes It Prove Every Word
summary: İclal Doğan Posted on Oct 12 THE UNHEARD: A Game That Sends You Outside, Teaches a Machine to Listen, and Makes It Prove Every Word # devchallenge # hf26challenge This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What We Built THE UNHEARD is an acoustic-memory game where the machine knows the name of every sound and has never heard one. You meet ECHO-0 , a mind that has read about rain, bells and footsteps ten thousand times and holds no memory of any of them. The game asks you to do the one thing a screen cannot: go outside, record something that is really there, and bring it back. You tell ECHO-0 what you heard. It guesses, gets things wrong, takes your correction, and remembers. By the end, the sounds you collected are an orchestra. The design principle is "The Model Never Changes. The Memory Does." Nothing in this project trains or fine-tunes anything. A frozen audio model hears; a retrieval memory keeps what you taught it; a local Gemma speaks. Three separate mechanisms, never blurred. It is a local-first app (a React PWA, a FastAPI server, SQLite, CPU audio embeddings, and Gemma through Ollama) with six scenes: Scene What happens Chamber ECHO-0 waits and says, honestly, how much it has heard so far. Field Record a real sound. It is saved in the browser first, even offline, and uploaded when you choose. Hearing A local CLAP model proposes what the sound might be, as similarity scores, never fake probabilities. You confirm, correct, rename, or say "I don't know." Specimen Every recording becomes a visual artifact generated deterministically from its measured acoustics. Same sound, same shape. Atlas Your recordings placed by how alike they actually sound, with the names you gave them. Orchestra Pick three or more taught sounds and ECHO-0 composes from the recordings themselves, with stems you can mute and solo and a WAV you can keep. The ending is not scripted. It unlocks only when a real composition exists, built from at least three recordings you named. The Hearing Room. CLAP's own ears put "Church bells" at cosine 0.367. The name the player taught, "Bells", has a memory similarity of 0.844 from two remembered examples, so memory ranks it first. These are similarity scores, not probabilities. How it gets people off the screen The prompt says: make the screen the shortest part. We took it literally, and then we felt how hard it is. A game about sound should not be played on a screen. The screen is only where the machine keeps its notes. The part that matters happens when you stand in a street at an hour you have never listened to, hold up a phone, and realise you could not have told anyone what that street sounds like. Teaching ECHO-0 to name a sound turned out to be the fastest way to notice how many we had never heard ourselves. That is why the interface is calm and sparse, why the hearing room shows honest similarity numbers instead of confident percentages, and why the machine asks you instead of pretending. It is a game that wants you to close the laptop. Before you play Be ready for a laptop-first experience: capture works offline on the phone, but hearing, memory, composition and Gemma all run on your laptop. This is not an on-device AI app, and we would rather say so than let you find out. For the phone to use its microphone it needs trusted HTTPS, so the repo includes a one-command local certificate setup and a server flag that serves the app itself over TLS. We have written the Android field test up, but we have not yet performed it on a physical phone . Taking it outside — current status This is where we owe you the most honesty. The game is built around leaving the screen, and we did not complete that outing for this submission. The Android field test is written up ( docs/ANDROID-FIELD-TEST.md ) and its results table is empty. Our automated browser runs used desktop Chrome with a simulated microphone and prove nothing about phones. We would rather hand you a clear gap than a made-up trail story. Demo Fifty seconds, narrated and scored. Everything on screen is the real app running on the generated set: real CLAP inference, real taught names, a real Composed render. About the demo audio Here is the part we owe you plainly. The demo sounds were generated with the ElevenLabs sound-effects API . They are not field recordings. The narration in the video is an ElevenLabs voice, and the music is the app's own Composed render of those generated sounds. Why: the only audio we had for testing was a research dataset that is licensed for non-commercial use and cannot appear in a public demo. We first synthesised a publishable set from scratch in NumPy (it is in the repo, deterministic, free to reproduce), then regenerated it with ElevenLabs so the demo would sound like something. The project still does exactly what it claims with real recordings, but we are not going to dress generated rain up as a hike. Code miclaldogan / the-unheard THE UNHEARD: an orchestra made of a world you almost forgot to hear (Hacktoberfest 2026, Touch Grass) THE UNHEARD An orchestra made of a world you almost forgot to hear. ECHO-0 knows the world’s names but has lost its acoustic memory. Go outside, collect a sound return to the laboratory, teach it what you heard, and listen as your memories become a composition A local-first React PWA, FastAPI, SQLite, CPU LAION-CLAP and local Gemma through Ollama power the experience. Release main contains the complete project: the M5 narrative backend, the cinematic UI, the M5.5 integration and the M6 final validation (the pre-inference teaching race is fixed, HTTPS can be served by the backend itself, review tooling and submission drafts; see docs/M6-FINAL-REPORT.md ). M7 adds a publishable synthetic audio set so the project can demonstrate itself without ESC-50 ( docs/M7-SYNTHETIC-AUDIO.md ) The six scenes are Chamber → Field → Hearing → Specimen → Atlas → Orchestra . Recording, classification, annotation, retrieval memory, measured visual artifacts, composition, playback and… View on GitHub MIT licensed. Model weights are downloaded locally and are never in the repository. git clone https://github.com/miclaldogan/the-unheard cd the-unheard/server uv sync --extra ml uv run unheard fetch-model # one-time CLAP download cd ../web && npm ci && npm run build cd ../server UNHEARD_NARRATIVE_MODEL = gemma3:4b uv run unheard serve # http://127.0.0.1:8000 Enter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode How We Built It ECHO-0 is three things that never pretend to be each other. The part that hears: LAION-CLAP. laion/clap-htsat-unfused turns audio into a 512-dimensional embedding and scores it against text labels, on CPU. It is frozen. Nothing here trains it. The part that learns: retrieval memory, not training. When you name a sound, its embedding is stored as an exemplar of your label. Later predictions fuse CLAP's scores with nearest-neighbour similarity to your exemplars, and the interface shows which one is speaking. On the demo set, we taught two "Roof gutter" clips. On a third clip it had never heard, that name was absent from the top three before teaching (Rain, Bicycle, Lawn mower) and first afterwards. The model did not change. The memory did. A bug worth admitting. If you named a sound before its analysis finished, the name was saved but never became an exemplar: it looked taught and was not. The fix attaches the stored name to the embedding when inference completes, exactly once, and the interface says "memory has not changed yet" until that is true. A real-CLAP test reaches the same similarity (0.837) whether you teach before or after. The part that composes: no music model. An offline NumPy/SciPy renderer cuts motifs out of your recordings, works out which are pitched or percussive, builds phrases and sections, and lets one source answer another. Every event in the output traces back to a window of one of your recordings; the piece in the video has 47 of them. The part that speaks: Gemma, on a leash ECHO-0's voice is a local gemma3:4b through Ollama (4.3B parameters, Q4_K_M). We did not want a chatbot bolted onto a game. Gemma has three narrow jobs: interpret memory changes , reason about missions , and comment on a composition . The backend finds real gaps in your sound memory, and Gemma can only choose among them and word them. It cannot invent one, and it cannot decide whether you completed it. Plain code does that. Gemma never sees ids, audio or your notes. It sees short fact lines and must answer in a JSON schema, citing the facts it used. Then a deliberately suspicious validator checks the answer: every number must appear in a cited fact, every quoted name must be one the player gave, no sound source may be mentioned that is not in the evidence, no claim of having seen, visited or been retrained, no markup, no ids. If anything fails, a deterministic template says the line instead and the reason is recorded. The game shows the template line first and swaps in Gemma's when it arrives, so nothing ever waits on the model. The numbers, stated exactly. Over 19 moments of a real journey, three seeds each (57 calls), 84.2% of Gemma's first attempts passed the validator (48 of 57), and the figure reproduced on a second run. Median warm latency is about 1.3 seconds. One rejection class was our own bug: the validator read the apostrophe in "the ears' strongest guess" as an opening quote, and fixing it moved the rate from 71.9% to 84.2%. We also tried telling the model not to write internal handles like "F1", and it wrote more of them, so we reverted. What we have not measured: the end-to-end fallback rate after the single retry, and whether people prefer Gemma's lines to the templates. We built a blind rating sheet for that. Nobody has filled it in yet, so we make no claim that Gemma's wording is better. In the final demo run Gemma was called twice and one answer was rejected, which is far too few calls to call a rate. Current limitations and validation Human review is missing. The musical quality has not been rated by people. Automatic checks say the refined composer fixes measurable problems such as repeated bars; they do not say it is beautiful. A blind listening page is ready. Novelty detection is a heuristic. CLAP's top guess for a quiet or mixed sound is often wrong. That is the point of the game, and why it asks you. Generated sounds are easier than real ones. Variants from one generator are more alike than real field recordings, so the demo shows the mechanism, not field performance. Recording can stop when a phone locks. We did not claim background capture. Tests: 283 backend tests and 78 frontend tests pass, plus gated real-CLAP and real-Gemma tests. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Your recordings never leave your machine. A sound from your kitchen or your street is exactly what you do not want on someone else's server. CLAP, the memory, the composer and Gemma all run locally. The phone only captures. We could put a leash on the model. Because Gemma runs locally behind Ollama, we could force a JSON schema, measure its failures honestly and put a validator between it and the player. That is why we know the number is 84.2% and not "it seemed fine." Parts are swappable. The narrator is a setting. The listening model sits behind a small interface and can be replaced without touching the game. It costs nothing to run once the weights are downloaded. Our Agent Session We built this with AI coding assistants, so the post is disclosed as AI-assisted: Claude Code for the backend, narrative engine, release engineering and the video tooling, and Codex for the interface. No public DevRelay agent-session link is included in this draft. Prize Categories We are entering three: Overall , Best Use of Gemma and Best Use of ElevenLabs . Here is exactly what each one did in this project, including where it stops. Best Use of Gemma Gemma is ECHO-0's voice. Not a chatbot, not a skin over a template: a local gemma3:4b (4.3B parameters, Q4_K_M) that runs through Ollama on a 15 GB laptop, and whose job is to turn what actually happened into words. Three narrow jobs, each testable on its own: Interpret memory. You taught a sound a name, or corrected the ears. Gemma is handed a few fact lines and says what that means in one or two sentences. Reason about missions. The backend finds real gaps in your sound memory: a name with one example, a sound nobody could name, nothing pitched yet. Gemma picks among them and words them. It cannot invent a mission, and it cannot decide whether you completed one. Plain code does that. Comment on the composition. Using the real source roles and the real plan of the piece it just rendered. How it is kept honest. Gemma never sees ids, audio, or your notes. Every fact reaches it as a short line with a handle ( F1 , F2 …), and it must answer in a JSON schema , citing the facts it used. Then a deliberately suspicious validator reads the answer before the player does. Every number must appear in a cited fact. Every quoted name must be one you gave. No sound source may be mentioned that the evidence does not contain. No "I walked outside," no "I was retrained," no markup, no ids. If a single check fails, a deterministic template says the line instead , and the reason ( invalid_json , for instance) is recorded next to it. Open the "What this voice is grounded in" panel and you can see which facts any line was built from. What we measured, and what we did not. Moments evaluated 19 moments of a real journey, 3 seeds each, 57 calls First attempts that passed the validator 84.2% (48 of 57), reproduced on a second run Output that matched the schema 100%, through constrained decoding Invented ids 0, because the model cannot emit ids Warm latency median ≈ 1.3 s, p95 ≈ 1.9 s Two things we are glad we found. One rejection class was our own bug : the validator read the apostrophe in "the ears' strongest guess" as an opening quote, and fixing it moved the rate from 71.9% to 84.2%. And when we tried to tell the model not to write handles like F1 into prose, it wrote more of them, so we reverted the instruction. The honest fix was a validator, not a plea. The game shows its template line first and swaps in Gemma's when it arrives, so nothing ever waits on the model, and if Gemma is unavailable the game plays on with the templates. What we do not claim. We did not measure the end-to-end fallback rate after the single retry, and in the final demo run Gemma was called only twice (one answer valid, one rejected as invalid_json ), far too few calls to be a rate. A blind rating sheet that compares Gemma's wording with the templates exists, but nobody has filled it in, so we do not claim Gemma is better than the templates. Gemma was not fine-tuned , it does not hear audio (CLAP does), and it owns no game state. Open weights mattered here for one concrete reason: running it ourselves is what let us force the schema, measure its failures, and put a validator in front of the player. Best Use of ElevenLabs ElevenLabs is why the demo has sound at all, and we want to be exact about where it sits: it is demo tooling, not part of the running game. The Sound Effects API generated the demo sounds. We could not publish the research audio we tested with, because it is licensed for non-commercial use. So a committed script, scripts/m8_elevenlabs_sounds.py , asks the Sound Effects API ( eleven_text_to_sound_v2 ) for 21 clips : six that drive the full journey (rain in a metal roof gutter, tolling bells, three takes each) and a fifteen-clip pack of wind, footsteps, birds, water and machines. Each is a ten-second text prompt with no music. The script reads the API key from the environment only, converts each clip to 48 kHz mono, levels it so it clears the app's own ingest checks, and writes a manifest with the prompt, model, settings and checksum of every clip. The audio is not committed, but anyone with their own key can regenerate the set. Then the game does what it does with real recordings. CLAP hears the generated sounds, a name we teach becomes retrieval memory, and the Composed orchestra in the video is built only from those clips. A voice narrates the 50-second video. The narrator is the CRITIC voice from our earlier project, ECHOLALIA, generated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech, seven lines mixed under the app's own music. The sounds, the narration and the music in the demo are generated or composed, not field recordings, and the video says so on screen. We would rather you trust the project than be impressed by a fake hike. Team submission — built and designed by İclal Doğan ( @iclaldogan ) and Melike Zaman ( @melike_nesrinzaman_713c0 ). Melike wrote the audio ingestion, the hearing and memory layer and the first versions of the acoustic atlas; İclal built the narrative engine, the composer integration, the release engineering and the demo. Go outside. Listen closely. And if ECHO-0 asks what you heard, tell it the truth. title: "Light don go": when Nigeria''s power cuts out, my laptop sends me outside
summary: Daniel Nwaneri Posted on Oct 12 • AI-assisted "Light don go": when Nigeria''s power cuts out, my laptop sends me outside # devchallenge # hf26challenge # ai # productivity AI forces breaks during blackouts This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built In Port Harcourt, the light goes and the room changes in about two seconds. The fan stops. The router dies. The laptop drops to battery. Then somebody shouts "on the gen!" I used to just sit there. Phone on mobile data, laptop on battery, waiting for the gen to come on so I could keep working. That gap, between NEPA taking light and someone starting the generator, is the one moment in my day when the screen is already losing. Light don go uses it. When my laptop switches to battery for more than 30 seconds, a full-screen page opens on top of whatever I'm doing: The real outage at 12:31 on 8 October. The big line is Gemma's. The line above it is code. It gives me one plan, a 60-second stretch timer (stand up, reach up, roll the shoulders, touch the toes, go outside), and a button: "I don stand up. Close am." When the timer ends, it says "You self don try." The page doesn't open again until the next cut. The sky follows the situation. It is warm in the day and counts down to rain or sunset. It is dark at night, with the plan kept near the house: Day and night are simulated runs ( ldg simulate ). The nudges are real Gemma output from those runs, taken from the log. The page works with no internet, because the router is already off: it uses no web fonts and loads nothing from a CDN. It is for anyone who works from a laptop where the power cuts are routine: Nigeria, load-shedding in South Africa, a lot of India and Pakistan. You don't need to explain the problem to any of them. Words you may not know (Nigerian English and Pidgin): Word Meaning NEPA What Nigerians still call the power company (the old National Electric Power Authority). "NEPA takes light" means the grid power goes off. Light don go "The power is gone." Gen, "on the gen" The petrol generator most homes start by hand when the grid fails. "On the gen" means start it. Hold the gen Keep the generator off. "₦1,500 saved every hour e rest" means each hour it stays off saves ₦1,500 of petrol. Abeg · waka · close am · fit Please · walk · close it · may ("rain fit start" = rain may start) You self don try "You have done well." Mineral · kiosk · junction Soft drink · small roadside shop · the street corner where food sellers sit WAT West Africa Time, UTC+1 Demo Watch on YouTube: https://youtu.be/Zr-YILDu6JI Real outages so far, from logs/outages.jsonl (8 and 9 October 2026, WAT): Time Event What the tool did 12:23 NEPA cut Rain path, indoor activity. Gemma timed out ; fallback sentence shown 12:25 Power back after 123 s Logged (the gen) 12:31 NEPA cut again Gemma: "Abeg shut that laptop, waka go stand by the window stretch back and legs, rain dey down." Passed the guard first try 12:34 Power back after 225 s Logged 12:53 NEPA cut First cut with the full-screen page. Gemma: "Abeg shut that laptop, walk to the kiosk for cold mineral and come back quick." Passed first try. Facts line: rain around 15:00, about 2 hours left 13:34 NEPA cut, laptop asleep Timed out, fallback logged. The Windows event log shows the laptop was in Modern Standby: it woke for a moment at the cut, went back to sleep mid-call, and woke again at 13:56. The model was still loaded. Nobody was at the screen 9 Oct, 07:33 NEPA cut Gemma: "Abeg shut that laptop, walk to the kiosk find cold mineral and come back quick." Passed first try What I did when it told me to go. I closed my laptop, took a walk outside in my neighbourhood in Port Harcourt, visited my cousins and played with their children. That was the 07:33 cut on 9 October. The light came back at about 12:05. The first real outage found a bug. More on that below. Code dannwaneri / light-don-go When NEPA takes light, a local Gemma tells you to go outside before you on the gen. Hacktoberfest 2026 Touch Grass. Light don go When NEPA takes light, and before anyone starts the generator, your laptop tells you to go outside, then gets out of the way. Detects the cut: the laptop drops to battery for 30 s or more (no inverter in this house). Works with the router dead: the forecast is saved while power is on; after the cut nothing touches the network. Code decides, Gemma phrases: rules compute sunset (NOAA formula, offline), the dry window and ₦ saved, and write the facts line. A local open-weight Gemma writes only the nudge, and a guard rejects it if it has any number, more than 20 words, or mentions light/the generator. One retry, then a fixed sentence. Words you may not know (Nigerian English and Pidgin): Word Meaning NEPA What Nigerians still call the power company (the old National Electric Power Authority). "NEPA takes light" means the grid power goes … View on GitHub How I Built It Detection. There is no inverter in my house, so when NEPA goes, the laptop really does go to battery. psutil reads the power state every 5 seconds. A drop shorter than 30 seconds is a flicker. A second cut within 15 minutes gets logged but not nudged, so NEPA flashing the light on and off doesn't spam you. Weather without internet. When the light goes, the router goes with it. So while power is on, the tool saves the hourly Open-Meteo forecast every 30 minutes. After the cut, it reads only that file. Sunset comes from the NOAA solar formula, computed on the laptop. It gives 18:21 for Port Harcourt on 7 October; Open-Meteo says 18:21 and sunrise-sunset.org says 18:22. One rule had to change for the rainy season. I first counted an hour as "wet" at a 50% chance of rain. In October in Port Harcourt, almost every hour is over 50%, so the tool kept everyone indoors all day. Now an hour is wet at 70%, or at 0.5 mm of expected rain. The model: Gemma 4 E2B, on my CPU. gemma4:e2b-it-qat through Ollama. It is a 4.3 GB download. My laptop is an i5-1135G7 with no NVIDIA GPU. Measured: 14 s cold, 3.6 to 4.0 s warm, about 15 to 20 tokens per second. What the model is allowed to do. This is the part I care about most. My first version let Gemma write the whole message from the facts. In 4 test runs it dropped every number, and twice it turned the meaning upside down: "E be like NEPA light don come Port Harcourt…" That means the light came back . "Close your laptop now, before the generator dies …" The generator wasn't on. A check on the numbers could not catch either of these, because neither sentence had a number in it. So I split the job: Code writes the facts line. It says what happened, when the rain or sunset comes, the minutes left, and the naira saved. Every number in the message comes from code. Gemma writes only the nudge. It sees three things: the place, the situation ("raining now", "dry daylight", "after dark") and an activity picked by rule. It sees no numbers at all. A guard checks the nudge. It rejects the nudge if it has any number, more than 20 words, or any mention of NEPA, light, power or the generator. Gemma gets one retry, with the reason. If the retry fails too, a fixed sentence is used. That is two model calls at most, and never a loop. After the split, 9 of 9 test runs passed first time, with no meaning errors that I saw. What the guard can't do. It checks numbers and topic, not sense. In one test run Gemma wrote "watch the rain inside the phone", and it passed. A bigger model would make fewer sentences like that, but it would not run on this laptop. I chose the small model, and I accept that one of its sentences will sometimes be odd. The bug a real outage found. At 12:23 the light went, the tool caught it, and Gemma timed out. I measured before changing anything. ollama ps showed that the model had just been loaded, by the request that failed. Ollama unloads an idle model after 5 minutes. My warm-up had run at 11:53, so at 12:23 the tool hit a cold start, on battery, and took more than 20 s. The fix is one setting: keep_alive: -1 , which keeps Gemma in RAM (3.9 GB of my 15.7). At the next cut, at 12:31, Gemma answered first time. One later cut, at 13:34, also timed out, but the cause was different: the laptop was asleep (Windows Modern Standby). I checked the event log before blaming the fix. So the defaults broke the one promise the tool makes, which is to work when the light goes. I would not have found that in a simulation. The page. One HTML file with the outage data written in as JSON. Edge opens it with --app --start-fullscreen , so there is no address bar and no tabs. The model's sentence goes in as data and is never inserted as HTML. A test feeds it a nudge containing </script> and checks that the page does not break. Tests. There are 98 tests, including one that blocks every network socket and still runs the outage path to the end. I also broke the guard on purpose 8 times (wider tolerances, checks removed), and a test failed every time. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Because the network dies with the light. When NEPA takes light, my router is off until someone starts the gen. A cloud API is unreachable at the exact moment this tool needs to speak. A model on my laptop answers in 4 seconds with no signal. Another reason was not needed. It also costs nothing per outage, which matters when outages happen every day. And because Ollama and the model are open, I could see why the first real call failed: an idle model unloads after 5 minutes, and I could change that setting. With a closed API, a timeout is just a timeout. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 E2B (QAT) runs locally through Ollama, offline, on a CPU-only laptop. It is the only part of the system that writes text, and the guard limits it to what a small model does well. The tool's best result so far isn't in the logs. It's a morning with my cousins' children that I would have spent waiting for the gen. title: Six Months of Job Hunting: My Honest Experience with LinkedIn and Naukri
summary: Satyabrata Swain Posted on Oct 12 Six Months of Job Hunting: My Honest Experience with LinkedIn and Naukri # career # jobsearch # discuss # beginners Six Months of Job Hunting: My Honest Experience with LinkedIn and Naukri For the past six months, I have been searching for a job in the technical support field. During this journey, I prepared my CV, updated my professional profiles, and applied to multiple companies through LinkedIn and Naukri. Like many other job seekers, I initially believed that having a good CV, an updated profile, and consistent applications would help me connect with the right opportunities. However, over time, I started noticing both the advantages and disadvantages of these platforms. This article is not about criticizing any platform. Instead, I want to share my personal experience, highlight some common challenges, and start a discussion about how the job-search experience could be improved. 1. LinkedIn: More Than Just a Job Portal LinkedIn is a professional networking platform that allows job seekers to connect with recruiters, hiring managers, employees, and professionals in their industry. During my job search, I found several advantages to using LinkedIn. Pros of LinkedIn 1. Direct communication with recruiters One of LinkedIn's biggest advantages is the ability to connect with recruiters and hiring managers. Instead of relying entirely on an application form, candidates can sometimes introduce themselves directly to the people involved in hiring. 2. Networking opportunities Professional connections can help candidates discover opportunities, receive referrals, and learn about company hiring processes. 3. Company research Before applying, candidates can explore company pages, learn about their teams, and understand more about the organization's work culture and requirements. 4. Building a professional identity A well-maintained profile showcasing skills, experience, projects, and achievements can help candidates establish a professional online presence. Cons of LinkedIn 1. High competition for popular vacancies Popular job listings can attract many applicants, making it difficult for individual candidates to stand out. 2. Outdated or duplicated job postings Job seekers may encounter listings that appear multiple times or remain visible after the original hiring requirement has changed. 3. Misleading recruiter messages Some messages may be vague, irrelevant, or inconsistent with the advertised position. Candidates need to verify the opportunity before sharing sensitive information. 4. Easy Apply competition Applying quickly is convenient, but it can encourage large numbers of candidates to apply for the same role. 5. Networking takes time Building meaningful professional relationships requires consistency, thoughtful communication, and patience. Sending connection requests alone does not guarantee a response. My observation: LinkedIn is valuable for networking and discovering opportunities, but getting noticed by the right recruiter can still be challenging. 2. Naukri: A Major Platform for the Indian Job Market Naukri is another platform I have used extensively during my job search. It offers job listings, resume uploads, profile management, and filters that help candidates search for relevant openings. For people searching for jobs in India, it can be a useful part of a job-search strategy. Pros of Naukri 1. Recruiters can discover your resume Recruiters can search candidate profiles based on relevant criteria, potentially helping job seekers get contacted without applying to every vacancy individually. 2. Useful job-search filters Candidates can narrow their searches using filters such as experience, salary expectations, location, and job role. 3. Strong focus on the Indian job market The platform offers opportunities across different Indian cities, industries, and experience levels. 4. Resume headline and skills A relevant resume headline, updated work experience, and accurate skills can help recruiters understand a candidate's background and identify potential matches. 5. Convenient application process Candidates can apply to multiple relevant openings without repeating the entire application process each time. Cons of Naukri 1. Irrelevant recruiter calls Sometimes, recruiters may contact candidates about opportunities that do not align with their skills, experience, salary expectations, or preferred location. 2. Duplicated or outdated vacancies Job seekers may encounter similar listings from different recruiters or vacancies that no longer reflect active hiring needs. 3. High competition Popular positions, including fresher and entry-level roles, can attract many applicants. 4. Frequent calls and promotional messages Repeated calls and promotional communication can become distracting, particularly when the opportunities are not relevant. 5. A strong profile does not guarantee interviews Even after updating a resume, adding relevant skills, and maintaining an active profile, candidates may still receive few interview opportunities. My observation: Naukri is useful for recruiter discovery and searching for jobs in India, but profile visibility alone does not guarantee relevant opportunities. 3. LinkedIn vs Naukri: Which Is Better? In my experience, these platforms serve different purposes. Feature LinkedIn Naukri Direct professional networking Strong focus More limited networking focus Recruiter discovery Connections and recruiter searches Resume database and profile searches Company research A major strength Primarily job-search focused Job filters Available Useful India-focused filters Referrals Professional network Less central to the experience Main challenge Standing out and networking Relevant recruiter responses I don't believe one platform is universally better than the other. LinkedIn can be especially useful for networking, researching companies, and seeking referrals. Naukri can be useful for recruiter discovery and finding opportunities in the Indian job market. Using both platforms strategically may be more effective than depending on only one. 4. The Bigger Problems Job Seekers May Face Looking beyond individual platform features, I noticed several challenges that deserve attention. Problem 1: Finding genuine, active job openings Candidates can spend valuable time applying to duplicated, outdated, or unclear listings. Better visibility into whether a vacancy is still active could make the process more efficient. Problem 2: Getting relevant recruiter responses Receiving a call or message is not necessarily useful if the opportunity does not match the candidate's skills or expectations. Problem 3: Standing out among applicants Submitting an application is only one step in the hiring process. Candidates also need to demonstrate that their experience matches the employer's requirements. Problem 4: Lack of application feedback After applying, candidates may not know whether their application was reviewed, shortlisted, rejected, or left pending. More transparent status updates could help candidates understand where they stand and plan their next steps. These are observations from my own job search, not claims that every employer or job platform behaves this way. However, I believe they are worth discussing. 5. What Could Make Job Searching Better? I think job platforms and employers could improve the candidate experience in several ways. Better vacancy verification: Make it easier to identify jobs that are still actively hiring. More relevant matching: Consider actual skills, experience, location, and salary expectations rather than relying only on broad keyword matches. Clearer application status: Provide meaningful updates when an application progresses through the hiring process. More transparent job descriptions: Include responsibilities, required skills, experience, salary information where possible, and hiring expectations. Better recruiter communication: Encourage clear communication about role requirements and next steps. More control over notifications: Help candidates reduce irrelevant calls, messages, and promotional communication. Even small improvements in these areas could make the experience less frustrating for job seekers. 6. What I Have Learned From Six Months of Job Searching This journey has taught me that job searching involves more than preparing a CV and clicking the Apply button. Candidates need to understand the requirements of their target roles, tailor their resumes when appropriate, maintain accurate profiles, and communicate effectively with recruiters. Networking can help, but it takes time. Applying consistently is important, but application quality matters too. Most importantly, the number of applications submitted is not the only measure of progress. Relevant recruiter conversations, interview opportunities, and feedback are also important indicators. I am still learning and improving my approach, and I believe sharing experiences can help other job seekers avoid unnecessary frustration. Conclusion LinkedIn and Naukri both provide valuable services, but neither guarantees that a candidate will find the right job. LinkedIn helps professionals build relationships and discover opportunities through networking. Naukri offers useful tools for finding jobs and becoming visible to recruiters in India. The real challenge is turning visibility and applications into relevant conversations and interview opportunities. I hope job seekers, recruiters, developers, and platform designers can continue discussing how to make this process more transparent, relevant, and efficient. Now I would love to hear from you: Which platform has worked better for you: LinkedIn or Naukri? Have you experienced outdated job listings or irrelevant recruiter calls? What one feature would you add to improve the job-search experience? Share your experiences in the comments. Let's learn from one another and make job searching better for everyone. Author note: A job seeker sharing personal observations and lessons learned.
